title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
Preface
This is the practitioner edition of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning. It is for engineers, data scientists and auditors who build or review machine-learning systems that handle personal data, and it tells them what each result says, when it applies, how to use it and what goes wrong, without proofs.
It covers the same topics as the full edition, in the same parts and chapters, but it is organised around the work rather than the theory. Each topic states the result with its formula, says why it matters, and gives a recipe with a worked example. It ends with what goes wrong. Each chapter closes with a cheat sheet and a link to the matching chapter of the full edition, which derives every result step by step. A separate exercise book, keyed to the full edition, has worked solutions.
You need some Python and NumPy, basic probability, and enough machine learning to know what a loss and stochastic gradient descent are.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
How this book is organized

Prerequisites is a mathematical reference to dip into when a later chapter cites it.
Threat models and attacks shows how models and data leak.
Differential privacy foundations defines the guarantee and builds its mechanisms.
Privacy accounting tracks the guarantee through private training.
Differential privacy in machine learning trains, tunes and audits private models.

You do not need to read Part 1 first. With a background in statistics or machine learning, start at Part 2 or Part 3 and follow the links back when you need a fact.
The numbers in the text come from the scripts in the repository’s code/ directory, which the full edition also uses, and tests check that the scripts still produce them. To rerun one, run uv run python code/<part>/<topic>.py.

title: Prerequisites
text:
What each chapter is for
This part is a mathematical toolkit, and it contains no privacy yet. You do not need to read it first. Later chapters link back to the facts they use, so come here when a link sends you.
Two ideas run through the part. The first is the likelihood ratio, how many times more likely an output is under one dataset than under a neighbouring one. The second is the effect of one input, how far a single example can move a result.
Probability distributions and Concentration inequalities give you the noise families, their scales and the error bars you publish with noisy numbers, which Parts 3 and 4 use constantly. Divergences compares the output distributions on two datasets with a single number, the language of Parts 3 and 4. Hypothesis testing shows how to read a detector’s trade-off curve at low false positive rates, which Parts 2 and 5 rely on. Information theory bounds what an output reveals about a hidden value, which Part 2 uses.
Optimization gives the constants, step sizes and clipping that Part 5 needs. Algorithmic stability and generalization explains why regularization and early stopping limit how much a model depends on one example, and why a reused holdout set misleads you. Cryptography basics teaches you to read a security claim stated as a game or a simulator, which later parts need.

title: Prerequisites
text:
How to use the chapters
Each chapter states its results, shows how to use them with a worked number, and links to its derivations in the full edition. Every number comes from a script you can rerun, such as uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/concentration.py. The scripts draw their randomness from seeded NumPy generators, numpy.random.default_rng, so reruns give the same numbers.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.1 Why this matters
Most of the random numbers in a machine-learning system are either counts or draws of noise. The number of mistakes a model makes on a test set is a count, and so is the size of a randomly sampled minibatch. The noise a system adds on purpose is the other kind, usually drawn from a Laplace or a normal distribution. Before you trust any of these numbers, you need to know where each one usually lands and how rare its large values are.
A handful of families covers almost every case. For a count, you need its spread, so that you can size a test set. For noise, you need its tail, so that you can calibrate its scale to an error bar.

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.2 Means, variances and the square-root law
text:
1.2 Means, variances and the square-root law
The mean of a random quantity \(X\), written \(\mathbb E[X]\), is the long-run average of many independent draws of it. The variance measures the spread around it, as the average squared distance from the mean: \[\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb E\big[(X - \mathbb E X)^2\big] = \mathbb E[X^2] - (\mathbb E X)^2. \tag{1.1}\] The standard deviation \(\sigma\) is its square root, in the same units as the quantity, so it is the number to compare with the mean.
Three rules cover almost every calculation. The mean of a sum is the sum of the means, always. Scaling a quantity by a constant \(c\) multiplies its variance by \(c^2\). And when two quantities are independent, their variances add: \[\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y). \tag{1.2}\] Without independence the last rule fails. Add a quantity to an exact copy of itself, and the variance of the sum is four times the original, not twice.
Together, the second and third rules give the square-root law. An average of \(n\) independent draws has the variance of one draw divided by \(n\), so its standard deviation is that of one draw divided by \(\sqrt n\). The law breaks when the draws are not independent, for example when one user contributes many rows, so count independent units, not rows.

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.3 Counts and rates: binomial and Poisson
text:
1.3 Counts and rates: binomial and Poisson
A yes-or-no outcome, such as whether a test example is misclassified, is a Bernoulli variable. It is 1 with probability \(p\), so its mean is \(p\) and its variance is \(p(1-p)\). Counting the yeses over \(n\) independent trials gives a binomial count, with mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\). Every measured rate, such as accuracy or a false-positive rate, is such a count divided by \(n\), so its standard deviation is \[\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}. \tag{1.3}\]
This formula is how you size a test set. Suppose a classifier errs on each of 2,000 test examples independently with probability 0.05. Then the measured error rate is typically within about half a percentage point of the true 5%. But if the true error rate is 0.001, the same test set expects only 2 mistakes, so the relative error of the count is about 70%. So what sets the relative precision is the expected number of events \(np\), not \(n\).
That is also why the normal approximation to a binomial count needs its variance \(np(1-p)\) to be about 10 or more, and fails for rare events. The snippet in Section 1.9 turns a target precision into a test-set size. For a relative standard deviation of 10%, a 5% error rate needs 1,900 examples, while a 0.1% rate needs 99,900.
When the trials are many and each is rare, the binomial depends almost only on the expected count, written \(\mu\). It then becomes the Poisson distribution \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\). Its variance equals its mean, so its relative spread is \(1/\sqrt\mu\), and independent Poisson counts add up to a Poisson count. The main use in this book is the batch size under Poisson sampling, where each example joins a batch independently with a sampling probability \(q\). Out of \(n\) examples, the batch size is then binomial with mean \(qn\). It is close to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(qn)\), so its standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{qn}\). For example, when each of 60,000 examples joins with probability 0.01, the standard deviation is about 24.5. A batch of 550 or 650 is then unremarkable.
So code that assumes a fixed batch size under this kind of sampling, such as a preallocated buffer or a per-batch average over a constant, is wrong. You can simulate the sizes with NumPy’s rng.binomial(n, q) or rng.poisson(q * n).
The waiting time until the first rare event follows the exponential distribution \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\), whose mean is the scale \(b\). In this book it serves mainly as half of a Laplace distribution. The size of a Laplace draw is exponential, and the difference of two independent exponential draws is a Laplace draw, which is one way to sample it.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.4 Tails and heavy tails
The mean and the variance describe the bulk of a distribution, but a guarantee that must hold except in rare cases depends on the tail, the chance of landing far from the mean. The Laplace tail shrinks exponentially with the distance, and the normal tail shrinks much faster, like the exponential of the squared distance. The tail bounds of Concentration inequalities work through the moment generating function, the average of \(e^{\lambda X}\) for a number \(\lambda\) you choose. A heavy-tailed quantity, such as an unclipped loss or gradient, has none, so those bounds do not apply to it, which is one reason to clip values before adding noise.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.5 Laplace and normal noise
The two standard noise distributions are the Laplace and the normal. The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b\) is an exponential density mirrored around zero. Its variance is \(2b^2\), so its standard deviation is \(\sqrt2\,b\), not \(b\). A draw \(X\) lands at least a distance \(t\) from zero with probability \[\Pr[|X| \ge t] = e^{-t/b}. \tag{1.4}\] Setting this chance to 5% gives the 95% half-width \(b\ln 20\), about three scales, which scipy.stats.laplace(scale=b).ppf(0.975) computes. So a count reported with Laplace noise of scale 2 is within 5.99 of the true count with 95% probability. The normal distribution has a mean \(\mu\) and a standard deviation \(\sigma\), written \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Its 95% half-width is \(1.96\sigma\), from scipy.stats.norm.ppf(0.975).
Figure 1.1 compares the two at the same variance. On a log scale the normal’s density is a parabola and the Laplace’s is two straight lines, so the Laplace has a sharper peak and much heavier tails.






Figure 1.1: Normal and Laplace densities with variance 2, on linear and log scales. The log of the normal density is a parabola; the log of the Laplace density is two straight lines.



Calibrating noise means solving the tail for the scale. Say the noise must stay within a width \(t\) of zero, except with a failure probability \(\beta\). Then the Laplace scale and the normal standard deviation can be at most \[b = \frac{t}{\ln(1/\beta)}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{t}{z_{1-\beta/2}}, \tag{1.5}\] where \(z_{1-\beta/2}\) is the normal quantile at \(1 - \beta/2\). Table 1.1 shows that the two multipliers grow very differently as \(\beta\) shrinks.

The two families also combine differently. A weighted sum of independent normal quantities is again normal, with the weighted means added and the variances added with squared weights: \[\sum_i a_iX_i \sim \mathcal N\Big(\sum_i a_i\mu_i,\ \sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2\Big). \tag{1.6}\] So the total noise of many noisy normal measurements is one normal draw that you can analyse exactly. A sum of Laplace draws is not Laplace, and its error bar needs the bound in Concentration inequalities. Either way, a noisy mean computed as a noisy sum divided by \(n\) has its noise standard deviation divided by \(n\), on top of the sampling spread of the data itself.
The most common bug with these distributions is a mismatched parameter. With rng = numpy.random.default_rng(seed), NumPy’s rng.laplace(0, b, size) and SciPy’s scipy.stats.laplace(scale=b) take the scale \(b\), whose standard deviation is \(b\sqrt2\). By contrast, NumPy’s rng.normal(loc, scale), Python’s random.gauss(mu, sigma) and scipy.stats.norm(scale=...) take the standard deviation, never the variance. So before you trust a noise level, check which one a call expects, and draw a million samples to confirm the variance.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.6 Normal noise in many dimensions
Noise is often added to a whole vector, such as a model’s parameters, as \(d\) independent normal coordinates with standard deviation \(\sigma\) each. Along any direction fixed in advance, this noise is a single draw from \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). Yet the vector’s length is large and predictable, close to \(\sigma\sqrt d\). For example, with a million parameters and a standard deviation of 0.01 on each, the noise vector has a length of about 10. So judge high-dimensional noise by its effect along the directions you care about, not by its total length.
The same picture explains noisy gradient descent. Suppose each example’s gradient is clipped to a length of at most \(C\), and normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) per coordinate is added to the sum of a batch of \(B\) clipped gradients. The noise vector then has length about \(\sigma C\sqrt d\), which can dwarf the clipped sum, whose length is at most \(BC\). Along the gradient’s own direction, though, the noise is only \(\sigma C\). Dividing the sum by the batch size divides both, leaving per-coordinate noise \(\sigma C/B\) on the averaged gradient, so larger batches shrink the noise relative to the signal.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.7 The central limit theorem
The central limit theorem says that a standardized sum of many independent draws with finite variance looks normal, whatever each draw’s distribution, which is what justifies a normal error bar on an average. The approach is slow for skewed data. For a sum of 30 exponential draws, the largest gap between its distribution function and the normal one is still 0.0243. And it describes the bulk, so for small tail probabilities use Concentration inequalities instead.

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.8 A density against its shifted copy
text:
1.8 A density against its shifted copy
Later parts keep asking how strongly one noisy observation can favour one underlying value over another that differs by a shift \(s\). The answer is the ratio of the noise density to its shifted copy at the observation. Laplace noise with scale \(b\) caps this ratio at \(e^{|s|/b}\), so no observation is very telling. Normal noise leaves it unbounded, so an observation far out in the tail can be overwhelming, although such observations are rare. With the shift and both scales set to 1, for example, Laplace noise never favours either value by more than a factor of about 2.72. Later parts rely on this difference, and Divergences averages this ratio.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.1 Why this matters
Almost every number in a machine-learning system is random. Some are random by design, like noise deliberately added to a published count, and others because of how they were measured, like an error rate on a test set. Before you publish or act on such a number, you need an error bar for it. And before you collect data, you need to know how much data buys the error bar you want.
A concentration inequality gives you both. It bounds the chance that a random quantity lands more than some distance from its mean. This chapter calls that event a failure, its chance the failure probability \(\beta\), and the distance the width. You use every inequality the same way: fix \(\beta\) and solve for the width, or fix the width and solve for the number of samples. Which inequality to use depends on what you know about the quantity, and the more you know, the narrower the error bar. At \(\beta = 0.05\) the choice matters little, but at the one-in-a-million level that later chapters need, the wrong choice makes an error bar a hundred times too wide.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.2 Mean or variance only: Markov and Chebyshev
text:
2.2 Mean or variance only: Markov and Chebyshev
Markov’s inequality needs only the average of a quantity \(X\) that cannot be negative, such as a cost or a latency. It bounds the chance that \(X\) reaches a threshold \(a\): \[\Pr[X \ge a] \le \frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}. \tag{2.1}\] Setting the right side to \(\beta\) says that \(X\) stays below \(\mathbb E[X]/\beta\) except with probability \(\beta\). If requests take 2 ms on average, at most a quarter take 8 ms or more. The condition matters, because a quantity that can be negative can hide large values behind negative ones.
Chebyshev’s inequality adds the variance. Write \(\mu\) for the mean and \(\sigma^2\) for the variance. The chance of landing a distance \(t\) from the mean is then \[\Pr[|X - \mu| \ge t] \le \frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}. \tag{2.2}\] So the width is \(\sigma/\sqrt\beta\). For an average of \(n\) independent samples, divide it by \(\sqrt n\). It holds for every distribution, which makes it safe when you distrust the shape of the data. The price is steep at small \(\beta\), though. At a 95% level it asks for 4.5 standard deviations where a normal-shaped tail needs 2.4. At one in a million, it asks for 1,000 where the normal needs 5.3. So use it for a quick 95% error bar and for nothing stricter.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.3 Noise you added: Laplace and Gaussian
text:
2.3 Noise you added: Laplace and Gaussian
When the randomness is noise you added yourself, you know its distribution exactly, so you read the width off its tail and need no inequality. Laplace noise with scale \(b\) stays within its width \[b\ln(1/\beta) \tag{2.3}\] of zero, except with probability \(\beta\). For normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\), multiply \(\sigma\) by the normal quantile at \(1-\beta/2\), which is 1.96 at 95%. The bound \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\beta)}\) is a convenient upper limit for mental arithmetic. In code, scipy.stats.laplace.isf and scipy.stats.norm.isf give the exact quantiles, as does the standard-library snippet in Section 2.8.
The typical use is the error bar you publish with a noisy count. If the count carries Laplace noise of scale 2, the published value is within 5.99 of the true one with 95% probability. Later parts choose the noise scale; this chapter only reads off its error bar. Publish that number next to the count, because an analyst who treats it as exact will over-read small differences.
A sum of \(k\) noisy counts needs care. Near its centre the total noise looks normal, with standard deviation \(b\sqrt{2k}\), but its far tail decays like a single Laplace draw, so the normal approximation understates rare failures. For a sum of 10 draws, it understates the chance of a large total about ninefold. A valid one-sided width is the larger of \[\sqrt{8kb^2\ln(1/\beta)} \quad\text{and}\quad 4b\ln(1/\beta). \tag{2.4}\] For two sides, use \(\beta/2\), which gives 17.18 at 95% for 10 counts of scale 1. If that is too wide, simulate the noise a million times and read off the quantile, since you know its distribution exactly.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.4 Many numbers at once: the union bound
text:
2.4 Many numbers at once: the union bound
A dashboard of \(k\) noisy counts should be right everywhere at once, not just count by count. The union bound says the chance that any of several failures happens is at most the sum of their chances. So give each count the failure probability \(\beta/k\). Because the widths above depend on \(\beta\) only through a logarithm, this is cheap. For 1,000 counts with Laplace scale 2, the width that covers them all is 19.81, against 5.99 for one. The union bound needs no independence, so it is always valid, and for rare independent failures it is nearly exact.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.5 Counts: the Chernoff bound
Batch sizes under random sampling, the records that match a query and the errors on a test set are all counts of independent yes-or-no outcomes. Write \(\mu\) for the mean of a count \(S\), and \(\delta\) for a relative deviation between 0 and 1. The Chernoff bound then says \[\Pr[S \ge (1+\delta)\mu] \le e^{-\delta^2\mu/(2+\delta)}, \qquad \Pr[S \le (1-\delta)\mu] \le e^{-\delta^2\mu/2}. \tag{2.5}\] For example, suppose each example joins a batch with probability 0.01, so that the batch size has mean 600. It leaves \(600 \pm 20\%\) with probability at most \(2.4\times10^{-5}\) per step. Over 1,000 steps, that is about 0.024. That is good enough for sizing memory, but code that silently assumes a fixed batch size will still break on the rare large batch, so handle it explicitly.
Two things go wrong in practice. The bound depends on the expected count, not on the number of trials, so a count of rare events has a wide relative error bar however many trials you run. And it needs independence: with several rows per user, count users.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.6 Averages of bounded values: Hoeffding, Bernstein, Clopper–Pearson
text:
2.6 Averages of bounded values: Hoeffding, Bernstein, Clopper–Pearson
Often you know only that each value lies in an interval of length \(R\), as for a clipped loss or a 0/1 mistake. Then Hoeffding’s inequality bounds the error of an average of \(n\) independent values. With probability \(1-\beta\), the average is within \[R\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}} \tag{2.6}\] of its mean. Its main use is planning, because it needs nothing you don’t know in advance. Solving for \(n\) gives \[n \ge \frac{R^2\ln(2/\beta)}{2t^2} \tag{2.7}\] for a width \(t\), so measuring accuracy to within one percentage point at 95% takes 18,445 test examples. When you pick the best of \(m\) models on a validation set, replace \(\beta\) by \(\beta/m\), because the winner is the one most likely to look too good.
Hoeffding’s inequality is too loose for small rates, because it assumes the largest variance the range allows. For a classifier with 1 false positive in 1,000 negatives, it adds 0.039 to the measured rate. Bernstein’s inequality uses the variance \(\sigma^2\) instead, with a one-sided width of about \[\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ln(1/\beta)}{n}} + \frac{2\ln(1/\beta)}{3n} \tag{2.8}\] for values in \([0, 1]\), and adds only 0.0045 here. Plugging in a variance estimated from the same data is a heuristic, though. For rates, use the exact binomial answer instead, the Clopper–Pearson interval. For the classifier, its 95% upper bound is 0.0047. With no errors at all it would be 0.0030, the “rule of three”: zero failures in \(n\) trials bound the rate by about \(3/n\). Plan with Hoeffding and report with Clopper–Pearson (Hypothesis testing).

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.7 Functions and adaptive processes: McDiarmid and Azuma
text:
2.7 Functions and adaptive processes: McDiarmid and Azuma
McDiarmid’s inequality extends Hoeffding’s to any function of independent inputs, as long as changing one input, the \(i\)-th, moves the result by at most \(c_i\). The tail is then \(\exp(-2t^2/\sum_i c_i^2)\), and Algorithmic stability and generalization uses it for the error of a retrained model. The \(c_i\) is the worst-case influence of one record, a quantity later parts return to.
Azuma’s inequality gives the same tail for a running total whose steps may depend on the past but have expected value zero given it, a martingale, with \(c_i\) replaced by the length of each step’s interval. Use it when an analyst or a training loop picks each step after seeing the last, which breaks the independence the other bounds need.

Rules of thumb

Use the most you know: an exact distribution beats any bound. Knowing only the variance costs a width growing like \(1/\sqrt\beta\), a normal-shaped tail like \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)}\), and a Laplace-shaped tail like \(\ln(1/\beta)\).
Publish the error bar with every noisy number.
For \(k\) numbers at once, divide \(\beta\) by \(k\).
Match the sides: a one-sided width covers only one direction, so for a two-sided error bar use \(\beta/2\).
Hoeffding needs bounded values: clip unbounded data first, and use the clipping range as \(R\).
Plan sample sizes with Hoeffding; report rates with Clopper–Pearson.
Never use the normal approximation for a guarantee in the far tail.
Independence is a condition: with several records per person, count people.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.1 Why this matters
Many questions in machine learning come down to putting a number on how different two distributions are. A feature drifts in production, and you want to know how far it moved. A test set changes slightly, and you want to know how far a classifier’s accuracy can move. A divergence gives that number. It is zero when the two distributions are equal and grows as they become easier to tell apart. The cheat sheet says which divergence answers which question.
All of them summarize one quantity. Call the two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\). For an outcome \(x\), write \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) for the probabilities they give to it. Their quotient is the likelihood ratio \[r(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. \tag{3.1}\] Its logarithm, written \(L(x)\) and called the log likelihood ratio, is the evidence that the outcome gives for \(P\) over \(Q\). Later parts use it to bound how much an output reveals.
Natural logarithms give divergences in nats, and base-2 logarithms give bits, with one nat about 1.443 bits. This chapter uses nats, so check the base of any library you use.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.2 KL divergence
The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is the average evidence per observation when the data come from \(P\): \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\left[\ln\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = \sum_x p(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. \tag{3.2}\] It is never negative, and it is zero only when the two distributions are equal. It is not symmetric, because it averages under its first argument, so always say which direction you computed. Maximum likelihood minimizes the KL divergence of the model from the data, while variational inference minimizes the reverse direction.
Its most useful property is that it adds up over independent observations: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\times P_2\,\|\,Q_1\times Q_2) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\|Q_1) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_2\|Q_2). \tag{3.3}\] So \(n\) independent observations carry \(n\) times the divergence of one. That makes it easy to work with many samples or many steps: add up the divergences, and convert to the quantity you need only at the end. Independence is a condition, though, because correlated observations partly repeat each other.
To compute a KL divergence from data, bin both samples on the same edges and call scipy.stats.entropy(p, q), which normalizes the two histograms and returns nats, or sum scipy.special.rel_entr(p, q). For example, take the feature histograms in Section 3.10, where the last of four bins was empty last month but holds a tenth of this month’s data. The KL divergence of last month from this month is 0.1116 nats, or 0.1610 bits. In the other direction it is infinite, because this month has mass in a bin that last month never used. So add a small pseudocount to every bin or use coarser bins, and report the choice. Compare only estimates made with the same bins and sample sizes, because they change with both.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.3 Rényi divergence and the max-divergence
The KL divergence reports the typical evidence. The Rényi divergence is a dial from the typical evidence to the worst case, set by a number \(\alpha\) greater than 1 called its order: \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big]. \tag{3.4}\] As the order goes to 1 it becomes the KL divergence, and it never decreases as the order grows. As the order goes to infinity, it becomes the max-divergence, the largest log ratio that any outcome, or any event \(A\), can give: \[D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_x r(x) = \ln\max_{A}\frac{P(A)}{Q(A)}. \tag{3.5}\] Like the KL divergence, every Rényi divergence adds up over independent observations.
The Rényi divergence also bounds how often the evidence is large. For every order, the chance under \(Q\) that one observation gives at least \(c\) nats of evidence for \(P\) is at most \(\exp(-\alpha c + (\alpha - 1)D_\alpha)\), and the full edition derives this tail bound. Different orders give different bounds, and none is best for every question. So in practice you compute the divergence on a grid of orders, add each order’s values over independent observations, and keep the order that gives the tightest final bound.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.4 Shifted normal and Laplace pairs
The most common pair in practice is a noise distribution and a copy shifted by \(s\), such as the same noise added to two values that differ by \(s\). For normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\), write \(\mu = s/\sigma\) for the shift in standard deviations. Then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \frac{\mu^2}2, \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{\alpha\mu^2}2, \qquad D_\infty(P\|Q) = \infty. \tag{3.6}\] At \(\mu = 1\), for example, the KL divergence is 0.5. Order 2 gives 1, and order 10 already gives 5. Because the dependence on the shift is quadratic, a small shift costs very little. A drift of 0.1 standard deviations gives a KL divergence of only 0.005.
For Laplace noise with scale \(b\), write \(t = s/b\) for the shift in scales. The worst case is then just the shift: \[D_\infty(P\|Q) = t, \tag{3.7}\] and the KL divergence is \(t + e^{-t} - 1\), which is 0.3679 at \(t = 1\). The evidence never exceeds \(t\), and it equals \(t\) on half the mass of \(P\).
This difference decides how the two noises are analysed. Laplace noise has a finite worst-case ratio, which you read straight off the noise scale as \(s/b\). Normal noise has an infinite max-divergence, because some rare outputs are overwhelming evidence. So any worst-case statement about normal noise must either leave out a small probability of rare outputs or use a finite Rényi order instead. Which pair is “more different” depends on the divergence, too. At equal variance and a shift of one Laplace scale, the Laplace pair has the larger divergence at small orders, but the normal pair overtakes it above order 2.98.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.5 Total variation
The total variation (TV) says directly how often a test is right. It is the mass of \(P\) that does not overlap with \(Q\): \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \max_A|P(A) - Q(A)| = \frac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{3.8}\] It is symmetric and lies between 0 and 1. When \(P\) and \(Q\) are equally likely a priori, the best possible test from one observation is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{correct}] = \frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q). \tag{3.9}\] No classifier can beat this. For two normal curves one standard deviation apart, the total variation is 0.3829, so the best test is right with probability 0.6915.
The total variation also bounds how far any fixed statistic between 0 and 1 can move. Accuracy is such a statistic, so when a test distribution moves by a total variation of at most 0.01, the accuracy of any fixed classifier moves by at most 0.01.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.6 Hockey-stick divergence
Scale \(q\) up by a factor \(\gamma\) of at least 1, and measure the mass of \(p\) that still sticks out above \(\gamma q\). That mass is the hockey-stick divergence: \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \max_A\big[P(A) - \gamma Q(A)\big] = \sum_x\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big)_+. \tag{3.10}\] Here \((y)_+\) is the positive part of \(y\). With no scaling it is the total variation. It falls as \(\gamma\) grows, and reaches zero once \(\gamma\) reaches the largest likelihood ratio.
So the hockey-stick divergence measures how much of the difference between two distributions comes from likelihood ratios above \(\gamma\), and later parts use it in that form. It also gives the best test when the two hypotheses are not equally likely, with \(\gamma\) set to the prior odds. For a normal pair shifted by \(\mu\) standard deviations, with \(\Phi\) the standard normal cumulative distribution function, \[E_\gamma = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big) - \gamma\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big). \tag{3.11}\] It is positive for every \(\gamma\), because the normal likelihood ratio is unbounded. At \(\mu = 1\) it gives 0.1906 for \(\gamma = 2\).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.7 f-divergences
The KL divergence, the total variation and the hockey-stick divergence are all members of one family. Each is the average under \(Q\) of a convex function \(f\) of the likelihood ratio, with \(f(1) = 0\): \[D_f(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_Q\big[f(r(X))\big]. \tag{3.12}\] The \(\chi^2\) divergence and the squared Hellinger distance are two more members. Every f-divergence obeys the data processing inequality below, and the Rényi divergence, which is an increasing function of one, inherits that.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.8 The data processing inequality
You rarely use raw outputs, because you threshold a score, round a statistic, fine-tune a model, or pass it through any other algorithm. The data processing inequality (DPI) says that none of this can make two distributions easier to tell apart. Describe the processing as a channel \(K\), which maps each input to a distribution over outputs, and write \(PK\) and \(QK\) for the two output distributions. Then every f-divergence and every Rényi divergence satisfies \[D_f(PK\|QK) \le D_f(P\|Q). \tag{3.13}\] That is because processing averages likelihood ratios together, and averaging can only weaken evidence.
The condition is that the processing behaves the same whatever the input came from, so it must not look at the original data again. Under that condition, thresholding, rounding or retraining on other data can never make the two distributions easier to tell apart. How much processing loses depends on the divergence. For two unit normal curves one standard deviation apart, a single bit that says whether the observation lies below the midpoint keeps 0.3090 of the KL divergence of 0.5. But it keeps all of the total variation, because it is the best test.
Every divergence here is an average or a maximum over outcomes, and only the maximum controls every output. A small KL divergence can hide a few outputs that are overwhelming evidence. So when every output matters, bound the worst case, through the max-divergence, a high Rényi order or the hockey-stick divergence, not only the average.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.9 Pinsker’s inequality
Pinsker’s inequality converts a KL divergence into a bound on the total variation: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) \le \sqrt{\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}. \tag{3.14}\] It is a quick conversion, but often loose, and it says nothing once the KL divergence exceeds 2. It also gives a floor on sample sizes. For a drift of 0.1 standard deviations, no test reaches 95% accuracy with fewer than 324 samples, while the exact answer for this normal pair is 1,083.

Rules of thumb

KL is not symmetric, so state its direction.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.1 Why this matters
A spam filter must call an email legitimate or spam, and a fraud detector must call a transaction normal or fraudulent. A monitoring job must likewise decide from a batch of readings whether a sensor has drifted. In each case an observation came from one of two distributions, and you must decide which. So every detector and every binary classifier is a hypothesis test, and evaluating one means measuring a test’s two error rates.
This chapter gives you the best possible test, the curve that says how good any test can be, and a way to measure a real detector’s error rates on a finite set of trials. Throughout, a single summary number such as accuracy or the area under the curve hides how a detector behaves when false alarms must be rare. That regime is often the one that matters.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.2 Tests and their two errors
The default assumption, called the null hypothesis \(H_0\), is that the observation comes from a distribution \(P\), such as the scores of normal transactions. The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) is that it comes from a distribution \(Q\), such as the scores of fraudulent ones. A test decides whether to reject the null, which here means flagging the transaction.
A test can make two kinds of mistake. Flagging a normal case is a false positive, and its probability is the false positive rate (FPR), written \(\alpha\). Missing a real case is a false negative, with probability \(\beta\), the false negative rate (FNR). The power \(1 - \beta\) is the true positive rate (TPR), the share of real cases the test catches. Catching more of them always means more false alarms. So the convention is to fix a budget for the FPR first, called the level, and then to find the most powerful test within it.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.3 The Neyman–Pearson lemma
Write \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) for the probabilities, or densities, of an observation \(x\) under the two hypotheses. Their quotient is the likelihood ratio \[\Lambda(x) = \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}, \tag{4.1}\] which puts the alternative on top, unlike Divergences. A likelihood ratio (LR) test picks a threshold \(\eta\) and rejects wherever the ratio exceeds it. The Neyman–Pearson lemma says that this is the most powerful test at its level. The reason is that rejecting \(x\) costs \(p(x)\) of false-alarm budget and buys \(q(x)\) of power, so the best test spends its budget on the best exchange rates first. On discrete data the LR test may have to reject a boundary value only with some probability, a randomized test, to hit a budget exactly.
So the best test looks at an observation only through its likelihood ratio. A single global threshold on a raw score is not that test when the score behaves differently for different items. For example, some merchants’ normal transactions score high anyway, while for others a high score is rare unless something is wrong. The better test models each merchant’s own two score distributions and thresholds the ratio between them. With a number \(n\) of independent observations, the LR test thresholds a sum of log ratios. Its FNR at a fixed FPR then falls like \[e^{-n\,\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)}, \tag{4.2}\] where \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. This is the Chernoff–Stein lemma.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.4 Trade-off curves
To say how hard it is to tell \(P\) from \(Q\), record the best FNR at every level. As a function of the budget, this is the trade-off function \(T(\alpha)\), and you compute it by sweeping the LR threshold. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve holds the same information upside down, as TPR against FPR. Any particular detector traces its own ROC curve, which lies on or below the best one. Every trade-off curve lies on or below the coin-flip line \(1 - \alpha\) and is convex, because randomizing between two tests reaches every point between them.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.5 The Gaussian trade-off curve
The most common pair in practice is a score that is normal under both hypotheses, with the same spread. Write \(\mu\) for the distance between the two centres in standard deviations, and \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The best test thresholds at \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\), and its FNR is \[T(\alpha) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{4.3}\] In SciPy this is norm.cdf(norm.ppf(1 - alpha) - mu), and at a tiny \(\alpha\) use norm.isf(alpha) for the threshold, because \(1 - \alpha\) loses the digits that matter. So a single number \(\mu\) fixes the best TPR at every FPR.
For example, take \(\mu = 2\). At an FPR of 5%, the best test has a TPR of 0.6388. If false alarms must be rare, at a rate of \(10^{-3}\), the TPR drops to 0.1378.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.6 The Laplace trade-off curve
For a Laplace distribution and a copy shifted by \(\kappa\) scales, the likelihood ratio is capped between \(e^{-\kappa}\) and \(e^{\kappa}\) (Probability distributions). No test can buy power faster than the cap per unit of FPR, so every test has \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\kappa\,\mathrm{FPR}. \tag{4.4}\] At \(\kappa = 1\) and an FPR of 0.05, the best TPR is 0.1359. The full curve has two more pieces, which the full edition gives. The same cap holds for any pair whose likelihood ratio is bounded by \(e^\kappa\), so at a low FPR every test on such a pair has a very small TPR.
A Laplace pair at \(\kappa = 1\) and a normal pair at \(\mu = 1.0301\) have the same best advantage. At a level of \(10^{-6}\), though, the best test on the normal pair has 36 times the power, because the unbounded normal ratio lets it find rare, overwhelming observations. So plan for the level you will actually use.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.7 Best advantage and total variation
The advantage of a test is its TPR minus its FPR, called Youden’s index in medicine. The best advantage over all tests is the total variation (TV) distance of Divergences: \[\max(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}) = \mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \frac12\sum_x |q(x) - p(x)|. \tag{4.5}\] It is reached by the test that rejects exactly where \(q\) exceeds \(p\). For the normal pair it is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), or 0.3829 at a shift of one standard deviation. Accuracy on a balanced set of positives and negatives measures the same point. But that point says nothing about the ends of the curve, as the Laplace and normal pairs above show. So never report only accuracy or advantage for a detector.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
section: 4.8 ROC summaries: why AUC hides the low-FPR regime
text:
4.8 ROC summaries: why AUC hides the low-FPR regime
Detectors are often compared by the area under the curve (AUC) of their ROC curves. It is the chance that a random positive scores higher than a random negative: \[\mathrm{AUC} = \Pr[S_+ > S_-]. \tag{4.6}\] But the AUC weighs mostly false-alarm rates nobody would operate at, while the question is often whether a detector can flag some cases with confidence, as when a fraud team can review only a few transactions.
Two detectors with standard normal scores on negatives make the point. Detector A’s positives score normal with mean 1 and standard deviation 1. Detector B’s positives are more spread out, with mean 1.5811 and standard deviation 2. Both have an AUC of 0.7602. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), though, A catches 0.0183 of the positives, while B catches about 12 times as many. A few of B’s spread-out positives score far above every negative, and those are exactly the cases a strict threshold catches.
So plot the full ROC curve on log–log axes, and report the TPR at fixed low FPRs such as \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-3}\). In scikit-learn, sklearn.metrics.roc_curve(y_true, y_score) returns the FPRs and TPRs to read them from, and roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score) gives the AUC for comparison with older work. Don’t read a TPR at an FPR below one over the number of negatives, though, because there the curve rests on a single false positive or none, and it is noise.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.9 The Bayesian view
Often you know a base rate \(\pi\), such as one transaction in a thousand being fraud. Bayes’ rule says that the odds of \(H_1\) after seeing \(x\) are the odds before, multiplied by the likelihood ratio: \[\frac{\Pr[H_1 \mid x]}{\Pr[H_0 \mid x]} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \times \Lambda(x). \tag{4.7}\] So the decision with the fewest errors says \(H_1\) when the ratio exceeds \((1 - \pi)/\pi\), which is again an LR test.
The same rule applies to an alarm, whose likelihood ratio is the TPR divided by the FPR. Take the test with \(\mu = 2\) in a population where 1% are positive. At an FPR of 0.05, a flagged case is positive with probability only 0.114, so most alarms are false. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the test flags fewer cases, but a flagged case is positive with probability 0.582. So when positives are rare, the FPR decides whether an alarm is worth believing.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.10 Measuring rates from finite trials
You measure a detector’s FPR by counting false positives among \(n\) test negatives. If each negative is flagged independently with the same probability, the count \(k\) is binomial, and its relative uncertainty is about \(1/\sqrt k\). So the precision of a measured rate depends on how many events you see, not on \(n\) alone.
The Clopper–Pearson interval gives the range of true rates that make the observed count unsurprising. Write \(1 - a\) for the confidence. Its lower end \(l\) and upper end \(u\) solve \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge k] = \frac a2, \qquad \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = \frac a2. \tag{4.8}\] It is exact, because it uses the binomial itself, and conservative, because it covers the true rate at least \(1 - a\) of the time. In SciPy, scipy.stats.binomtest(k, n).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact") computes it, and statsmodels’ proportion_confint(k, n, alpha=0.05, method="beta") does the same.
To claim that an FPR is below a target, use the upper end alone. The upper end of a two-sided 90% interval is a one-sided 95% bound, which is 0.0047 for 1 false positive in 1,000 negatives. With no events at all, the one-sided 95% bound is about \(3/n\), the rule of three. So certifying an FPR below \(10^{-3}\) takes 2,995 negatives with no false positive.
Even 10 false positives in 10,000 negatives give the interval \([0.00048, 0.00184]\), from about half to almost twice the target. As a rule of thumb, measuring an FPR of \(\alpha\) to within about 20% takes on the order of \(100/\alpha\) negatives. A common shortcut fails here, because the Wald interval, a normal approximation, is too narrow and collapses to \([0, 0]\) with no events.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
section: 4.11 Evaluating a detector at a low false positive rate
text:
4.11 Evaluating a detector at a low false positive rate
These results give a recipe for evaluating any detector or binary classifier.

Fix the target FPRs, such as \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-3}\).
Plan the trials with about \(100/\alpha\) negatives for a target FPR \(\alpha\).
Choose the threshold on one split and measure the rates on another, because a threshold tuned on the evaluation set looks better there than it is.
Report the TPR at each target FPR, with Clopper–Pearson intervals on both rates, and the full ROC curve on log–log axes.
Compare two detectors at the same FPR, never by AUC or accuracy alone. On a shared evaluation set, a paired test such as McNemar’s (statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.mcnemar) compares the positives each one catches.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.1 Why this matters
You often observe one thing and want to know how much it tells you about another thing you cannot see. A word in an email hints at whether the email is spam, and a noisy sensor reading carries a trace of a machine’s true state. Later parts ask how much a published output reveals about hidden data. Information theory turns “how much” into a number, in two different ways, because there are two different questions.
The first question is how many bits the output saves, on average, when you describe the secret. Shannon entropy and mutual information answer it, so they are the language of compression, of the cross-entropy loss and of feature selection. The second question is how much more likely a single best guess becomes once you have seen the output. Min-entropy and vulnerability answer that one, so they are the language of password strength and of anyone who gets one try. The two can rank the same channels in opposite orders, and both are averages, so neither says how exposed one particular value is.
Logarithms here are base 2, so every quantity is in bits. One nat, the unit of natural logarithms, is about 1.443 bits. SciPy’s scipy.stats.entropy(pk, base=2) returns bits, but its default and scikit-learn’s sklearn.metrics.mutual_info_score(labels_true, labels_pred) return nats, so convert before you compare numbers.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.2 Entropy
The entropy of a random variable \(X\) is its average surprisal, the logarithm of one over the probability of the value that occurs. Writing \(p(x)\) for the probability that \(X\) takes the value \(x\), it is \[H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x), \tag{5.1}\] where an outcome of probability zero adds nothing. It is also the average number of bits per value that the best possible code needs. For a coin that lands heads with probability \(p\), it is the binary entropy \(h(p)\), which is 1 bit for a fair coin and zero for a certain one. Even a coin with an 11% chance of heads still carries \(h(0.11) = 0.4999\) bits.
Entropy lies between zero, when one value is certain, and the logarithm of the number of possible values, when every value is equally likely. A uniform 4-digit PIN, for example, has \(\log_2 10{,}000 = 13.2877\) bits. The same bound sizes a combination of columns, such as birth date, sex and postcode. Its entropy is at most the logarithm of the number of combinations. Once it approaches the logarithm of the number of rows, many rows have a combination of their own.
For two variables, the conditional entropy \(H(X \mid Y)\) is the uncertainty about \(X\) left after seeing \(Y\), averaged over the values of \(Y\). It is never larger than \(H(X)\), but only on average. A particular observation can increase the uncertainty, for example when a rare word makes a probably-legitimate email look equally likely to be spam.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.3 Mutual information and data processing
How much does an output \(Y\) tell you about a secret \(X\)? The mutual information \(I(X; Y)\) is the drop in uncertainty it causes on average. It is also the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the joint distribution of the pair and the product of the two separate distributions: \[I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D\big(P_{XY}\,\big\|\,P_XP_Y\big). \tag{5.2}\] So it is never negative, it is zero only when the two variables are independent, and it is symmetric. Unlike a correlation, it detects dependence of any kind. Decision trees call it the information gain, and many feature-selection methods rank features by it.
To estimate mutual information from data, mutual_info_score puts the observed frequencies of two discrete columns into Equation 5.2. For continuous features, mutual_info_classif and mutual_info_regression in sklearn.feature_selection use a nearest-neighbour estimator instead. Both are biased. Plug-in estimates from small samples run high, so independent variables rarely give exactly zero. Compare an estimate with the same estimate on data whose pairing you have shuffled, which shows what independence alone produces.
The data processing inequality (DPI) says that processing cannot add information. Suppose a third variable \(Z\) is computed from \(Y\) alone, possibly with fresh randomness of its own. This is written \(X \to Y \to Z\), and then \[I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y). \tag{5.3}\] The condition is essential, because a \(Z\) that also looked at \(X\) directly could know more. In practice, denoising, feature extraction and training are all processing steps, so a bound on what the raw output reveals covers everything anyone computes from it.
A channel is the table of output probabilities for each input, and its capacity is the largest mutual information over all input distributions. It is the highest rate at which error-correcting codes can send data reliably. For the binary symmetric channel (BSC), which flips each bit with probability \(p\), it is \(1 - h(p)\).

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.4 Min-entropy and one-guess leakage
A guesser who gets one try wins with the probability of the most likely value. That probability is the vulnerability \(V(X)\), and its negative logarithm is the min-entropy: \[V(X) = \max_x p(x), \qquad H_\infty(X) = -\log V(X). \tag{5.4}\] Min-entropy is never larger than Shannon entropy, and the two are equal only for a uniform distribution. A value with a min-entropy of \(k\) bits is as hard to guess in one try as a uniform string of \(k\) bits, whatever its Shannon entropy.
A PIN shows why Shannon entropy is the wrong measure of guessing difficulty. Suppose 10% of people choose 1234, and the rest choose uniformly among the other PINs. Then the Shannon entropy barely moves, to 12.4278 bits. But the min-entropy falls to 3.3219 bits, because the guess “1234” succeeds one time in ten.
Now let the guesser see an output \(Y\) through a channel \(C\), whose entry \(C[x, y]\) is the probability of output \(y\) when the secret is \(x\). Write \(\pi\) for the prior, how likely each secret is to begin with, so that each entry of the joint table is \(\pi(x)C[x, y]\). The best strategy is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess, the secret most likely given the output. Its success probability is called the posterior vulnerability, and it is the sum of the column maxima of the joint table: \[V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x \pi(x)C[x, y]. \tag{5.5}\] The min-entropy leakage is the logarithm of the factor by which the output multiplies the chance of a correct guess: \[\mathcal L = \log\frac{V(X \mid Y)}{V(X)}. \tag{5.6}\] So a leakage of 1 bit doubles the guesser’s chance, which is a statement you can act on.
This is how to quantify one-guess risk on a small table. List the secret’s prior, write down the channel from secret to output, and compute the two vulnerabilities. In the example of Section 5.7, a secret with four values has a best prior guess that is right with probability 0.4. With the output, the guesser wins with probability 0.66, so the leakage is 0.7225 bits. Two shortcuts give wrong answers. Comparing channel entries instead of joint entries ignores the prior. Averaging the min-entropy of each posterior takes the logarithm too early, and gives 0.6548 bits instead of the correct conditional min-entropy of 0.5995 bits.
When you do not know the prior, use the worst case over all priors. That is the min-capacity, which needs only the column maxima of the channel itself, and which a uniform prior attains: \[\mathcal{ML}(C) = \log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]. \tag{5.7}\] For the example channel it is 1.2630 bits. For a channel that reports a hidden bit correctly with probability 0.75 and flips it otherwise, it is 0.5850 bits. So whatever the prior, seeing the output multiplies the chance of guessing the bit by at most 1.5.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.5 Shannon against min-entropy leakage
The two leakages agree for a channel that reveals the same bits every time. They disagree, by a lot, for a channel that reveals the secret completely on a few outputs and nothing on the rest. Shannon leakage averages the logarithm, so a rare full reveal contributes little. Min-entropy leakage takes the logarithm of a success probability, which the same reveal dominates. Table 5.1 compares two deterministic channels on a uniform 64-bit secret.



Table 5.1: Shannon and min-entropy leakage of two deterministic channels on a uniform 64-bit secret.











Channel
Shannon leakage
Min-entropy leakage
One-guess success




Reveal all if the low 3 bits are zero
8.1686 bits
61.0000 bits
0.1250


Reveal the low 9 bits
9.0000 bits
9.0000 bits
\(2.78\times10^{-17}\)






Shannon leakage says the second channel leaks more, yet a guesser with one try does better against the first by a factor of more than \(10^{15}\). So low mutual information does not mean that nothing is revealed. A channel can have little mutual information with its secret and still give some values away completely.
Min-entropy leakage has the same blind spot in a milder form, because it too is an average over secrets. A channel that reveals a 32-bit secret only when it is all zeros has a min-entropy leakage of exactly 1 bit, and a far smaller Shannon leakage. Yet for the one secret made of zeros, it reveals everything. Any measure that averages over the secret can hide a value that is fully exposed. So when every value matters, you need a worst-case bound on the likelihood ratio of each output, which later parts build.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.6 Fano’s inequality
Mutual information can also show that a problem is hard. Fano’s inequality concerns a secret that takes one of \(M\) values. It says that a guess computed from the output, wrong with probability \(P_e\), must satisfy \[H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1). \tag{5.8}\] So if much uncertainty remains after the output, every guess must often be wrong. For a label uniform over 8 classes, with features that carry at most 1 bit about it, every classifier errs at least 0.3730 of the time. Later parts use the same tool to show that some estimates need many samples.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.7 Code
This snippet computes the vulnerabilities, the min-entropy leakage and the min-capacity for a secret with four values and three outputs, and the min-capacity of a channel that flips a bit with probability 0.25.
from math import log2

prior = [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]
channel = [  # channel[x][y] = probability of observation y given secret x
    [0.8, 0.2, 0.0],
    [0.1, 0.8, 0.1],
    [0.0, 0.5, 0.5],
    [0.0, 0.2, 0.8],
]


def posterior_vulnerability(prior: list[float], channel: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Success probability of the best one-shot guess: the sum of the joint table's column maxima."""
    joint = [[px * c for c in row] for px, row in zip(prior, channel)]
    return sum(max(col) for col in zip(*joint))


def min_capacity(channel: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Leakage in bits under the worst prior: log of the sum of the channel's column maxima."""
    return log2(sum(max(col) for col in zip(*channel)))


v_prior = max(prior)
v_post = posterior_vulnerability(prior, channel)
print(f"{v_prior:.4f} {v_post:.4f}")  # 0.4000 0.6600
print(f"{log2(v_post / v_prior):.4f}")  # 0.7225
print(f"{min_capacity(channel):.4f}")  # 1.2630
flip = [[0.75, 0.25], [0.25, 0.75]]  # report the hidden bit correctly with probability 0.75
print(f"{min_capacity(flip):.4f} {2 ** min_capacity(flip):.4f}")  # 0.5850 1.5000

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.1 Why this matters
Almost all training is done by gradient descent (GD), or by its cheaper and noisier variant, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and two practical questions come up every time. The first is how to set the step size and the number of steps, and how much noise in the gradients slows training down. The second is how much the trained model depends on any one training example, which is the quantity that later parts of the book have to control.
Both are answered by a few constants of the loss and by the variance of the random gradients. So the first job is to know these constants for your loss, or to enforce them.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.2 The constants of a loss, and how to enforce them
text:
6.2 The constants of a loss, and how to enforce them
Throughout, the model is a parameter vector \(w\), and the training set has \(n\) examples. Write \(\ell(w, z)\) for the loss on an example \(z\), and \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) for the training examples. Training minimizes the empirical risk, the average loss \[F(w) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w, z_i), \tag{6.1}\] and this chapter writes \(w^*\) for its minimizer and \(F^*\) for its smallest value.
A loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz when its gradient never has length more than \(L\), so it caps how far one example can push a model. It is smooth when its gradient changes by at most a constant \(\beta\) per unit of distance. That bounds how far you can trust a step, and it sets the safe step size \(1/\beta\).
A loss is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex when it curves upward by at least \(\lambda\) in every direction, so that a point with a small gradient must lie close to the minimizer. The ratio \(\kappa = \beta/\lambda\) is the condition number, the ratio of the steepest curvature to the flattest. Table 6.1 gives the constants for the losses this book uses, for features of length at most 1.

The table shows that the constants come from three choices you control. Normalizing every feature vector to length at most 1 is what makes the logistic and hinge losses 1-Lipschitz, so a single unnormalized outlier breaks the guarantee. A ridge term \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) is the usual source of strong convexity, because the logistic loss has none of its own. But the ridge term makes the gradient grow with the parameters. So you also keep \(w\) in a ball by projection, which pulls it back to the nearest point of the ball after any step that leaves it.
For a neural network, whose constants nobody can compute, you instead clip each example’s gradient to a chosen length \(C\). Clipping enforces the Lipschitz bound by construction, with \(L = C\), but only if it happens per example. In PyTorch, torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ clips the gradient of a whole batch, which bounds nothing about any single example. Per-example clipping, which Part 5 uses, needs per-example gradients.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.3 Gradient descent and SGD
Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the full gradient, with a step size written \(\eta\). The safe step is \(1/\beta\), because smoothness guarantees that such a step never overshoots. On a strongly convex risk the error then shrinks by a factor \(1 - 1/\kappa\) per step. So a badly conditioned problem is slow, which is why rescaling features to similar ranges speeds training up.
SGD replaces the full gradient with that of one example, or the average over a small random minibatch. The random gradient equals the true gradient on average, but only if the examples are sampled uniformly, and a sampler that favours some examples minimizes a reweighted risk instead. Its scatter around the true gradient, the variance, is what every SGD rate pays for. With a constant step it keeps the iterates jittering around the minimizer, and averaging them or shrinking the step removes the jitter.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.4 Convex losses: the step size and the averaged iterate
text:
6.4 Convex losses: the step size and the averaged iterate
The basic guarantee covers convex losses with bounded gradients, including the hinge loss. It runs projected SGD inside a closed convex set that contains the minimizer. It returns the averaged iterate \(\bar w_T\), the average of the parameters over a run of \(T\) steps. Write \(G^2\) for a bound on the average squared length of the random gradients, and \(R\) for a bound on the distance from the start to the minimizer. With the step size \[\eta = \frac{R}{G\sqrt T}, \qquad \mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{RG}{\sqrt T}. \tag{6.2}\] For an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss, \(G = L\).
To use it, take \(R\) as the radius of the projection ball and \(L\) from Table 6.1, choose \(T\), and start from the step the formula gives. For logistic regression on the ball of radius 5, a run of 10,000 steps gives a step of \(0.05\). No method does better than this \(1/\sqrt T\) rate on this class.
Treat the bound as a guarantee and the step as a starting point. The formula assumes the worst gradients and the farthest start, so on the full edition’s logistic problem the best step on a grid is \(3.6\) times larger. So tune the step on a grid around the formula’s value, and return the averaged iterate, which the guarantee covers, rather than the last one.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.5 Strongly convex losses: a decaying step
text:
6.5 Strongly convex losses: a decaying step
With a ridge term the rate improves from \(1/\sqrt T\) to \(1/T\), so halving the error takes twice the steps rather than four times. Use the steps \(2/(\lambda(t + 1))\) at step \(t\), and average the iterates with weights proportional to \(t\). Then \[\mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{2G^2}{\lambda(T + 1)}. \tag{6.3}\] The simpler schedule \(1/(\lambda t)\) with a uniform average costs an extra factor that grows like \(\ln T\). Here \(G\) bounds the gradients on the projection ball, since a ridge term makes them grow with the weights.
In practice, scikit-learn’s SGDClassifier with learning_rate="optimal" uses a step of this \(1/(\lambda t)\) shape, with its alpha equal to \(\lambda\), and average=True returns an averaged iterate. Its LogisticRegression is parameterized differently. It multiplies the summed loss by C instead of penalizing the weights, so its ridge strength in this chapter’s terms is \(\lambda = 1/(Cn)\). A large C therefore means a weak ridge term.
The schedule needs a value of \(\lambda\) no larger than the true curvature. If you overestimate it, the steps shrink too fast and the iterates can stall far from the minimizer.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.6 Gradient noise and minibatches
Gradients get noisier from small batches, low-precision arithmetic or compression, and later parts add noise to them on purpose. Write \(\sigma_1^2\) for the variance of a single-example gradient. A batch of \(B\) examples divides it by \(B\), and drawing the batch without replacement does slightly better: \[\mathbb E\|g_B - \nabla F(w)\|^2 = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{B}\cdot\frac{n - B}{n - 1}. \tag{6.4}\] Noise of a fixed size added to the summed gradient of a batch is also divided by \(B\) when the sum is averaged. So larger batches dilute added noise, which is why noisy training prefers them.
Now add noise of mean zero whose average squared length is \(\sigma^2\). It simply adds to \(G^2\), so the convex recipe becomes \[\eta^* = \frac{R}{\sqrt{(L^2 + \sigma^2)T}}, \qquad \mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{R\sqrt{L^2 + \sigma^2}}{\sqrt T}. \tag{6.5}\] To reach the same bound, the number of steps must grow by the factor \(1 + \sigma^2/L^2\), so noise of size \(\sigma = 3L\) multiplies the steps you need by 10. On the full edition’s logistic problem with 10,000 steps, the formula’s step falls from 0.0500 without noise to 0.0158 at \(\sigma = 3\), and the error at that step grows about 20-fold. The best step on a grid falls too, from 0.178 to 0.056. So a step tuned without noise is too large once noise is added, and the formula’s step is conservative throughout. Retune on a grid whenever the noise level changes.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.7 Non-convex losses
Neural networks have non-convex losses, and no gradient method can promise to find their global minimum. With a smooth loss and a step of at most \(1/\beta\), SGD only guarantees a point where the gradient is small. Noise slows that down, just as it does for convex losses. A small gradient can sit at a saddle point or a poor local minimum, so nothing here says how far the risk is from its best value. A step above \(2/\beta\) can even raise the risk, which is what a diverging loss curve usually means.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.8 How far one example moves the model
text:
6.8 How far one example moves the model
Regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) minimizes the average loss plus a ridge term, \[J(w; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w, z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2, \tag{6.6}\] where \(D\) is the training set and \(w^*(D)\) its minimizer. If each loss is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz, replacing one example moves the minimizer by at most \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.7}\] One example tilts the gradient by at most \(2L/n\), and strong convexity turns a small tilt into a small move. The loss on any example then changes by at most \(2L^2/(\lambda n)\), a property called uniform stability, which the next chapter turns into a generalization bound.
Later parts calibrate noise to this per-example influence, so read the bound as a design rule. Ten times more data gives a tenth of the movement, and halving \(\lambda\) can double it. For the logistic loss with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and 1,000 examples, the bound is \(0.02\), while the largest movement observed on the full edition’s data is \(6.66\times10^{-3}\).
The bound needs strong convexity, and without it no bound of this kind exists. The absolute loss is convex and 1-Lipschitz, but its minimizer is the median, and replacing one example can move the median from 0 to 1 however large \(n\) is. For a non-convex loss, one example can decide which of two valleys is deeper. So for neural networks, any statement about the influence of one example must be about the training algorithm, not about the minimizer.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.1 Why this matters
What matters is a model’s loss on new data, not on its training data. The difference between the two is the generalization gap, and you measure it on data the model has not seen. This chapter tells you in advance which knobs shrink it, which examples carry it, and when a held-out measurement stops being honest.
The one idea is that a model generalizes when it does not depend much on any single training example. For regularized training and for stochastic gradient descent (SGD), that dependence shrinks with a stronger regularizer and a shorter run. It can also be measured example by example, and Part 2 shows why it matters beyond accuracy.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.2 Training loss, test loss and the gap
text:
7.2 Training loss, test loss and the gap
Take a training set \(S\) of examples drawn independently from one distribution \(\mathcal D\). Write \(n\) for the number of examples, and \(A(S)\) for the model that a learning algorithm \(A\) returns. A loss \(\ell(w, z)\) that is never negative measures how badly a model \(w\) does on an example \(z\). The test loss \(R(w)\) is the average loss on a new example from \(\mathcal D\), and the training loss \(\hat R_S(w)\) is the average over the training set. The gap of the trained model is \[\mathrm{gap} = R(A(S)) - \hat R_S(A(S)). \tag{7.1}\]
For a model fitted to the data, the training loss is biased downward, because the algorithm chose the model that does well on these particular examples. So estimate the test loss on a held-out set that played no part in training and comes from the same distribution as future data.
The chapter’s running example is logistic regression on features in 10 dimensions with noisy labels, plus a ridge penalty whose strength is written \(\lambda\).

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.3 The gap and uniform stability
The tool here is the replace-one neighbour \(S^{(i)}\), the training set with example \(i\) replaced by a fresh draw from \(\mathcal D\). The expected gap is then exactly the average damage that training without an example does to that example’s loss: \[\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\Big[\ell\big(A(S^{(i)}), z_i\big) - \ell\big(A(S), z_i\big)\Big]. \tag{7.2}\] It holds for any algorithm, because a training example and a fresh draw are interchangeable. In other words, overfitting is dependence on individual examples.
To bound that dependence, call an algorithm \(\beta\)-uniformly stable when replacing any one training example by any other moves the loss by at most \(\beta\). That must hold at every test point \(z\): \[\big|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z)\big| \le \beta. \tag{7.3}\] Every term of the identity then lies within \(\beta\) of zero, so the expected gap does too: \[\big|\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}]\big| \le \beta. \tag{7.4}\] It works for large models too, but \(\beta\) is a worst case over training sets, replacements and test points, so it can sit far above the true gap.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.4 High probability: the Bousquet–Elisseeff bound
You train once, so you may want a high-probability bound. The bound of Bousquet & Elisseeff gives one for losses bounded by some maximum, but only when \(\beta\) falls faster than \(1/\sqrt n\), and it is loose at realistic sizes. At 95% confidence, for regularized logistic regression with 10,000 examples at \(\lambda = 0.1\), it adds 0.614 to the training loss, which says nothing useful. So measure the gap on held-out data, and use the bounds only to compare settings.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.5 Regularized ERM is stable
Regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) covers ridge regression and regularized logistic regression. It picks the weights that minimize the training loss plus a ridge penalty, \[w_S = \arg\min_w \Big(\hat R_S(w) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\Big). \tag{7.5}\] Suppose each loss is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz, which means that its gradient never has length more than \(L\) (Optimization). Then replacing one example moves the weights by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\), and the algorithm is stable with \[\beta = \frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}. \tag{7.6}\]
To compute \(\beta\), normalize the features to length at most 1, which makes \(L = 1\) for the logistic and hinge losses, and plug in \(\lambda\) and \(n\). Logistic regression with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and 1,000 examples then has \(\beta = 0.02\). In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression(C=...) sets \(\lambda = 1/(Cn)\), so a large C means a weak penalty and a large \(\beta\).
On the full edition’s running example, the measured gap falls like \(1/n\), as the bound predicts, but it stays between about 3% and 13% of the bound. So the bound tells you how the gap scales with \(\lambda\) and \(n\), not how large it is. Doubling \(\lambda\) halves \(\beta\), but a larger penalty also pulls the weights away from the best fit. The test loss is therefore U-shaped in \(\lambda\), so choose \(\lambda\) on held-out data and use the bound to know which direction helps.
Both conditions matter. Squared loss is Lipschitz only on a bounded region, so ridge regression needs bounded features and labels. Without convexity, one flipped label can move the minimizer from one valley to another, however large \(n\) is.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
text:
7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
Large models are trained by SGD rather than to an exact minimizer. Write \(\eta_t\) for the step size at step \(t\), and \(T\) for the number of steps. Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016) showed that \[\beta \le \frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t. \tag{7.7}\] With a constant step \(\eta\) over a number of epochs \(E\), the bound becomes \(2L^2\eta E\). So for a fixed number of epochs, more data does not improve it.
The bound needs a convex, \(L\)-Lipschitz and smooth loss, with steps small enough not to overshoot. It also needs examples picked uniformly at random, so shuffling once per epoch, as most implementations do, is not covered as stated.
The practical reading is that training time is a stability knob, which makes early stopping a trade-off rather than a trick. Take the running example without regularization, with 100 examples and a step of 0.25. One epoch then gives \(\beta \le 0.5\). The gap grows from 0.036 after one epoch to 0.121 after 40. The test loss is lowest after about 5 epochs and rises afterwards, while the training loss keeps falling. The bound gets the direction right but the size wrong, by a factor of 165 after 40 epochs. For non-convex losses the bound grows polynomially in the number of steps, so treat it as a direction, not a number.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.7 An unstable algorithm: 1-nearest neighbour
The nearest neighbour (NN) rule with one neighbour, 1-NN, predicts the label of the closest training point. Like a lookup table that stores the training set, it has training error 0 and, under the 0-1 loss, stability \(\beta = 1\). That is because replacing a point by the same point with the opposite label flips the prediction there. So with noisy labels its gap never closes, and in the running example its test error never falls below 0.338. In scikit-learn, KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1) is this rule, and its perfect training score is a warning, not a result.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
text:
7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
Each term of Equation 7.2 measures how much one example depends on its own presence, and it is called the example’s memorization score, or self-influence, \[\mathrm{mem}_i(S) = \ell\big(A(S^{(i)}), z_i\big) - \ell\big(A(S), z_i\big). \tag{7.8}\] Their average is the expected gap, so the scores show which examples carry it.
To measure a score, train on \(S\) and record the example’s loss. Then replace the example by a fresh draw, retrain with the same settings, and record its loss again. That costs one retraining per example, which is affordable only for small models. For a large model, score a sample of examples, or train many models on random subsets and compare each example’s loss with and without it.
The scores are uneven in a predictable way. A typical example is fitted well whether or not it is present, because its neighbours carry the same information. An atypical one, such as a mislabelled point or a member of a rare subgroup, is fitted only if it is there itself. In the running example, the examples whose label goes against the trend have three times the average score of the others. Regularization flattens that profile. A small average gap therefore leaves room for a few heavily memorized examples, so a small train-test gap does not mean that no example was memorized. Look at the largest scores, not only the mean, and see Part 3 for a stronger, worst-case guarantee. Feldman (2020) shows that on data with a long tail of rare subgroups some memorization is needed for accuracy, so a large score is not always a defect.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.9 Choosing what to measure after looking
text:
7.9 Choosing what to measure after looking
A held-out set is honest only for questions fixed before you look at it. Call a question a rule that gives each example a score between 0 and 1, such as whether a model classifies it correctly. Questions fixed before the holdout set is drawn are safe. For some number \(k\) of them on \(n\) examples, their largest error is on average at most \(\sqrt{\ln(2k)/(2n)}\). But you usually look at a verdict, change something, and ask again. Each new question then depends on the holdout set, so you have become a learning algorithm trained on it, and the bound no longer holds.
Freedman’s paradox shows the size of the effect. A holdout set has 1,000 examples, each with many random features and a label independent of them all, so no rule beats 50% on new data. An analyst keeps the features that agree with the label noticeably more or less than half the time, and measures their majority vote on the same holdout set. With 1,000 features, the questions fixed in advance stay within the bound of 0.0616. But the vote, chosen after looking, reports an accuracy of 0.8053.
The fix is sample splitting, which means never letting an example answer a question it helped to choose. Choosing the features on one half and measuring the vote on the other brings the accuracy back to 0.5018. You need a fresh part of the data for every round of choices, not for every question. So split the data with scikit-learn’s train_test_split before you start, and tune with cross_val_score on the training part. Then use the test set once, for the final verdict.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.10 Code
This calculator gives the stability of regularized ERM and of SGD, and prints the numbers quoted above.
import math


def erm_beta(lipschitz: float, lam: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Uniform stability of ridge-regularized ERM."""
    return 2 * lipschitz**2 / (lam * n)


def sgd_beta(lipschitz: float, step: float, epochs: float) -> float:
    """Stability bound for SGD with a constant step on a convex, smooth, Lipschitz loss."""
    return 2 * lipschitz**2 * step * epochs


print(f"{erm_beta(1, 0.1, 1000):.3f}")  # 0.020
print(sgd_beta(1, 0.25, 1))  # 0.5
print(sgd_beta(1, 0.25, 40))  # 20.0
