title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.1 Why this matters
To build or review a system that hides data, you need to know which tool does the job, how much data one key can protect, and what a security claim promises. The last question has a precise answer, because security is a game. A challenger secretly flips a fair coin to pick one of two worlds, such as encrypting one message or another. An adversary sees the result and guesses which world it is in. A scheme is secure when no efficient adversary beats the coin by more than a tiny amount.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.2 Which tool for which job
Never build your own scheme. Use a vetted library, and pick the construction by the job, as in Table 8.1.



Table 8.1: The construction to use for each job, and the mistake to avoid.











Job
Use
In Python
What goes wrong




Encrypt data
Authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD): AES in GCM (Galois/Counter Mode), or ChaCha20-Poly1305
AESGCM or ChaCha20Poly1305 from the cryptography package
A nonce reused under one key reveals data

A pseudorandom function, in practice the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC)
hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256)

Every operation spends a noise budget

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.3 Advantage
The simplest adversary sees one sample and answers with a bit. It is called a distinguisher, written \(A\), and its answer 1 means “I think this sample came from the second world”. Write \(X\) and \(Y\) for the distributions of the sample in the two worlds. The advantage of the distinguisher is the gap between how often it says 1 in the two worlds: \[\mathrm{Adv}_A(X, Y) = \big|\Pr[A(X) = 1] - \Pr[A(Y) = 1]\big|. \tag{8.1}\] A distinguisher whose answer 1 points to the second world wins the coin game with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}_A\), so the advantage is twice its edge over a coin flip. For example, take a fair coin against a coin that lands heads with probability 0.6. Saying 1 on heads has advantage 0.1, and so it wins with probability 0.55.
No distinguisher, however long it runs, can do better than the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions (Divergences).
So if that distance is 0, security is perfect, and if it is tiny, it is statistical. Most of cryptography is computational instead, where no efficient adversary can find where the two worlds differ.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.4 Efficient adversaries and concrete security
Textbooks define security asymptotically, requiring a negligible advantage, one that eventually falls below one over every polynomial in the key length. But “eventually” says nothing about the key length you use, so never read an asymptotic claim as a concrete one.
Practitioners use concrete security instead. A scheme has \(\kappa\)-bit security if no attack does better than trying keys by brute force over \(2^\kappa\) keys. An attacker that runs for time \(t\) then gets an advantage of at most about \[\frac{t}{2^\kappa}. \tag{8.2}\] Take an attacker who tests \(10^{18}\) keys per second for a year. Against a 128-bit key, it succeeds with probability only \(9.3\times10^{-14}\). That is why AES uses keys of 128 bits or more.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Hybrid arguments
Proofs compare two worlds through a chain of intermediate worlds called hybrids, each differing from the next in one thing, and the advantages of the steps add up. So if one sample cannot be told apart, a number \(m\) of independent samples cost at most \(m\) times the one-sample advantage, a safe but pessimistic factor.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 Pseudorandom generators and functions
A pseudorandom generator (PRG) stretches a short random seed into a long string that looks random to any efficient observer. Stream ciphers such as ChaCha20 are treated as PRGs. A pseudorandom function (PRF) is a keyed function, written \(F_k\) for the key \(k\), whose outputs look like a random table to anyone without the key. HMAC is assumed to be one, which is what makes a keyed pseudonym safe. A plain hash has no key, so anyone can hash every possible identifier and match the results.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
section: 8.7 The birthday bound and the data limits of a key
text:
8.7 The birthday bound and the data limits of a key
Many arguments fail only if two random values coincide. Write \(q\) for the number of values drawn independently and uniformly from a set of size \(N\). The birthday bound says that the chance of a repeat is \[1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \le \Pr[\text{collision}] \le \frac{q(q-1)}{2N}. \tag{8.3}\] A collision becomes as likely as not after about \(1.18\sqrt N\) draws, so random values of \(\kappa\) bits start to collide after about \(2^{\kappa/2}\) draws. This needs uniform values, because others collide more often.
Collisions come early in practice. With the hashing trick, for example, 1,000 features hashed into about a million buckets collide with probability 0.379. Random 32-bit identifiers reach even odds of a clash at 77,164 records, as the snippet computes. So size identifiers until \(q^2/(2N)\) is tiny for the largest \(q\) you expect.
The same bound limits how much data one key may protect, because treating a block cipher as a PRF costs the birthday bound on the blocks processed. With 128-bit blocks, this switching lemma reaches one half at \(2^{64}\) blocks, so change keys long before that, and ciphers with 64-bit blocks need new keys far sooner.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.8 Encryption
The one-time pad encrypts a message \(m\) as \(m \oplus K\), the bitwise exclusive or (XOR) with a uniformly random key \(K\) as long as the message. That gives perfect secrecy, but only with a key as long as all the data. It must also never be reused, because the XOR of two ciphertexts under one pad is the XOR of the two messages.
Practical schemes use short keys and aim for security under chosen-plaintext attack (CPA). In its game, the adversary may ask for encryptions of any messages it likes, then guesses which of two messages of equal length a challenge encrypts. Ciphertexts usually reveal length, so pad messages when their length is sensitive.
The game forces encryption to be randomized. If the same message always gave the same ciphertext, the adversary would ask for the encryption of its first message and compare, with advantage 1. Deterministic tokens of email addresses can even be reversed, because anyone who can compute the token reverses it by running a dictionary of addresses through it. The fix is a fresh random value for every encryption, called a nonce and written \(r\), drawn from a set \(\mathcal R\) of possible values. The PRF’s output on \(r\) then serves as a one-time pad, and the ciphertext is \((r, m \oplus F_k(r))\). After \(q\) requested encryptions, its advantage is at most \[2\,\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} + \frac{q}{\lvert\mathcal R\rvert}. \tag{8.4}\] The second term is a real attack, because a repeated nonce reuses a pad.
Over the life of a key, any two nonces may repeat, so the birthday bound sets the limit. Take the 96-bit nonces of AES in GCM. If they are random, the chance of any repeat after \(2^{32}\) messages is about \(1.2\times10^{-10}\), and it grows with the square of the count. So rotate keys well before that, or use a counter as the nonce. And since a CPA-secure scheme does nothing against tampering, use authenticated encryption.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Simulation and secret sharing
Many procedures among several participants must reveal the result and nothing else, and simulation makes “nothing else” precise. Write \(\mathrm{View}(x)\) for everything a participant sees on the inputs \(x\), and \(L(x)\) for the leakage, what it is allowed to learn. The procedure reveals nothing more if an efficient simulator \(S\), given only \(L(x)\), can fake a view with the same distribution: \[S(L(x)) \equiv \mathrm{View}(x). \tag{8.5}\] Whether revealing \(L(x)\) is acceptable is a separate decision.
Additive secret sharing is the basic example. Take a number \(h\) of holders and a prime \(p\). To split a secret \(x\), draw \(h - 1\) shares uniformly at random modulo \(p\), and choose the last share so that all of them add up to \(x\): \[s_h = x - (s_1 + \dots + s_{h-1}) \bmod p. \tag{8.6}\] Any \(h - 1\) shares are then independent uniform numbers whatever the secret is, so a simulator just outputs random numbers and the security is perfect. Holders can add their shares of two secrets to get shares of the sum. Part 3 builds on this, and the sum itself is never hidden.
The wrap-around modulo \(p\) is a condition, not a detail, because without it the range of a share moves with the secret. With a mask uniform on 0 to 15 and no reduction, the shares of the secrets 0 and 7 have a TV distance of \(7/16\). So choose \(p\) larger than any sum you will compute, and reduce every result modulo \(p\).

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.10 Learning with errors
Learning with errors (LWE) is the hard problem behind post-quantum key exchange and homomorphic encryption. It hides a secret vector \(s\) behind slightly wrong linear equations modulo \(p\), and each sample pairs a uniformly random vector \(a\) with a number \[b = \langle a, s\rangle + e \bmod p. \tag{8.7}\] Here \(\langle a, s\rangle\) is the inner product, and \(e\) is a small random error drawn fresh for each sample.
Regev encryption shows how such schemes compute on ciphertexts. It hides a bit in a fresh sample, and decryption works while the error stays below a quarter of \(p\). Adding ciphertexts adds the bits, but it also adds the errors. So if every error lies within an error bound \(B\) of zero, a sum of \(k\) ciphertexts is guaranteed to decrypt when \[k < \frac{p}{4B}. \tag{8.8}\] With \(p = 4096\) and \(B = 32\), the guarantee covers 32 ciphertexts, but independent errors partly cancel, so failures become measurable only around 256.
This noise budget is the central parameter of homomorphic encryption. SEAL, TenSEAL and OpenFHE implement schemes such as BFV for exact integers and CKKS for approximate real numbers. In each, a larger modulus buys more operations at the cost of bigger, slower ciphertexts.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.11 Code
This snippet shares and adds secrets, and sizes identifiers and nonces.
import secrets


def union_bound(q: int, n: int) -> float:
    """Upper bound on the chance that q uniform draws from n values repeat."""
    return q * (q - 1) / (2 * n)


def share(secret: int, holders: int, p: int) -> list[int]:
    """Split a secret into additive shares modulo p."""
    shares = [secrets.randbelow(p) for _ in range(holders - 1)]
    return [*shares, (secret - sum(shares)) % p]


def reconstruct(shares: list[int], p: int) -> int:
    return sum(shares) % p


def even_odds_draws(n: int) -> int:
    """Smallest number of uniform draws from n values with a repeat at least half the time."""
    no_repeat, q = 1.0, 0
    while no_repeat > 0.5:
        no_repeat *= 1 - q / n
        q += 1
    return q


p = 2**61 - 1
a, b = share(42, 3, p), share(100, 3, p)
print(reconstruct(a, p))  # 42
print(reconstruct([x + y for x, y in zip(a, b)], p))  # 142
print(even_odds_draws(2**32))  # 77164
print(f"{union_bound(2**32, 2**96):.1e}")  # 1.2e-10

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
This part teaches you to attack your own models and releases before someone else does. You need the attacks even if you plan to use differential privacy, because they are how you check that an implementation keeps its promise. Every attack here is a game, in which a model or a release depends on a hidden secret and an adversary sees what the threat model allows. Its guess counts only by how much it beats a baseline that never looks at the model.
Start with Threat models and privacy games, and then read Membership inference. After those two, pick the chapter whose secret matches your question. For a trained model, membership inference asks whether one record was used, and Attribute inference seeks a person’s sensitive field. Property inference seeks a fact about the whole training population, and Memorization and extraction seeks text the model memorized. In federated learning, Gradient inversion rebuilds a client’s input from its updates.
For released data, read the last three chapters in order, because together they tell one story about releasing less. Records without names still fall to linkage (Linkage and re-identification). Records hidden in crowds still give away sensitive values (Syntactic anonymity). And accurate aggregates alone can give away the whole dataset (Reconstruction attacks). This is the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: answering too many statistics too accurately reveals the data. So “we removed the names” and “we only release aggregates” are not anonymization, and the next part starts from differential privacy instead.
Two lessons drive every audit in this part. First, report the true positive rate at a low false positive rate, such as one in a thousand, not accuracy or the area under the curve. Second, the worst-off records leak first, such as outliers, duplicates and people with a unique combination of attributes, so an average over all records misleads. A failed attack proves little, because an attack only gives a lower bound on the leak.
At the end of this part you will be able to write a threat model, run a membership audit you can defend, test a table for unique records, and decide whether a dataset called anonymized really is. The full edition’s scripts in code/part02-attacks/ reproduce every number at toy scale.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model on patient records and offers it to doctors through a web service. Whether the model is private has no answer until you say against whom. One attacker reads only predicted labels, while another holds the weights, knows the other patients or slips crafted records into the training data. A threat model pins these assumptions down. Without one, “the model leaks” is a claim nobody can test.
Once the threat model is fixed, an attack becomes a game. The adversary guesses a hidden secret, such as whether one patient’s record was used, from what the threat model lets it see. This chapter gives you a worksheet for the threat model, the baseline every attack must beat, and the way to report a result. Behind all three is one idea: an attack counts only by how much it beats a guess made without the model.
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.2 Writing down the threat model
Before you run or read an attack, answer five questions.

Goal: what is the secret? A membership attack asks whether a record was in the training data, and an attribute attack seeks a sensitive field of a known record. A reconstruction attack seeks the records themselves, and a property attack a statistic of the whole dataset.
Access: what does the adversary observe? The weakest is label-only access, the model’s decisions on inputs the adversary chooses. Next is black-box access to scores such as confidences or losses, then white-box access to the weights. The strongest is the transcript, everything training exposed along the way, such as per-step gradients.
Behaviour: does it follow the rules? An honest-but-curious adversary only analyses what it legitimately sees. A malicious one may choose its queries adaptively or insert crafted records into the training data, which is called poisoning.
Trust: who sees the raw data? In the central model a trusted curator holds the data and the adversary sees only the release. In the local model nobody is trusted, so each person’s data are protected on their own device before collection.
Side information: what does it know already? It may know the population, a public dataset, some or all of the other records, or the target’s non-sensitive fields.

For example, a service that returns only the top class gives label-only access, while published weights give white-box access to anyone. A federated-learning server holds the transcript of per-client updates, and it may be malicious. One model can sit in several such deployments at once, and its risk is set by the most exposed one.
Access is ordered, because each level can compute the one below it. A label is a function of the scores, and the scores are a function of the weights. So for the same model and side information, the best attack can only get stronger along the chain \[\text{labels} \;\le\; \text{scores} \;\le\; \text{weights} \;\le\; \text{transcript}. \tag{9.1}\] The same holds for side information and behaviour, since an adversary can always forget what it knows or choose not to deviate. It also means that rounding or noising an output can never make the best attack stronger, though it may not weaken it much either.
The chain compares the best attack at each level, and the attacks people run are often far from it. Against a simple anomaly detector, calibrating each target’s score against how typical the target is raised a black-box attack’s advantage from 0.0407 to 0.2789, the white-box optimum. So “the attack we tried failed” proves little. Membership inference builds that calibration into a practical attack.
Side information is the axis you control least, so assume an adversary who knows every record except the target’s unless you can argue otherwise. Trust decides who the adversary is. If the curator is inside the threat model, protection must happen before the data leave the user (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.3 Scoring an attack against its baseline
text:
9.3 Scoring an attack against its baseline
State every attack in the same four parts: the challenger, the secret, the adversary’s view and its guess. The simplest games ask the adversary to guess one hidden bit. In the membership game, the bit says whether the target’s record is in the training set, which makes the target a member.
Two rates describe an attack. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags. Neither rate depends on how often members occur, but the win rate does, which is why it misleads. Write \(\pi_1\) for the probability that the target is a member and \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1\) for the opposite. The attack then wins with probability \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,(1 - \mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.2}\] If only one target in ten is a member, always saying “not a member” wins 90% of the games. So an attack that is right “90% of the time” may reveal nothing. So score every attack against a baseline, the best score of a guess that never looks at the model.
With a fair prior, half members and half non-members, the baseline is one half. Write the attack’s advantage as \(\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\). The win rate is then \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac12 + \frac12\,\mathrm{Adv}. \tag{9.3}\] So an attack with 55% accuracy at a fair prior has advantage 0.1. Whether 55% is a problem depends on where those wins come from, which the next section shows how to read. Because both rates are measured inside one world, the advantage does not change with the prior. No attack’s advantage exceeds the total variation distance between the adversary’s views in the two worlds (Divergences), which differential privacy later bounds.
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.4 Reporting: TPR at a low FPR
text:
9.4 Reporting: TPR at a low FPR
The advantage is the best height of the attack’s receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve above the diagonal. It says nothing about the region where false positives are rare, which is where privacy breaks. An attack that flags 1% of members with no false alarms has a tiny advantage, but it identifies those members with certainty. But the 55%-accurate attack of the last section may flag members and non-members at similar rates, and then it identifies nobody with confidence. So Carlini et al. (2022) report membership attacks by their TPR at a low FPR such as \(10^{-3}\), or lower, on log axes. This part does the same. The full ROC ceiling of the two worlds is their trade-off curve, which Gaussian differential privacy turns into a guarantee.
A flagged person cares about a third number, the chance that the verdict is right. That is the precision, \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flagged}] = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{9.4}\] When members are rare, even a small FPR applied to the many non-members swamps the true positives (Jayaraman et al., 2021). So a precision is meaningless without the prior it assumes.
Take a count of people with a condition, released with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1, and an adversary who knows the other records. The count is centred on 50 without the target and on 51 with it. The best attack thresholds the count, and its advantage is 0.3829. Held to an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), it catches members with probability 0.0183. That is fewer than 2% of members, but when it fires at a fair prior its precision is 0.948. If only one target in a hundred is a member, the precision drops to 0.156.
A report you can act on states the following.

The threat model, from the worksheet above, and the game.
The TPR at a stated low FPR, \(10^{-3}\) or lower, and the ROC curve on log axes.
The number of non-members the FPR rests on, and a confidence interval for both rates, such as a Clopper–Pearson interval (Hypothesis testing).
The baseline, and the prior behind any precision.
Whether targets were random records or chosen worst cases.

To compute these, scikit-learn’s roc_curve returns the FPR and TPR at every threshold from labels and scores, and auc gives the area under that curve. Then numpy.interp reads off the TPR at your target FPR. scipy.stats.binomtest(k, n).proportion_ci(method="exact") gives the Clopper–Pearson interval for a count. An FPR of \(10^{-3}\) rests on few false positives unless you have far more than 1,000 non-members. To see a given number of false positives at an FPR \(\alpha\), you need about that number divided by \(\alpha\).
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.5 Average case and worst case
An evaluation can draw the data and the target from the population, which gives the average case. Or it can let the adversary know or pick the other records and the target, which gives the worst case. Audits of real models measure the first, but a guarantee must control the second. The best advantages are ordered: \[\text{does not know the others} \;\le\; \text{knows them} \;\le\; \text{chooses them}. \tag{9.5}\] Not knowing the other records acts like extra noise that blurs the two worlds.
The gap can be large. Suppose the noisy count has 100 other records. The adversary who knows them reaches an advantage of 0.3829, and one who does not reaches only 0.0779. But a malicious adversary who planted the other records knows them, so a defence that relies on the crowd fails against exactly the adversary it most needs to stop.
Averaging over targets hides the worst-treated person in the same way. A mechanism that publishes one record chosen at random from 1,000 has an average-case advantage of only 0.001, yet every run exposes one person completely.
So treat an average-case number as a lower bound on the risk, never as an upper bound. Audits narrow the gap by planting canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible (Memorization and training-data extraction). The definition of differential privacy bounds the worst case directly, for every pair of datasets that differ in one record.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.6 Code
The snippet computes the best TPR at any FPR, and the precision, when the attack’s score is standard normal for non-members and shifted by 1 for members, as in the noisy count.
from statistics import NormalDist

Z = NormalDist()


def tpr_at_fpr(fpr: float, shift: float) -> float:
    """Best TPR at a given FPR when the attack score is N(0, 1) for non-members, N(shift, 1) for members."""
    return 1 - Z.cdf(Z.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - shift)


def precision(tpr: float, fpr: float, prior: float) -> float:
    """Fraction of 'member' verdicts that are right when a fraction `prior` of targets are members."""
    return prior * tpr / (prior * tpr + (1 - prior) * fpr)


advantage = 2 * Z.cdf(0.5) - 1  # best TPR - FPR for a shift of 1: the total variation distance
tpr = tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 1.0)
print(f"{advantage:.4f}")  # 0.3829
print(f"{tpr:.4f}")  # 0.0183
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.5):.3f}")  # 0.948
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.01):.3f}")  # 0.156

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 Why this matters
A hospital publishes a model that predicts a disease, and you hold a patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, the patient was treated there for that disease. This is membership inference, the standard measure of leakage, since a model that cannot hide whether a record was used will hide little else.
The one idea of this chapter is that membership is a test about one record. Some records are predicted well whether or not the model trained on them, so their outputs reveal almost nothing. Others are predicted well only if it did. An attack that applies one rule to every record mixes the two kinds and identifies almost nobody. The attack to use in an audit is the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA). It compares the model’s output on a record with how that same record fares under models trained with and without it.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.2 Membership as a test about one record
text:
10.2 Membership as a test about one record
The game is the one of Threat models and privacy games. The attacker gets a training member or a fresh record with equal chance. It is scored by its true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR), and its advantage is the TPR minus the FPR.
Fix one target record, written \(z\), and look at the model’s output on it, such as its loss. Over many training runs with \(z\), that output has one distribution, and over runs without \(z\) it has another. Call them the IN and OUT distributions of \(z\). The best test thresholds their likelihood ratio (Hypothesis testing).
A simple case sets the scale. Suppose the attack’s score is normal with standard deviation 1 and mean 0 for non-members, and shifted for members by an amount \(s\), called the separation. Then, writing \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function and \(\alpha\) for the FPR you allow, the best TPR is \[\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s\big). \tag{10.1}\] For example, at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) a separation of 0.5 gives a TPR of only 0.0048, but a separation of 4 gives 0.8185. Typical records have small separations and outliers have large ones, so the low-FPR end of any attack is made of outliers.
The numbers below come from the full edition’s experiment, which trains logistic regression on random halves of a pool in which 5% of points are outliers. The attacker attacks 128 target models, with 64 shadow models of its own.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.3 The quick check: the generalization gap
text:
10.3 The quick check: the generalization gap
Before any attack, compare the training and test errors. A model fits its training data, so its loss is lower on members. Yeom et al. (2018) showed that the attack “member if correctly classified” has an advantage equal to the gap between the errors: \[\mathrm{Adv} = \text{test error} - \text{training error}. \tag{10.2}\] In the running example, the gap between the two errors, and so the advantage, is 0.1168.
This gives a lower bound for free, since a model with a generalization gap leaks membership by at least the gap. The converse fails, because the gap is an average over records, and an average hides who is exposed. Yeom et al. even construct models that leak with no gap at all, so a small gap does not mean a private model. At a low FPR the loss attack is near chance, as Table 10.1 shows.
The classic attack of Shokri et al. (2017) trains shadow models, copies of the target trained on the same population, and learns to tell their members from non-members. It learns a rule that treats all records alike, so it is mostly superseded, but shadows remain the way to calibrate a threshold for the target.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example
text:
10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example
LiRA, from Carlini et al. (2022), estimates each record’s own IN and OUT distributions from shadow models trained with and without it. Its statistic is the logit of the model’s confidence. Writing \(p_y\) for the confidence in the true label \(y\), the logit is \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}. \tag{10.3}\] LiRA uses it because it is close to normal over retrainings, while the confidence itself piles up against 1. For each record, fit a normal distribution to its logit under the shadow models that trained on it, with the mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}}\) and the standard deviation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}}\). Fit another to the shadow models that did not, with mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\).
Online LiRA scores the target model’s output \(\phi_z\) by how much more likely it is under the IN fit than the OUT fit. Writing \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) for the normal density, the score is \[\ln\Lambda_z = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}}^2\big). \tag{10.4}\] Offline LiRA uses only OUT models, which can be trained once and reused for every target record. It asks how many OUT standard deviations the output lies above its usual value, \[\frac{\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}}. \tag{10.5}\] Both put one threshold on the score for all records. Online LiRA is stronger, because it weighs each record’s evidence by its own separation, while offline LiRA is cheaper. Table 10.1 compares them with the older attacks by their area under the curve (AUC) and by their TPR at a low FPR.



Table 10.1: Every attack on the running example: 128 target models, 64 shadow models, 64,000 member and 64,000 non-member pairs.

The table shows why the AUC is the wrong summary, because by AUC the attacks are close. But at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) the loss and shadow attacks are at chance, since their TPR is no higher than the FPR. Online LiRA’s TPR is 17.0 times the loss attack’s there, although both use the same statistic, so comparing each record with itself is the whole gain.
The main practical failure is noisy fits. Each record’s variance is estimated from half the shadow models. An underestimated variance makes an ordinary output look like a far-tail event, and that produces false positives exactly at the strict thresholds that matter. Carlini et al. therefore recommend one global variance, estimated from all records at once, when shadow models are few. For example, with 16 shadow models online LiRA reaches a TPR of only 0.0023 at an FPR of one in a thousand with per-record variances. With a global variance it reaches 0.0151.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.5 Running LiRA on your model
The full-scale benchmark, CIFAR-10 with 16 shadow models, takes hours of GPU time, but the recipe is the same for any model.

Split the data. For each of \(N + 1\) models, where \(N\) is the number of shadows, choose a random half of the training pool. One model plays the target, and rotating that role adds pairs.
Train every model with exactly the target’s recipe, augmentation included.
Compute the logit for each model and record. Compute it from the class scores \(f\) before the softmax, as \(f_y - \ln\sum_{y' \ne y}e^{f_{y'}}\), which never forms \(1 - p_y\) and so never rounds to 0 for a confident model. Carlini et al. also query a few augmented copies of each input, such as flipped images, and fit over all of them.
Fit IN and OUT normals for each record over the shadows, with a global variance if you have fewer than about 64.
Score each pair of model and record with Equation 10.4, or with Equation 10.5 if you only have OUT models.
Evaluate. Pool all pairs, sweep one threshold, and plot the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve on log axes.

The cost is \(N + 1\) training runs, so the shadow count is the budget decision, and a global variance makes 16 shadows enough.
The members and non-members must come from the same distribution, and violating this is the most common way a membership audit goes wrong. If non-members come from a later period, another site or another preprocessing pipeline, the attack measures that shift rather than the model. So draw both from one pool, split at random, as step 1 does.
When shadows cost too much, there are cheaper options. Offline LiRA reuses one set of OUT models. Reference-model attacks, such as the relative membership inference attack of Zarifzadeh et al. (2024), are designed to stay strong with only a few reference models. Against a service that returns labels only, a label-only attack measures how much an input must be perturbed before its label flips (Choquette-Choo et al., 2021).
For the computation, scipy.stats.norm.logpdf gives the two terms of the online score, and sklearn.metrics.roc_curve gives the curve. TensorFlow Privacy’s membership-inference tests take losses or logits of members and non-members in an AttackInputData object, and run_attacks runs simple threshold attacks on them. LiRA’s reference implementation lives in the same repository. The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox offers MembershipInferenceBlackBox, a trained attack model, and LabelOnlyDecisionBoundary, and ML Privacy Meter implements reference-model attacks.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.6 Reading the result
Report the TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or lower, with the ROC curve on log axes (Threat models and privacy games), because averages hide breaches. An attack that exposes 5% of members with certainty can have the same AUC as one that nudges every score slightly, yet catch 38 times as many members.
Measuring a low FPR takes many non-members, because an FPR is estimated by counting false positives. A count of \(k\) events has a relative error of about \(1/\sqrt k\). So to see \(k\) false positives at an FPR \(\alpha\), you need about \(k/\alpha\) non-members. For example, the running example’s 64,000 non-members give about 64 false positives at one in a thousand. Even then, the Clopper–Pearson 95% interval for online LiRA’s FPR runs from 0.00077 to 0.00128.
Then check three things.

The TPR’s interval is clear of the FPR. If not, the attack is at chance there, like the loss attack in Table 10.1.
The top-scored records make sense. Inspect them, because they are usually outliers, rare subgroups or mislabelled points.
The thresholds were set on separate data. Setting them on the data that measure the rates is usual but optimistic.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.7 Who is exposed, and what helps
text:
10.7 Who is exposed, and what helps
The exposed records are those whose IN and OUT distributions lie far apart. A record’s separation is large when the rest of the data contradict its label or its features are unusual. In the running example, at an FPR of one in a thousand, a share of 0.873 of the members online LiRA finds are outliers.
That points to what does and does not help.

Removing the exposed records does not. Carlini et al. (2022b) removed the most exposed records and retrained, and the next layer became exposed. They call this the onion effect.
Closing the generalization gap is not enough. More data or stronger regularization shrink the average, but the low-FPR end is set by the worst records.
Masking the output does not bound the leak, because label-only attacks still work.
Differential privacy does. It bounds every record’s separation at once. Private training provides it, and an audit with planted canaries checks it.

Expect a trade-off, because memorizing rare cases can be what makes a model accurate on long-tailed data (Feldman, 2020).

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 Why this matters
A hospital’s public model predicts a lung disease from a patient’s age band and whether they smoke. An insurer knows your age and, from a claim, that you have the disease. It can use the model to guess whether you smoke, but that alone is not a privacy failure, since a published study on smoking would allow the same guess. The question that matters is this. Does the model reveal more about your attribute because your record was in its training data?
Attribute inference tries to recover one sensitive field of a record, such as smoking status or a genotype, from its other fields and a model. The one idea of this chapter is to separate two kinds of success. Population inference works equally on everyone, and no defence that limits what one record contributes can stop it. The individual leak is the extra success on people who were in the training data.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 The attribute game
“The attack recovered 78% of smoking statuses” means nothing on its own, so Yeom et al. (2018) defined a game (Threat models and privacy games). In it, the adversary wants the sensitive attribute \(s\) and already knows the public features \(x\). It also sees the label \(y\), which the model predicts.
The challenger trains a model, then picks the target either from the training set, making it a member, or fresh from the population, with equal chance. The adversary sees the target’s \(x\) and \(y\) and queries the model, and then guesses \(s\). The score is the attribute advantage, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{member}] - \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}]. \tag{11.1}\] Population inference helps members and non-members equally, so it cancels in the difference, and what is left is what the model knows about its own training records.
A toy experiment shows how small the advantage can be. Against 200 small logistic regressions, model inversion is right on 0.7832 of members. Yet the attribute advantage is only 0.0569. Most of the attack’s 78% would be there even if the person had never been in the training data.
Any attribute attack is also a membership attack that says “member” when its guess is right, with the same advantage. So a model that leaks nothing about membership leaks nothing about attributes, though the converse fails. As a membership test it is weak, because in the toy experiment being right is only 1.08 times as likely for a member as for a non-member.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 The imputation baseline
The imputation baseline is the success of the best possible guess of \(s\) from \(x\) and \(y\), made by someone who knows the population exactly. Jayaraman & Evans (2022) found that many published attacks do no better than imputation, so this is the number to beat.
The best guess for each pair of \(x\) and \(y\) is the most probable value of \(s\), the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess. Write \(p(s, x, y)\) for the probability that a record from the population has these three values. The MAP guess then succeeds with probability \[\text{baseline} = \sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y). \tag{11.2}\] This is also a ceiling for non-members. A model trained without the target is independent of it, so no attacker does better on a non-member. Attacks that ignore the model have zero advantage, because without the model a member is just another draw from the population.
Table 11.1 works this out for the smoking example. Smokers make up 30% of the population and tend to be older, and the disease is more likely with age and with smoking.



Table 11.1: The smoking table: the joint distribution of smoking status \(s\), age band \(x\) and disease \(y\), with the column maxima in bold and the probability of smoking in each column.

With no observation, the best guess is “non-smoker”, right 70% of the time. But the chance of smoking crosses one half in the two disease columns, so there the MAP guess becomes “smoker”. Its success is the sum of the bold entries, 0.748.
Every one of these numbers comes from the population, not from any model. So dropping the sensitive column from the model’s inputs does not stop this inference, because the correlates in \(x\) and \(y\) remain. As Dwork & Roth (2014) put it, a study showing that smoking causes cancer discloses a fact about the world, not about its participants. Do not count such a finding as a breach. Population inference can still hurt, but it is a question for policy and fairness.
In practice you never know \(p(s, x, y)\), so estimate the baseline from data. Take records from the same population that the model never saw, then fit the best imputer you can on half of them and measure its success on the rest. With a few discrete fields, the imputer is a table of the most common \(s\) in each cell, as in the snippet of Section 11.7. For continuous fields, train instead any good classifier to predict \(s\) from \(x\) and \(y\), such as scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoostingClassifier. The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox packages this as AttributeInferenceBaseline. Your imputer may fall short of the true ceiling, so the estimate errs low. An attack that seems to beat it on non-members points to a weak imputer, not a leak.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 Model inversion: the MAP attack
The imputation guess needs the probability of the label given the other fields, \(p(y \mid x, s)\), and a model that predicts the label from them estimates it. Fredrikson et al. (2014) called the attack built on this model inversion. Writing \(f_y(x, s)\) for the model’s confidence in the known label when it is fed the public features and a candidate value of \(s\), the MAP inversion attack guesses \[\hat s(x, y) = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.3}\] The first factor comes from the adversary’s knowledge of the population, and using the overall frequency \(p(s)\) instead throws away what the public features say. The second comes from one query per candidate, which against a scikit-learn model is a call to predict_proba, reading the column of the known label.
Take an old patient with the disease, and a calibrated model, one whose confidences equal the population’s probabilities. An old person smokes with probability 0.3913, and the model gives the disease a probability of 0.7 for a smoker. So “smoker” scores 0.2739 against 0.1826 for “non-smoker”, and the attack guesses “smoker”. With a calibrated model, inversion simply is imputation, with zero advantage.
A trained model differs from the population in two ways. On members it is too sure of the truth, which is the generalization gap of Membership inference seen through the attribute. On non-members its confidences are noisy, so its guesses fall below the ceiling. In the toy experiment, inversion beats the ceiling of 0.7517 on members but not on non-members. So measuring an attack only on fresh records understates what it achieves on members.
More data closes both gaps. With 25 training records the advantage is 0.1610, and with 1,600 it is only 0.0052.
The same idea can invert a whole input. For example, MIFace in the toolbox recovers a typical face of a class, which is a privacy problem when the class is one person.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 Confidence masking
Many interfaces round their confidences or return only the top label, a defence that Fredrikson et al. (2015) suggested. Such confidence masking cannot help the best attacker, because whoever holds the full answers can apply the mask themselves. But it bounds nothing about the gap between members and non-members, which is the leak, and the gap can shrink or grow.



Table 11.2: MAP inversion success through three interfaces, averaged over 200 models trained on 100 records each. Guessing from \(x\) alone gives 0.7045, and imputation with the true population 0.7517.

In Table 11.2, rounding changes almost nothing. With labels only, non-member success drops close to the guess from \(x\) alone, but member success drops less, so the advantage grows. Masking has hurt population inference more than the individual leak, and label-only membership attacks exploit the same asymmetry.
So don’t count a drop in overall attack success as a privacy gain. Less overfitting shrinks the member gap, and differential privacy bounds it for every attacker and every output format.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
section: 11.6 Deciding whether there is a leak
text:
11.6 Deciding whether there is a leak
An audit of attribute leakage follows four steps.

Estimate the baseline from held-out data, as in Section 11.3.
Run MAP inversion, or your strongest attack, on training members and on as many held-out non-members. The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox’s AttributeInferenceBlackBox is a ready-made attack. For synthetic data, Anonymeter’s InferenceEvaluator measures the same risk.
Compare the two rates, with a confidence interval for each. If member success is not clearly above non-member success, this attack finds no individual leak.
Classify what remains. Success up to the baseline is population inference, a policy question. Success on members beyond non-members is the individual leak, which more data or differential privacy addresses.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.7 Code
The snippet estimates the imputation baseline from held-out records of the smoking population, and its estimate lands close to the exact 0.748.
import random
from collections import Counter
from collections.abc import Hashable

P_SMOKER = 0.3
P_OLD = {0: 0.4, 1: 0.6}  # Pr[old | s]
P_DISEASE = {(0, 0): 0.1, (0, 1): 0.3, (1, 0): 0.4, (1, 1): 0.7}  # Pr[disease | s, old]
Record = tuple[int, Hashable]  # (sensitive value s, the fields the attacker sees)


def draw(rng: random.Random) -> Record:
    s = int(rng.random() < P_SMOKER)
    old = int(rng.random() < P_OLD[s])
    return s, (old, int(rng.random() < P_DISEASE[(s, old)]))


def imputation_baseline(fit: list[Record], test: list[Record]) -> float:
    """Learn the most common s for each observed cell on `fit`, and return its success on `test`."""
    counts: dict[Hashable, Counter[int]] = {}
    for s, seen in fit:
        counts.setdefault(seen, Counter())[s] += 1
    fallback = Counter(s for s, _ in fit).most_common(1)[0][0]
    guess = {seen: c.most_common(1)[0][0] for seen, c in counts.items()}
    return sum(guess.get(seen, fallback) == s for s, seen in test) / len(test)


rng = random.Random(0)
held_out = [draw(rng) for _ in range(20_000)]
print(f"{imputation_baseline(held_out[:10_000], held_out[10_000:]):.4f}")  # 0.7468

\(\sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y)\)
Population inference; estimate on held-out data


MAP inversion
\(\hat s = \arg\max_s p(s \mid x)\,f_y(x, s)\)
One query per candidate value; use \(p(s \mid x)\), not \(p(s)\)


Masking
Cannot help the best attacker
But the member/non-member gap can grow






Rules of thumb

Report success on members, on non-members, and the imputation baseline. One success rate, such as 80%, says nothing about privacy until you know the other two.
An attribute attack is a weak membership test, so measure membership with a dedicated attack.
Rounding confidences or returning labels only changes the attack, not what the model memorized.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a readmission model on its 1,000 patients and shares it with a research partner. Suppose you have checked that no attack on the model can tell, much better than a coin flip, whether any one patient was in the training set. The partner can still learn whether 45% or 55% of the hospital’s patients are over 65, and be right almost every time.
None of these secrets is about a single record. Each is a property of the training set as a whole, such as the fraction of records in some subgroup. Property inference is the attack that recovers it from a trained model. The one fact to keep from this chapter is that a property changes many records at once, so it moves the model far more than any single record does. That is why defences sized for one record do not cover it, and why the attack gets easier, not harder, as the dataset grows.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.2 The property game and its ceiling
text:
12.2 The property game and its ceiling
Threat models and privacy games writes every attack as a game. In the property game, a challenger flips a fair bit and trains a model on records drawn with one of two subgroup shares, \(t_0\) or \(t_1\), depending on the bit. The attacker knows both shares, has data from both groups and can train models the way the victim does. It sees the weights or only the model’s answers, and guesses the bit. Each dataset carries a single secret, so the natural score is the accuracy, the chance that the guess is right. It is tied to the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) by \[\text{accuracy} = \tfrac12(1 + \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}), \tag{12.1}\] so a coin flip scores one half.
First ask whether the property is a secret at all. Learning that smokers get more lung cancer is the purpose of a medical study, not a breach. A property is a harm to reveal only when the property describes the data owner rather than the world, such as one hospital’s patient mix or one lab’s machine configuration. When the dataset is a small sample of a public population, its property is public anyway.
There is a ceiling on what any attacker can learn. When each record shows its group, no model can leak more than the count of subgroup records, so the best advantage is the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions of that count (Hypothesis testing). Write \(n\) for the number of records. For the hospital’s 1,000 patients the ceiling is 0.9985, so it is no comfort, only a scale against which to read a measured attack. An attacker who can add a few records of its own to the training set can make a property far easier to infer (Mahloujifar et al. 2022).

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
text:
12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
The simplest release, the count of subgroup records, shows why. One attacker asks whether one subgroup record is in the data, while another asks whether the share was \(t_0\) or \(t_1\). Write \(t\) for the population share in the first question. Then the best membership advantage is about \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{mem}} \approx \frac{1 - t}{\sqrt{2\pi(n - 1)t(1 - t)}}, \tag{12.2}\] which falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). Write \(\bar t\) for the midpoint of the two shares and \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function. The best property advantage is about \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{prop}} \approx 2\Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big) - 1, \tag{12.3}\] which rises towards 1.



Table 12.1: Exact best advantages from a released count of subgroup records, which the formulas match closely. Property: \(t_0 = 0.45\) against \(t_1 = 0.55\). Membership: one subgroup record, population share \(t = 0.5\).





\(n\)

Membership

In Table 12.1, at 10,000 records, the attacker who asks about one patient is right with probability 0.502, while the one who asks about the share is never wrong to four decimals.
Two practical rules follow. Size and gap enter only through \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\), so doubling the gap has the same effect as four times as much data. And moving from share \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, which for the hospital is 100 of its 1,000 patients. Differential privacy (DP) protects one record at a time. Its group-privacy guarantee for a group of records multiplies the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) by the size of the group, here 100 (Properties of differential privacy). So a model trained with DP at a useful \(\varepsilon\) still reveals the property, and a small membership risk says nothing about it either.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.4 Running the attack: shadow models and a meta-classifier
text:
12.4 Running the attack: shadow models and a meta-classifier
Nobody can write down the distribution of a real model’s weights, so the attacker samples it instead (Ateniese et al. 2015). The recipe is the shadow-model idea of Membership inference, with whole models as the data points.

From auxiliary data, draw many datasets of the victim’s size with share \(t_0\) and as many with share \(t_1\).
Train a shadow model on each one, with the victim’s architecture, hyperparameters and training code.
Turn each shadow model into a feature vector, either its parameters or its outputs on fixed probe inputs.
Train a classifier, the meta-classifier, to tell the two shares apart from those vectors, and measure its accuracy on fresh shadow models.
Apply it to the victim’s model.

A linear meta-classifier is a sensible default. Models fitted by minimizing an average loss on many records have roughly normal parameters, and for those the best possible test is linear. In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression from sklearn.linear_model serves well, and LinearDiscriminantAnalysis from sklearn.discriminant_analysis is the linear test itself. Fit either on the shadow features with the share as the label, and read its accuracy with score on held-out shadow models. No mainstream privacy library ships a standard property-inference attack, so this short pipeline is the usual tool.
meta = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(shadow_features, shadow_shares)
print(meta.score(heldout_features, heldout_shares))   # attack accuracy
The full edition also predicts how well the best attack can do. Write \(\theta'\) for the slope of the fitted parameters, how fast they move as the share changes, and \(\Sigma_1\) for their noise, the covariance that one record would give. Their ratio is a constant \(\kappa\), and for a small gap the best accuracy is about \[\text{accuracy} \approx \Phi\big(\kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|/2\big), \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{\theta'^\top\Sigma_1^{-1}\theta'}. \tag{12.4}\] The released count has \(\kappa = 2\) at a midpoint of one half, so a model leaks as much as the count would on a fraction \((\kappa/2)^2\) of the records. If the property does not change what the model fits, nothing leaks to first order. If it does, the leak is a side effect of fitting the data well, and no care in the training code removes it.
For example, the full edition’s logistic regression never sees the group but has \(\kappa = 0.647\), so it leaks the share about as well as one record in ten would.
What goes wrong is mostly on the attacker’s side. With few records and a small gap, noise in the shadow models hides the shift, so the measured attack falls short of the best one and a weak result is not evidence that the model is safe. Report the measured accuracy, and the predicted one next to it when you can estimate \(\kappa\). The auxiliary data must also match the victim’s population, or the meta-classifier learns the difference between the populations rather than the share.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.5 Neural networks: choose the right representation
text:
12.5 Neural networks: choose the right representation
A neural network can be written down in many ways. Swap two hidden units, together with their incoming and outgoing weights, and the network computes the same function. With the tanh activation, flipping the signs of one unit’s weights also changes nothing. Training treats all these equivalent weight vectors alike, so every raw weight has the same mean under both shares, and a meta-classifier fed the flattened weights sees nothing (Ganju et al. 2018).
The fix is a representation that ignores the order of the units. The full edition compares four on small tanh networks, for shares 0.2 against 0.8. A linear meta-classifier on raw parameters scores 0.497, which is chance, while one on the network’s outputs at 16 fixed probe inputs scores 1.000. Sorting the units by their outgoing weights recovers most of the signal, but it is fragile when two units have nearly equal weights. Sums over the units, the idea behind DeepSets (Zaheer et al. 2017), need no sorting and extend to deeper networks layer by layer. Probes do best, because the property changes the function the network computes and probes measure it directly.
Probe outputs need only query access, so a model behind an application programming interface is not safe either, and Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko (2021) attack properties through queries alone.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.6 Defences and their limits
Because a property is a large group of records, there is no cheap defence. A released statistic hides it only if its noise is on the scale of \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, and that much noise also destroys what the statistic was for. Removing the group column does not help, because whatever correlates with the group still moves the model.
If the property is a secret (Section 12.2), the strongest option is not to release a model trained on that mix, and query access is no way out. Pooling data with other owners is no fix, because Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko (2021) attack exactly that multi-party setting, and in federated learning the same attack can target one client’s updates. If you must release, run the attack recipe with your own data as the auxiliary data. Then report its accuracy for the shares an adversary would plausibly compare, and state in the release notes that DP protects individuals only.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is”, and it may finish the sentence with the real number. Nobody queried a database, and no breach leaked anything, because the number is stored in the model’s weights and comes out through its normal interface. This is training-data extraction. Membership inference needs the record in hand to ask whether it was used, while extraction hands the attacker the record itself.
One idea runs through the chapter. Fix the context in which a secret appears, say “my pin is”, and list every possible filler from the most likely to the least likely under the model. The rank of the true secret is its position in that list, which is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries the fillers in that order. A model has memorized a string when it ranks it far above the strings that could have stood in its place.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Which memorization to measure
The notions of memorization below give rates that differ by orders of magnitude, so a report must say which one it measures. All use greedy decoding, which writes out the most likely next token at each step.



Table 13.1: The notions of memorization and when to use each. Discoverable implies extractable, and verbatim implies approximate.











Definition
The string counts as memorized if
Attacker it fits
Use it for




Discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023)
Its training prefix makes greedy decoding produce it
One who holds the prefix
Measuring memorization on a model you own


Extractable (Carlini et al. 2021)
Some prompt, any at all, makes greedy decoding produce it
One who has only the model
The real risk; found by attacks, not measured


\(k\)-eidetic
It is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) documents
As extractable
Flagging the dangerous case, \(k = 1\)


Approximate (Ippolito et al. 2023)
Greedy decoding comes within a set edit distance of it
Any reader of the output
Near copies, such as a number with one digit changed






Discoverable memorization is the one you can measure. Carlini et al. (2023) prompt with 50 tokens of a training sequence, decode 50 tokens greedily and count exact matches. Treat any verbatim rate as a lower bound on the leak. Ippolito et al. (2023) show that a filter blocking verbatim training text is easy to bypass with prompts that change the style, while approximate copies still come out.
Deployed systems sample rather than decode greedily, which turns memorization into a matter of budget. A sample at temperature 1 writes out a string \(x\) after a prompt with the model’s probability \(p\) of that string. Write \(\beta\) for the chance of failure the attacker accepts. Then a number \(m\) of independent samples suffices when \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p}. \tag{13.1}\] For example, a string of probability \(10^{-3}\) needs about 4,600 samples for 99% confidence. So report a sampling probability or a budget alongside the greedy rate, because a string that greedy decoding misses can still come out after a few thousand queries. Measure with the temperature and decoding settings you deploy.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.3 What gets memorized: copies, model size and rare data
text:
13.3 What gets memorized: copies, model size and rare data
Carlini et al. (2023) ran that test on open models, and the largest reproduced at least 1% of its training data. Memorization grew log-linearly with three things, so it rises by about the same amount each time one of them is multiplied by a fixed factor.
The first is the number of copies of a string. Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel (2022) found that a sequence repeated ten times is generated about a thousand times more often than one seen once.
The second is model size. A larger model separates contexts more finely, so rare strings end up with parameters of their own, and they are memorized from fewer copies. The third is prompt length, since a longer prefix pins down the context. Rare data are exposed first, because an atypical example can be fitted only by memorizing it (Algorithmic stability and generalization).
These findings give the order of defences. Deduplication is the cheapest, because it lowers the copies of every repeated string. Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often without losing quality, and released their exact-substring tool as deduplicate-text-datasets. For near duplicates, MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing is the usual method, for example MinHash and MinHashLSH in the datasketch package. Deduplication does nothing for a string seen once in a large model, though, because there one copy is enough.
The second defence is to remove personal data before training. A detector of personally identifiable information (PII), such as Microsoft’s Presidio, finds names, phone numbers and similar fields so you can mask them. It misses whatever its patterns do not cover, so measure what remains with canaries rather than trusting the filter. Filtering the model’s outputs is weaker still, because approximate copies pass a verbatim filter. The only defence with a guarantee for singletons is training or fine-tuning with differential privacy.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Auditing with canaries and exposure
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing, while an auditor wants a graded answer. Carlini et al. (2019) proposed planting canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits. You know each canary’s value and the number of values it could have taken, so after training you can see exactly where the model ranks it. Write \(\mathcal R\) for the set of possible values, \(|\mathcal R|\) for their number and \(\hat r\) for the planted value. The exposure is the number of bits of search the model saves an attacker: \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.2}\] Each bit halves the guesses the attacker needs, and an exposure near the maximum, \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\), means the secret can actually be extracted.
What makes exposure an audit tool is its known behaviour when nothing was memorized. A canary that was never inserted lands at a uniformly random rank, so for any threshold of \(t\) bits, \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge t\big] \le 2^{-t}. \tag{13.3}\] So \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\) bounds a p-value, the chance that an uninserted canary would look at least this memorized. The average exposure of an uninserted canary is about 1.44 bits.
The recipe for a real model follows.

Draw a few dozen canaries in a format your data could contain, each with a fresh random value. Insert each one a chosen number of times, from once to many.
Train as usual, and keep some canaries drawn but never inserted as a control.
For each canary, score its value and many random values of the same format by the model’s log-probability after the prefix. With Hugging Face transformers, pass the tokens as input_ids and as labels, with the prefix positions of labels set to -100. The returned loss is then the mean cross-entropy over the value’s tokens.
Estimate the rank as the share of random values that score at least as high as the canary, and convert it to exposure.
Check that the controls average about 1.44 bits, then report the exposure against copies. TensorFlow Privacy ships secret-sharer utilities that compute exposure, but the snippet in Section 13.6 does the same.

Three things go wrong. First, scoring \(m\) random values cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2 m\) bits, because a canary that beats them all only tells you that its rank fraction is below about \(1/m\). Carlini et al. (2019) extrapolate by fitting a skew-normal to the scores, because a plain normal fit overestimates exposure. Second, ties hide memorization, because when every candidate gets the same score, every exposure is 0. Third, the canary format must look like your data, or the model may treat it as unlike anything it learned. Comparing two training runs, such as with and without deduplication, then tests the defence.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted data from GPT-2 in three steps. The attacker generates many samples, ranks them by how likely each is to be memorized, and checks the top of the ranking against public sources. The ranking is the hard step, because a model finds a string likely either because it is ordinary text or because it was memorized. A reference model, trained on similar data but not on the target’s training set, stands in for ordinary text. Write \(p_\theta(x)\) for the target’s probability of a string \(x\), and \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) for the reference’s. Rank by the log-likelihood ratio \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x), \tag{13.4}\] which is the best possible ranking for a fixed rate of false alarms (Hypothesis testing).
Raw likelihood puts first the strings that any model finds likely, such as software licences and boilerplate, which reveal nothing, and the ratio cancels them. A crude reference works. Carlini et al. (2021) used a smaller model of the same family, and also the target’s own likelihood on lowercased text and the compressed length of the text, len(zlib.compress(text.encode())) from Python’s standard library. With Hugging Face transformers, model.generate with do_sample=True draws the samples, and passing output_scores=True and return_dict_in_generate=True lets model.compute_transition_scores return each token’s log-probability.
An attacker without the prefix extracts less than the discoverable rate suggests, but production models are still not safe. Nasr et al. (2023) asked ChatGPT to repeat one word forever, and about 200 US dollars of queries extracted over 10,000 unique memorized examples, so alignment hides memorization from casual use without removing it.

Question
Answer




Which rate to report

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type, and the raw text never leaves the phones. Instead, a server sends the current model to each phone, the phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples, and it sends back only that gradient. The server averages the gradients of many phones and takes a training step. This is federated learning (FL), often called private because “the data stay on the device”.
This chapter asks what a single client’s gradient reveals about its data, and the answer is often everything. A gradient holds one derivative for every parameter, and many of them are simple functions of the input, so the input can be read back. Averaging over a batch protects much less than people expect. So treat a per-client update as being as sensitive as the data it came from.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 The attacker and what it sees
text:
14.2 The attacker and what it sees
The attacker is the server. It is honest-but-curious in the sense of Threat models and privacy games, so it follows the protocol, sees each client’s own update and knows every parameter, since it chose them. A client holds a batch of \(B\) examples, each an input with its label. Write \(\theta\) for all the parameters, and \(\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i)\) for the loss on example \(i\) with input \(x_i\) and label \(y_i\). The client sends the average gradient \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i). \tag{14.1}\]
The numbers in this chapter come from the full edition’s experiments, on small grey-scale images and a network with one hidden layer of 32 units. Its gradient gives 2,212 numbers, one per parameter, against 64 unknown pixels per image.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
The most common first layer, a fully connected layer with a bias, gives its input back by one division. Each unit \(j\) multiplies the input \(x\) by its weights and adds a bias. Write \(\delta_j\) for the rate at which the loss responds to that unit’s output, its backward signal. The chain rule then makes the weight gradient and the bias gradient \[
abla_W\ell = \delta\,x^	op, \qquad 
abla_b\ell = \delta. 	ag{14.2}\] So row \(j\) of the weight gradient is the input scaled by \(\delta_j\), and entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is that same scale. For a single example, dividing one by the other gives the input exactly, for every unit whose bias gradient is not zero: \[x =  rac{(
abla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(
abla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. 	ag{14.3}\]
Everything above the layer, including the depth of the network, the loss and the label, sits inside the scale \(\delta_j\) and cancels. So the attack needs no optimization and no knowledge of the data, and it checks itself, because every usable unit gives the same answer. In the experiment, every switched-on unit gives back the image to rounding error. At a deeper fully connected layer, the same division gives that layer’s input.
Switched-off ReLU units give nothing, but one active unit is enough. Without a bias, every row still points along \(x\), so a one-dimensional search for the scale finds it. What stops the division is a convolutional first layer, because its filter is reused at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum that no division separates. For such models the attacker searches instead (Section 14.5).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
The label is often the most sensitive part of an example, such as a diagnosis. It can be read off the last layer without any search (Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen 2020). The rule needs a last layer with a bias, followed by the softmax and the cross-entropy loss. Write \(p\) for the predicted probabilities and \(e_y\) for the vector with a 1 at the position of the label \(y\). The last layer’s bias gradient is then \(p - e_y\), which is negative only at the true label. So for a single example \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.4}\] Without the bias, the same sign pattern shows in the last layer’s weight gradient when the hidden values cannot be negative. The one failure is a very confident model, whose true-label probability rounds to exactly 1, so the sign is lost.
A batch hides which example has which label, but not how many examples there are of each class. Write \(n_k\) for the number of examples of class \(k\), and \(p_{ik}\) for the probability the model gives that class on example \(i\). Then \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.5}\] The server does not know the sum of predictions, but it knows the model. So it estimates the sum from its own data of the same kind, and rounds the result. With that estimate, every count came out exact in all batches of 4, but larger batches miss more often, and the share exact falls to 52.5% for batches of 64.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Deep Leakage from Gradients
When the division does not apply, the attacker searches. Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) (Zhu, Liu & Han 2019) guesses an input and computes the gradient it would produce. It then moves the guess until that gradient matches the observed one. Write \(R\) for the matching loss, the squared distance between the two gradients. With the labels from Section 14.4, the attack looks for the guesses that make it smallest: \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\lVert\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\rVert^2. \tag{14.6}\]
In PyTorch the attack is a short loop. Its key call is torch.autograd.grad with create_graph=True, which keeps the gradient differentiable so that the optimizer can follow the slope of \(R\).
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x_guess), y_known)
grads = torch.autograd.grad(loss, model.parameters(), create_graph=True)
R = sum(((g - g_obs) ** 2).sum() for g, g_obs in zip(grads, observed_grads))
R.backward()   # then one optimizer step on x_guess; repeat
Three things decide whether it works. The activation must have a slope that varies, so Zhu et al. replaced the ReLU by the sigmoid. The search can get stuck, because \(R\) is not convex, but the final value of \(R\) tells you which case you are in. A loss at rounding error means an exact match, while one that stops falling above it means a restart from a new random guess. Finally, a failed run is an optimization failure, not a lack of information. Geiping et al. (2020) compared gradients by direction and added a smoothness penalty, and recovered recognizable images from trained networks and from batches. In the full edition’s experiment, one image comes back exact to about 13 digits after 600 steps of the Adam optimizer.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Batches and averaging
Clients usually send the average over a batch, or the parameter change after several local steps. Averaging breaks the division and makes the search harder, but much of the structure survives, because each example contributes one outer product to the first-layer gradient, so for a batch of \(B\) \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\delta_{1,i}\,x_i^\top, \qquad \operatorname{rank}\nabla_{W_1}\ell \le B. \tag{14.7}\] Every row of the gradient is a combination of the \(B\) inputs. So the server learns the few directions that every example is built from, which already rules out almost every input.
The division still recovers an example exactly when one ReLU unit is switched on for that example and off for the rest of the batch, because the unit then isolates the example. Suppose the \(m\) hidden units switched on like independent fair coins. Each example would then be isolated with probability \(1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m\), so an even chance at a batch of 10 needs only 710 units. Real data are worse than that formula, because images of the same kind make a unit fire on many examples or on few. With 1,024 units and a batch of 16, the formula predicts that 1.6% of the batch is exposed, while in fact 69.1% is. So wide layers with real data expose most examples of batches of 10 or more.
DLG suffers more from batching, and from a batch of 4 the median run gets stuck. That is a harder search, not less information, since the isolation attack recovered all four images of such a batch.
Several local steps, as in federated averaging, hamper the search but do not protect a single example. Every step’s first-layer gradient is an outer product with the same input, so the division still works on the total change. And a malicious server that chooses the weights can isolate most examples of even a large batch by design. It plants units that fire only on rare inputs or sort inputs into narrow bins (Boenisch et al. 2023; Fowl et al. 2022).

For an FL deployment, ask who can see one client’s update, using Table 14.1.

Two protections change the picture. Secure aggregation is a cryptographic protocol that lets the server see only the sum over many clients, never one client’s update. That removes the per-client view that every attack here uses. It needs a minimum number of clients per sum, though, because a sum over very few clients is close to a single update. So larger cohorts help, and clients that drop out mid-round must not leave a small group exposed.
Secure aggregation alone is not enough, because the sum and the final model still leak and a server can still choose malicious weights. For a guarantee, add training with DP. In DP federated averaging, each client’s update is clipped to a fixed norm and noise is added to the sum. That bounds what any update reveals, whoever sees it. Opacus provides per-example clipping and noise for PyTorch through its PrivacyEngine, and Flower and TensorFlow Federated both offer secure aggregation and differentially private aggregation of client updates. Heuristic defences, such as pruning small gradient entries or mixing inputs, raise the cost of the search but carry no guarantee.
To check your own setup, attack it with your own architecture, batch size and number of local steps. Geiping’s open-source breaching framework implements the published attacks for PyTorch models, and the full edition’s script, code/part02-attacks/gradient_inversion.py, runs every attack in this chapter.
