title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital wants to share its discharge records with researchers. It deletes the names but keeps the postcode, the date of birth, the sex and the diagnosis, because the research needs them. But anyone who holds a voter roll, with names next to those same three columns, can join the two tables and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification.
To judge whether a release is identifying, measure identifying information in bits, because bits add up. Write \(n\) for the number of people in a population. Singling out one of them takes \(\log_2 n\) bits, which is 27.9 bits for the United States of 1990 and 32.9 bits for the whole world. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 v\) bits, and the bits of independent attributes add. Once the bits an adversary knows exceed \(\log_2 n\) by a few, almost everyone is unique.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, like a name or an email address, name a person on their own, while sensitive attributes, like a diagnosis, are what the release is about. Quasi-identifiers sit in between. None of them names anyone alone, but together they often single out one person, and they appear in other datasets next to names. The most common “de-identification” removes the direct identifiers and keeps the quasi-identifiers, which is exactly the gap the linkage attack uses.
To score a release you hold, group its \(n\) records into equivalence classes, the sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers, and write \(J\) for the number of classes. An adversary who knows the target is in the release, and knows the target’s quasi-identifiers, finds a target alone in its class for sure and a target in a class of \(k\) records one time in \(k\). Averaged over targets, its success probability is \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] and no adversary that sees only the quasi-identifiers can do better.
For example, the hospital release in the Code section uses ZIP code, birth date and sex, and its records fall into 5 classes for a success of 0.625. Three of its records are unique, so anyone on a voter roll with one of those combinations has their diagnosis exposed with certainty. Latanya Sweeney estimated from the 1990 census that 87% of Americans were likely unique on those three attributes, because together they carry at most 31.1 bits. Coarser geography helps, and with the county in place of the ZIP code the figure fell to 18%.
If every class holds at least \(k\) records, the success is at most \(1/k\), but a class whose records share one diagnosis still leaks it (Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers
Many releases replace each identifier by a pseudonym, a code that stays the same across a person’s records, and such codes fail in two ways. The first is that an unkeyed hash, such as MD5, can be reversed whenever the possible identifiers can be listed. The adversary hashes every candidate once and looks each pseudonym up, which takes seconds to hours for phone, licence or identity numbers. The second failure survives any key. Because the pseudonym ties a person’s records together, linking any one record to them reveals all the others.
New York City’s 2013 taxi release showed both. Driver licences had been replaced by unkeyed MD5 hashes, and there were only about 2 million possible licences. So Vijay Pandurangan hashed every one in minutes, and public lists of licence holders put a name on every driver’s trips and income. Passengers were exposed by the trips themselves, because a pickup minute and place single out one trip.
So treat a pseudonymized release as identifiable, as the GDPR does, since it counts pseudonymized data as personal data. If you must keep a join key, derive it with a keyed hash, a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) such as Python’s hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256), and keep the key away from the data. That stops the dictionary attack, but the key still groups each person’s records into a history that is itself identifying. Use a fresh key for each release, because one pseudonym reused across releases joins them.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.4 Predicting uniqueness before a release
For a release you are still designing, you need a model rather than a count. Call a person’s combination of attribute values their cell, write \(p_c\) for the probability of cell \(c\), and assume that people fall in cells independently. The expected fraction of the \(n\) people who share their cell with nobody is then \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} = \sum_c p_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.2}\]
When all cells are equally likely and there are \(2^b\) of them, so that the attributes carry \(b\) bits, the formula becomes \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2 n - b}\big). \tag{15.3}\] This fraction depends only on the bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), and it is steep. Half the people are unique at 0.53 bits beyond it, and 99% at 6.64 bits.
Use Equation 15.3 for a first estimate. For the Sweeney attributes it predicts that 0.899 of Americans are unique, close to her 87%. Real attributes are skewed, and skew usually lowers uniqueness, so the uniform estimate is pessimistic. The full edition also gives a floor on uniqueness from the collision probability, the chance that two random people share a cell. Correlated attributes carry fewer bits than their sum. They need a model of the joint distribution, such as the Gaussian copula of Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Sparse data: the Netflix attack
Ratings, purchases and locations have no quasi-identifier columns, but they are even more identifying. In 2006 Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings, with subscribers’ names replaced by random numbers. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) matched its records to public reviews. Their attack scores how well each record \(r\) agrees with what the adversary knows, a few items \(i\) with approximate values \(\mathrm{aux}_i\): \[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{aux}, r) = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{aux}} w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i). \tag{15.4}\] Here the agreement \(\mathrm{Sim}\) is 1 when the record’s rating \(r_i\) is within one star of the known value, and 0 otherwise. The weight \(w_i\) favours rare items, because agreeing on an obscure film says much more than agreeing on a hit. Write \(s_i\) for the fraction of records that rated item \(i\). The weight \(\ln(1/s_i)\) works well, and the item carries \(\log_2(1/s_i)\) bits.
On Netflix, eight ratings identified 99% of records, even with two of them wrong and dates known only to within two weeks. Bits explain it again, since a film that 1% of subscribers rated carries 6.64 bits, and three such films single out one subscriber. Errors in the auxiliary data cost little because the score adds up evidence rather than demanding a perfect match.
The top score is the best guess only if the target is in the release. When it may not be, the eccentricity test declares a match only if the best score stands out. Write \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) for the two largest scores, and \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of all scores. The test requires the gap to clear a threshold \(\varphi\), \[\frac{S_1 - S_2}{\sigma} \ge \varphi. \tag{15.5}\] Calibrate the threshold on people known not to be in the data, because the published threshold of 1.5 falsely matched 26.3% of outsiders on the full edition’s synthetic ratings. So always report the rate at a stated false positive rate (Hypothesis testing).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Does releasing a sample protect?
Statistical agencies often release only a sample, arguing that a sample-unique record may not be unique in the population. Write \(\pi\) for the sampling fraction and \(\lambda\) for the expected number of other people in the target’s cell. Start from a known person who has exactly one match in the sample, and write \(\kappa\) for the probability that the match is right. Or start from a record alone in its cell in the sample, and write \(\xi\) for the probability that it is alone in the population too. For a rare cell, \[\kappa \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - \pi)}, \qquad \xi \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - \pi)}. \tag{15.6}\] Since \(1 - \pi\) is at most 1, sampling can never push them below \(1/(1 + \lambda)\) and \(e^{-\lambda}\), so it helps only when cells are crowded. For a rare cell, a match from a person is right with probability 0.910 even in a 1% sample.
In the full edition’s synthetic population, 0.8301 of the sample-unique records in a 1% sample were still unique in the population, and the adversary can tell which ones from the sample itself. So estimate uniqueness for the population, never just for the sample. Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye predicted that 99.98% of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset with 15 demographic attributes, and that sampling changes this very little. So a small sample protects only people who were not unique anyway.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.7 A pre-release risk check

List the quasi-identifiers. Include every column an adversary could find elsewhere next to a name, such as demographics, dates, locations, employers and rare events like a hospital stay in the news.
Measure the release. Group by the quasi-identifiers and report \(J/n\), the fraction of unique records and the fraction in classes smaller than your \(k\). In pandas, df.groupby(qi_cols).size() gives the class sizes.
Estimate the bits for planned releases. Add \(\log_2\) of each attribute’s number of values, and if the total is several bits above \(\log_2 n\), expect most people to be unique.
Reduce the risk. Coarsen geography and dates first, since they carry the most bits, then suppress the records that remain unique.
Know when to stop. If the analysis needs fine-grained or sparse data, release aggregates or a differentially private output instead (The definition of differential privacy).

Several tools automate these steps. ARX, an open-source Java application, measures risk and searches for generalizations, and the R package sdcMicro does the same from an object built with createSdcObj. To test a release by actually linking it, use the Python recordlinkage package, Splink, or Anonymeter’s SinglingOutEvaluator and LinkabilityEvaluator. No tool knows what auxiliary data exist, so the choice of quasi-identifiers stays your judgement.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.8 Code
The snippet computes the risk of a release you hold, and the uniform estimate of Equation 15.3 for Sweeney’s attributes.
from collections import Counter
from math import exp, log2


def linkage_report(rows: list[tuple[str, ...]]) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Linkage success J/n, fraction of unique records, and smallest class size of a release."""
    sizes = Counter(rows).values()  # one count per distinct quasi-identifier combination
    n = len(rows)
    return len(sizes) / n, sum(1 for k in sizes if k == 1) / n, min(sizes)



release = [
    ("02138", "1961-03-14", "F"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"),
    ("02139", "1958-06-21", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"),
    ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02141", "1983-09-30", "M"),
]
success, unique, k = linkage_report(release)
print(f"{success:.3f} {unique:.3f} {k}")  # 0.625 0.375 1
cells = 40_000 * 365 * 80 * 2  # ZIP code x birth date over 80 years x sex
print(f"{log2(cells):.1f} {exp(-248.7e6 / cells):.3f}")  # 31.1 0.899
The full edition’s script, linkage.py, computes every number in this chapter.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table, because the remaining quasi-identifiers, such as age, ZIP code and sex, single out most people. Between 1998 and 2008, researchers answered with definitions that constrain the released table itself. They are called syntactic because you can check each one by reading the published table.
Statistics offices, clinical data sharing under the HIPAA expert-determination route, and tools such as ARX and sdcMicro still use these definitions, so you will meet them in audits. The short answer to whether they are enough is that each is a property of one table against an adversary whose knowledge is fixed in advance. One unanticipated fact, or a second release, voids the guarantee.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
section: 16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
text:
16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
To anonymize a table, the custodian applies a generalization, which turns an age into a range, a ZIP code into a prefix, and so on. Records with the same generalized quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class, or class. An adversary who knows the target’s quasi-identifiers can find the target’s class \(E\), but the records in it look alike. So if it knows nothing else, its belief about the target’s sensitive value is the share of the class with that value.
Call that belief its posterior. Write \(\lvert E\rvert\) for the size of the class, and \(n_E(v)\) for the number of its records with a sensitive value \(v\). Then \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert} = P_E(v). \tag{16.1}\]
Background knowledge works by elimination. Ruling out a value crosses out its records, and the remaining shares grow, which is the calculation behind every attack in this chapter.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 k-anonymity and what it costs
Sweeney and Samarati proposed k-anonymity in 1998. A release is k-anonymous if every class has at least \(k\) records, for a crowd size \(k\) the custodian chooses. Generalizing gets there, with suppression of the records that still stand out. The linkage success of Linkage and re-identification is the number of classes \(J\) over the number of records \(n\), and it is then capped: \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.2}\] The guarantee is about names only, and it assumes the adversary knows the quasi-identifiers and nothing more. In sparse data every column is a quasi-identifier, so k-anonymity destroys a ratings matrix (Aggarwal, 2005).
What \(k\) to use is a policy choice that the mathematics does not settle, so data-sharing agreements fix it. What the mathematics does say is how coarse the quasi-identifiers must be. Counted in bits as in the linkage chapter, hiding 99% of people in classes of at least 2 allows about 9 bits fewer than making 99% unique.
Anonymizers search for a generalization that fits the data. For example, Mondrian keeps splitting groups of records at the median of one quasi-identifier, as long as both halves keep at least \(k\) records. Table 16.1 gives what each criterion costs on the full edition’s synthetic hospital table, where mean width is the average share of each quasi-identifier’s range that a class covers.

crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.4 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
Machanavajjhala and colleagues (2006) pointed out that k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to, but not what it says. If all three records of Alice’s class say heart disease, her posterior is 1 without anyone finding her record, which is the homogeneity attack. If Bob’s class says cancer, cancer and flu, a neighbour who knows he did not have flu learns he has cancer, which is the background knowledge attack. In the hospital table at \(k = 5\), 2.3% of patients sit in single-diagnosis classes.
l-diversity asks each class to hold enough different values. Its distinct version asks for at least \(\ell\) different values, and its entropy version asks for at least \(\log_2 \ell\) bits of entropy. Neither caps the share of the most common value, and a class over eight values can be entropy 3-diverse with one value in 73% of its records.
The recursive version targets background knowledge directly. Sort a class’s value counts from largest to smallest, and write \(r_1\) for the largest count and \(r_\ell\) for the \(\ell\)-th largest. A class is recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse, for a constant \(c\) the custodian picks, if \[r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + r_{\ell+1} + \dots). \tag{16.3}\] That condition caps the posterior even after the adversary rules out \(\ell - 2\) values: \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, \text{background}] < \frac{c}{1 + c}. \tag{16.4}\]
So l-diversity protects against certainty, not likelihood, since the cap is already one half at \(c = 1\). On the hospital table, distinct 3-diversity removes the certain disclosures at little cost, while recursive diversity forces some classes to hold hundreds of patients.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.5 Measuring what a release teaches
Compare every posterior with what the adversary would believe with no release, not with zero. The comparison is the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion, the most likely sensitive value given the target’s own quasi-identifiers under the population distribution. Only success beyond it is about the individual.
On the hospital table, guessing the most likely diagnosis for each patient’s age, with no release, is right for 53.6%, and a 5-anonymous release is right for 59.3%. So most of what the release teaches is the link between age and diagnosis, which any useful study would report, and only the excess of 0.057 is a leak.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian (2007) found two attacks that l-diversity misses. In the skewness attack, a class that is half HIV is 2-diverse, yet in a table with 1% HIV it raises its members’ posterior fifty-fold. In the similarity attack, a class of three stomach diseases is 3-diverse but reveals a stomach disease. t-closeness answers both. A release is t-close if every class’s distribution is within a distance \(t\) of the whole table’s.
With the total variation (TV) distance (Divergences), no belief moves by more than \(t\). Write \(P_E(A)\) and \(P(A)\) for the chance that a value from the class, or from the table, lands in a set \(A\). Then \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.5}\] The bound is additive, which protects rare values badly. A value held by 1% of the table may rise to 16% at \(t = 0.15\). Total variation also treats all diagnoses as equally different, so against the similarity attack Li and colleagues used the earth mover’s distance (EMD), under which similar values are close.
t-closeness also fights the purpose of the release, because at \(t = 0.15\) the hospital table’s guess accuracy falls far below what imputation from age achieves.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.7 The composition attack
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked what happens with two releases. Suppose that two hospitals in one city each publish a properly k-anonymous or \(\ell\)-diverse table, and a patient was treated at both. Write \(E_A\) and \(E_B\) for the patient’s classes in the two releases. The adversary keeps only the diagnoses that appear in both, \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}. \tag{16.6}\] When one candidate is left, the diagnosis is pinned down.
The full edition simulates two hospitals that each publish a 5-anonymous release. Together, the releases pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of their shared patients, more than three times what either pins alone. With distinct 3-diversity neither release pins anyone, yet together they still pin 18 patients.
No single-table definition can stop this, because the intersection of two tables is a table that neither custodian checked. A definition that survives must compose, hold whatever the adversary knows, and bound the ratio of beliefs to protect rare values. The definition of differential privacy starts from these requirements, and that is why regulators and the Census Bureau have moved towards it (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.8 Choosing and running an anonymization

Fix the quasi-identifiers with the risk check of Linkage and re-identification. Choosing them too narrowly is the commonest failure, since every column an adversary could know counts.
Choose the criteria. Use k-anonymity against linkage, add distinct l-diversity when a single-diagnosis class would be a disclosure, and use t-closeness only when the sensitive attribute is skewed or has similar values, since it costs the most.
Run the anonymizer. ARX, an open-source Java tool, takes a generalization hierarchy for each quasi-identifier, the privacy models above and a suppression limit, and searches for the generalization that loses the least information.
Audit the output yourself. In pandas, df.groupby(qi_cols)[sensitive].agg(["size", "nunique"]) gives each class’s size and number of distinct values, and the Code section computes entropy \(\ell\) and distance from the table. The Python package pycanon also reports \(k\), \(\ell\) and \(t\) for a table. Report guess accuracy next to the imputation baseline.
Move to differential privacy when overlapping views or other releases of the same people exist, when the sensitive attribute is rare, or when the data are sparse.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.9 Code
The snippet audits a 3-anonymous release and prints the smallest class size, the fewest distinct values, and each class’s entropy-equivalent \(\ell\) and distance from the table.
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from math import log2


def classes(rows: list[tuple[str, str, str]]) -> list[Counter[str]]:
    """Count the diagnoses in each class of (ZIP, age, diagnosis) rows."""
    groups: defaultdict[tuple[str, str], Counter[str]] = defaultdict(Counter)
    for zip_code, age, diagnosis in rows:
        groups[(zip_code, age)][diagnosis] += 1
    return list(groups.values())


def entropy_l(counts: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """The number of equally common values with the same entropy."""
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return 2 ** -sum(c / total * log2(c / total) for c in counts.values())


def tv_to_table(counts: Counter[str], table: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """Total variation between a class's distribution and the whole table's."""
    nc, nt = sum(counts.values()), sum(table.values())
    return sum(abs(counts[v] / nc - table[v] / nt) for v in table) / 2


rows = [
    ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"),
    ("148**", "4*", "cancer"), ("148**", "4*", "flu"), ("148**", "4*", "heart disease"),
    ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "flu"),
]
table = Counter(diagnosis for _, _, diagnosis in rows)
found = classes(rows)
print(min(sum(e.values()) for e in found))  # 3
print(min(len(e) for e in found))  # 1
print(" ".join(f"{entropy_l(e):.2f}" for e in found))  # 1.00 3.00 1.89
print(" ".join(f"{tv_to_table(e, table):.3f}" for e in found))  # 0.556 0.111 0.444
The full edition’s script, syntactic_anonymity.py, implements Mondrian and the attacks.

text:
16.10 Cheat sheet



Table 16.2: The syntactic definitions and the attacks on them.










Definition or attack
Condition
What it gives, and where it ends




k-anonymity
Every class has at least \(k\) records
Linkage at most \(1/k\); nothing about the sensitive attribute


Distinct, entropy l-diversity
At least \(\ell\) values, or entropy at least \(\log_2 \ell\)
No cap on the top value’s share


Recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diversity
\(r_1 < c(r_\ell + r_{\ell+1} + \dots)\)
Posterior below \(c/(1 + c)\) after ruling out \(\ell - 2\) values


t-closeness (TV)
Each class within \(t\) of the table
Every belief moves by at most \(t\), so a 1% value may reach \(1\% + t\)


Composition
Intersect the target’s classes in two releases
No single-table definition prevents it






Rules of thumb

k-anonymity protects names, not attributes, so check what each class’s sensitive values reveal.
Measure attribute disclosure against imputation from the population, or you will count the study’s findings as leaks.
A rare sensitive value needs a bound on the ratio of beliefs, not on their difference.
Assume another release exists, because a guarantee about one table is not a guarantee about a person.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.1 Why this matters
A hospital keeps one sensitive bit per patient, recording whether that patient tested positive. It only answers counting questions such as “how many of the patients on this list tested positive?”, with a little noise added to each answer. Dinur and Nissim (2003) showed that this is not safe unless the noise is large. Each answer is a linear equation in the patients’ bits, and enough equations with small enough errors determine the unknowns.
The protection can fail in two ways. The error can be too small, or there can be too many answers, because independent errors are averaged away as the attacker asks more. Dwork and Roth call this the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: overly accurate answers to too many questions destroy privacy. Any aggregate release must be checked against both.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.2 Counts are linear equations
Write the secret as a list of bits \(d = (d_1, \dots, d_n)\), one for each of \(n\) people. A subset-sum query names a set of people and asks how many of them have bit 1. The attacker’s \(m\) queries form a matrix \(A\) of zeros and ones, with one row per query and one column per person, so the true answers are \(Ad\).
The party that answers, the curator, publishes the answers with an error vector \(e\), \[a = Ad + e. \tag{17.1}\] Write \(E\) for a bound on the size of every error. The attacker is scored by the fraction of bits it recovers, against one half from guessing (Threat models and privacy games).

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.3 Exact and random queries: how much error is enough
text:
17.3 Exact and random queries: how much error is enough
An attacker who could ask all \(2^n\) subset sums would get at most \(4E\) bits wrong, whatever errors the curator chose. So a curator whose error is a vanishing fraction of \(n\) is blatantly non-private. A distortion the attacker can simulate, such as rounding to a multiple of 4, is not noise at all, because the attacker can round each candidate’s answers too.
Nobody can ask \(2^n\) questions, but random ones suffice. Each random query includes every person with probability one half. The Dinur–Nissim decoder solves a linear program, searching for fractional bits whose answers lie within \(E\) of the published ones, and then rounds. The price is that the error must now be well below \(\sqrt n\), not just below \(n\), because a random query picks up each wrong bit only half the time. A number of queries of order \(n \log n\) then suffices. The proved constants are pessimistic, and in practice least squares already works at errors of about \(0.2\sqrt n\) with \(4n\) queries.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.4 Least squares: the attack to run on your system
text:
17.4 Least squares: the attack to run on your system
Least squares needs no solver and no value of \(E\). It picks the vector whose answers come closest to the published ones in squared error, \[\hat x = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top a, \tag{17.2}\] and then clips and rounds each entry. Suppose the curator adds independent normal noise, and write \(\sigma\) for its standard deviation. A bit then comes out wrong when its error crosses one half, so write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The expected fraction of bits recovered is then about \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right). \tag{17.3}\]
Plug your system’s numbers into it. At a fixed number of queries per person only \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) matters, so \(\sqrt n\) is the scale of the threat, and recovery degrades smoothly rather than switching off at a threshold. On 500 people with 2000 queries, the prediction is within 0.013 of every simulated value in Table 17.1.



Table 17.1: Least-squares reconstruction of \(n = 500\) bits from \(m = 2000\) random subset sums with Gaussian noise.

The last column shows how a curator can look safe and still fail. With noise of twice \(\sqrt n\), four queries per person recover only 0.5875 of the bits. But if the curator answers any number of queries at that noise level, 106.1 queries per person are predicted to recover 90%. So the noise must grow like \(\sqrt m\) to hold the attack back.
Errors chosen against the decoder hurt more than random noise of the same size. Least squares amplifies errors most along the direction its queries see least clearly. A curator that pushed every error that way caused 143 wrong bits, where normal noise of the same size caused about 17. So test a system with errors aimed at the decoder, too.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.5 The Fundamental Law of Information Recovery
text:
17.5 The Fundamental Law of Information Recovery
Noise of order \(\sqrt n\) can stop reconstruction without giving privacy. A curator that answers from a secret random sample of half the people hides the others completely, yet enough queries reveal every sampled person’s bit exactly. The definition of differential privacy protects every individual instead.
Exact answers are also cheap to exploit. An exact count of up to \(n\) people carries at most \(\log_2(n + 1)\) bits. So any attack needs at least about \(n/\log_2(n + 1)\) counts to pin down the \(n\) bits, and least squares with exact answers needs only \(n\), close to that floor. Coarser answers carry fewer bits each, but they are no defence, because an attacker can simply ask more.
Weaker goals need far fewer aggregates. For example, a genome study’s published allele frequencies reveal whether a given person took part, as Homer and colleagues showed in 2008 (Lower bounds).

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.6 Attacking a deployed query system
In 2017 Aircloak offered a bounty for breaking Diffix, its commercial system for counting queries in a restricted form of SQL. Diffix added noise for each condition in a query, so the noise grew with the length of a query but not with the number of queries. The noise was sticky, so repeating a query gained nothing. Its language forbade OR, so naming an arbitrary subset took many noisy conditions.
Cohen and Nissim (2020) picked random short descriptions instead, and took whatever subset each one selected. A query multiplied a record’s public identifier by a prime, raised it to a fractional power, and kept the record when a chosen digit was divisible by 2 or 5. Diffix counted that as one condition, so each query carried little noise. On a real banking dataset, 3,500 such queries recovered every secret bit, with reported noise of standard deviation 4.
Least squares predicts this in advance. Write \(\rho\) for the fraction of records a query includes, and \(v\) for the average of \(\rho(1 - \rho)\) over the queries. From \(m\) queries, least squares then recovers about \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{v\,(m - n - 1)}}{2\sigma}\right) \tag{17.4}\] of the \(n\) bits. For the smallest range in the attack, of 73 records, the prediction is near-total recovery. Holding the attack to 75% would have needed noise 4.9 times larger. The lesson applies to any system, because many distinct queries average away noise that is fixed per query. A restricted language does not help either, since any short formula that splits records independently of their secrets acts as a random query.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.7 Reconstructing a census block
Each cell of a published table is a query. Garfinkel, Abowd and Martindale (2019) showed that a constraint solver rebuilds a census block from its statistics in seconds. The full edition repeats this with a fictional block of seven people. For six groups of them it publishes a count, a median age and a mean age, and means to two decimals give exact sums of ages.
A decoder lists candidate blocks and discards each one that contradicts a published number, and exactly one block survives. So eighteen numbers determine the age, sex, race and marital status of all seven people.
Real publications are more exposed, because the same people appear in thousands of overlapping cells. The usual protections also leave most constraints exact. For example, swapping changes a few households and leaves the rest, while coarsening and suppression remove some constraints but keep the others. A suppressed cell even adds an inequality, because it says the count is below the threshold.
The Census Bureau ran this attack on its own 2010 publications. It rebuilt a record for every person counted, and about 46% of the records matched a real person exactly on block, sex, age, race and ethnicity. Linking the records to commercial data then confirmed the identity of about 17% of the population. So the Bureau moved the 2020 Census to differential privacy, using its TopDown algorithm, and published the source code of its disclosure avoidance system.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.8 Auditing an aggregate release

Count the equations. If the published cells or allowed queries outnumber the people, reconstruction is possible in principle.
Classify the error. Rounding, swapping and suppression are not noise, because the attacker can simulate them or work around them. Fresh noise per answer is averaged away, and sticky noise only stops repeats, while restricting or auditing the allowed queries fails because ordinary-looking formulas act as random queries. Only noise calibrated to a budget over all answers holds up.
Predict least squares. Plug the noise and the number of queries into Equation 17.3 or Equation 17.4. A prediction far above one half means the system leaks.
Run the attack. For noisy counts, solve with numpy’s np.linalg.lstsq, as below, or pose the linear program with SciPy’s scipy.optimize.linprog, bounding each unknown between 0 and 1. For tables of counts, medians and means, write each cell as a constraint on whole-number unknowns. Then solve the integer program with SciPy’s scipy.optimize.milp, PuLP or Gurobi, and count the solutions.
Fix it with a budget. If the attack works, move to noise that grows with the number of answers, which is what differential privacy provides.

A = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 2, size=(m, n))   # random subset-sum queries
x = np.linalg.lstsq(A, answers(A), rcond=None)[0]           # least-squares estimate
recovered = np.mean(np.clip(x, 0, 1).round() == d)          # against a test secret d

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.9 Code
The functions below predict least-squares recovery at your noise level and the queries per person that reach a target.
from math import sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

PHI = NormalDist()


def ls_recovered(n: int, m: int, sigma: float) -> float:
    """Predicted fraction of n secret bits that least squares recovers from m noisy random subset sums."""
    sd = 2 * sigma * sqrt(n / ((n + 1) * (m - n - 1)))  # spread of each decoded bit's error
    return PHI.cdf(0.5 / sd)  # a bit comes out wrong when its error crosses 1/2


def queries_per_person(target: float, sigma_over_sqrt_n: float) -> float:
    """m/n at which least squares recovers a fraction `target` of the bits, for noise sigma = c * sqrt(n)."""
    return 1 + (4 * sigma_over_sqrt_n * PHI.inv_cdf(target)) ** 2



n, m = 500, 2000
print(" ".join(f"{ls_recovered(n, m, c * sqrt(n)):.4f}" for c in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)))  # 1.0000 0.9585 0.8069 0.6676 0.5858
print(f"{queries_per_person(0.9, 2.0):.1f}")  # 106.1
The full edition’s script, reconstruction.py, runs the attacks themselves.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
The previous part showed that anonymization and access control do not stop releases from leaking. This part introduces differential privacy (DP), the defence the rest of the book builds on. It is a property of the release process, not of a dataset. Changing one person’s data may change the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), set by a privacy level \(\varepsilon\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). That one condition caps every attack of Part 2. So every DP claim must state three things, namely \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and the unit of privacy, such as a record, a user or a user-day.



Table 1: Notation used throughout Part 3.









Symbol
Meaning




\(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\)
Privacy level and slack


\(\Delta_1f\), \(\Delta_2f\)
Sensitivity, the most one record moves the answer


\(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\)
Laplace noise of scale \(b\), normal noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\)






The part teaches one workflow. First fix the unit of privacy and the neighbouring relation, as The definition of differential privacy explains. Then clip the data, bound its sensitivity and calibrate a mechanism to it (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Next, account for every release (Post-processing, group privacy and composition and Advanced and optimal composition). Finally, post-process the outputs freely, since that costs nothing.
You need those four core chapters to ship a private statistic, while the next ones are per task. Selection picks the best of many options. Query release answers many queries through a synthetic dataset and Beyond global sensitivity handles data whose worst case is far from typical. Read Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms before sampling noise yourself, and Local, shuffle and distributed trust models when nobody can be trusted with the raw data. The last two chapters help you size a study. Lower bounds says when an accuracy is impossible at your \(\varepsilon\), and Private mean estimation says how many records a private mean needs.
The full edition proves every result, and this edition shows how to use them. Part 4 then replaces hand composition with accountants, and Part 5 applies all of it to training models. The tools used from here on are OpenDP, Tumult Analytics, diffprivlib, Google’s dp_accounting and Opacus.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.1 Why this matters
Every attack in Threat models and attacks runs an algorithm on one of two datasets that differ in one person, and guesses from the output which one was used. Differential privacy (DP) makes the two outputs look alike against every test, including tests nobody has invented yet. It is a property of the algorithm, not of the data, so you can check it before any data are touched. This chapter teaches you to read a privacy claim, which means knowing what it protects, what it promises and what it leaves out.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.2 Neighbouring datasets
The first question about any claim is what “differ in one record” means, and the neighbouring relation answers it. Under add/remove, two datasets are neighbours when one is the other with one record added or taken away. The guarantee then hides whether a person is in the data at all. Under replace, the two datasets have the same size and differ in the value of one record, so only what the record says is hidden. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition, so a guarantee at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) converts as \[\varepsilon\text{-DP under add/remove} \implies 2\varepsilon\text{-DP under replace}. \tag{18.1}\] The reverse fails, since only add/remove hides how many records there are.
You also choose the unit of privacy, what one record is. At the example level, it is one training example or one event, and at the user level, all the data of one person. Under example-level DP, a user who wrote 200 messages is a group of 200 records. The guarantee weakens quickly with the size of a group (Post-processing, group privacy and composition), so check that the claim protects the person. The guarantee must also hide every record the data format allows, even a person aged 900, which is why private algorithms clip their inputs before adding noise.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.3 The definition
Call a randomized algorithm that takes a dataset and returns an output a mechanism, written \(M\). Write \(D\) for a dataset and \(D'\) for one of its neighbours. The definition asks that no set of outputs become much more likely when one record changes. It measures “much more likely” by a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), for a non-negative privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\), and allows a small additive slack \(\delta\) on top. A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{18.2}\] The probabilities come only from the mechanism’s own randomness, with the data held fixed.
When \(\delta = 0\) the guarantee is called pure DP, and otherwise approximate DP. One consequence matters in practice. A private mechanism must be random, because a deterministic one gives some output that has probability 0 on a neighbour. So rounding, aggregating or suppressing small cells gives no guarantee by itself, however coarse the result looks.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.4 The privacy loss and δ
For an output \(y\), write \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) for its probability, or its density, when the mechanism runs on \(D\). The privacy loss of \(y\) is the logarithm of how much more likely the output is on \(D\) than on \(D'\), \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{18.3}\] A loss of 0 means that the output says nothing about which dataset was used. Independent outputs multiply their likelihood ratios, so their losses add, which is why the accountants of Part 4 work with the loss. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP is exactly the condition that every output has a loss between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise meets it, while the loss of Gaussian noise grows without limit in the far tail (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
Under approximate DP, \(\delta\) covers the outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\). It counts each one only by how far its probability on \(D\) goes beyond the ratio bound. This weighted total is called the hockey-stick divergence. So \(\delta\) is not the chance that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), which is a valid but often loose choice. Take a count with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Its loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability \(4.006\times10^{-2}\). The exact \(\delta\) is \(6.830\times10^{-3}\), less than a sixth of that.
Each \(\varepsilon\) has its own smallest \(\delta\), and the function \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the mechanism’s privacy curve. A quoted pair is one point on it, so report the noise parameters with the pair, and others can recompute the whole curve. Numerical accounting computes these curves from the distribution of the loss.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.5 Randomized response
The first private mechanism comes from survey design (Warner, 1965). Each person tells the truth with some probability \(t\) a little above one half, and lies otherwise, so a single answer proves nothing about them. A person who answers truthfully on heads, and with a second coin toss on tails, tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\), which gives pure DP at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). In general, randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \[t = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{18.4}\]
The guarantee is \(\varepsilon\) per person however many people answer, provided their coins are independent, but only under replace. Write \(\bar y\) for the share of “yes” reports among the \(n\) people. The estimate of the true fraction and its standard deviation are \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n}, \tag{18.5}\] which is about \(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\) for small \(\varepsilon\). For 1,000 people, the two-coin scheme gives 0.0274, about twice the sampling error that the survey already has. That is the price of the local model, in which nobody sees a true answer (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models). diffprivlib implements the mechanism as mechanisms.Binary.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.6 What ε means for an attacker
text:
18.6 What ε means for an attacker
A membership attacker looks at the output and decides whether to accuse the target of being in the data, so it has two error rates (Hypothesis testing). Its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it accuses a target who is out. Its true positive rate (TPR) is how often it accuses one who is in. The outputs on which it accuses form a set, which the definition bounds. So under add/remove, every attack at every FPR satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{18.6}\]
This is the form to use, because Part 2 judged attacks by their TPR at a low FPR. For example, take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Then at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no attack reaches a TPR above 0.002728. As the FPR falls towards 0, the \(\delta\) term takes over, so at a very low FPR the guarantee rests almost entirely on \(\delta\).
Read backwards, the cap turns an attack into an audit. Measure an attack’s FPR and TPR, and solve the cap for the smallest \(\varepsilon\) consistent with them, \[\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{18.7}\] Suppose a model is claimed to be \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and an attack reaches a TPR of 0.05 at an FPR of 0.001. If those rates are exact, \(\varepsilon\) is at least 3.91, so the claim is false. Audits plant a canary, a record built to be as easy to detect as possible, because the guarantee must hold for the worst record (Memorization and extraction).
Two summaries are easier to explain to a lawyer or an auditor. The membership advantage, the TPR minus the FPR, says how much better than a coin flip an attacker does. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP it is at most \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \tag{18.8}\] which is the hyperbolic tangent of \(\varepsilon/2\) when \(\delta = 0\). The posterior bound speaks about beliefs. One output can multiply an adversary’s odds between two neighbours by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), whatever it believed before. So a prior belief \(\pi\) that the data are \(D\) rises at most to \[\Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon\pi}{e^\varepsilon\pi + 1 - \pi}. \tag{18.9}\] Table 18.1 turns a claimed \(\varepsilon\) into both numbers.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.7 How small δ must be
A small \(\delta\) barely moves the advantage bound, but the advantage is an average that hides harm to a few people. For example, take a mechanism that publishes each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). Under add/remove it is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, because a record changes the output only when its own coin publishes it. Yet over \(n\) records it publishes at least one with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{18.10}\] With 10,000 records and \(\delta = 1/n\), someone’s full record is published with probability 0.6321.
Treat \(\delta\) as a per-person budget for catastrophe. Choose it well below \(1/n\), for example \(1/n^{1.5}\), and let \(n\) count people rather than records.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.8 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
18.8 What differential privacy does not protect
DP compares a world with your record and a world without it, so anything that can be learned in both worlds is outside the guarantee. A study that never used Alice’s record may show that smokers get cancer at a high rate. That changes what anyone believes about Alice, a smoker, yet the study is 0-DP with respect to her. Correlated records are a second gap. A household of five that always answers alike is protected only at five times the per-record \(\varepsilon\), unless the household is the unit of privacy. The third gap is the implementation, which needs its own review (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
When someone reports a privacy violation, ask three questions. Would the inference come out materially different without the person’s record? Does it succeed exactly when the model is accurate? And when, and by whom, was the revealing information given up? Only the first decides. If the answer is no, as when public “likes” predict someone’s politics, it is not a violation in the DP sense, even when it causes harm. A language model that completes a prompt with one user’s identification number does fail it, because a model trained without her messages would not.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Why this matters
A private mechanism is never the whole system. Its output gets rounded, plotted or fed into a model, the people in your data may each own many records, and an analyst rarely asks only one question. So you need to know what guarantee holds for what you actually publish in each case, without writing a new proof for every pipeline.
Three properties of differential privacy (DP) give that answer. The first, post-processing, says that anything computed from a private output without reading the data again is free. The second, group privacy, says what a guarantee about one record promises for a person who owns several. And composition says that running several mechanisms on the same data costs at most the sum of their budgets. Together they turn privacy into bookkeeping, because you can prove each building block once and then keep a ledger of what you spend.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.2 Post-processing
Take a private mechanism, written \(M\). Write \(\varepsilon\) for its privacy level and \(\delta\) for its slack, so that it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Apply to its output any function \(f\), which may use random coins of its own but never reads the data. Then the processed release is just as private, \[f(M(D)) \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.1}\] Processing can merge outputs that point in different directions, and so it can lower the privacy loss, but it can never raise it.
This is what makes DP practical. Rounding a noisy count, clamping it at zero, or making noisy totals consistent with their parts costs no extra budget. A model trained on private synthetic data, a plot and a dashboard all inherit the guarantee with no further proof too. So a private system adds noise at one narrow point, such as noisy counts or noisy gradients, and treats everything after it as public. The same rule covers attackers. A membership-inference attack is a function of the output, so the attack cap of the definition holds even for attacks invented after the release.
The condition is that \(f\) never reads the data. “Take the noisy top category, then report its exact count” breaks it, because the second step is a new and non-private mechanism. So does “publish the noisy count, unless the true count is 0”, which peeks at the raw data to decide. A finer histogram computed after an odd bin catches your eye is a second mechanism too, whose cost adds by composition.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.3 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but a user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages. If the guarantee is per record and a person owns \(k\) records, you need a guarantee for datasets that differ in \(k\) records. For pure DP, the losses of the \(k\) steps from one dataset to the other add up, so \(\varepsilon\)-DP per record becomes \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for the group. With a slack, each step also adds its own \(\delta\), and every later step multiplies the earlier ones by \(e^\varepsilon\). For a group of \(k\) records, an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \[\Big(k\varepsilon,\ \delta_k\Big)\text{-DP}, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{19.2}\] The simpler form on the right is looser, so compute the sum when you can.
The price is steep. A user with 50 rows under a row-level guarantee of \(\varepsilon\) is protected only at \(50\varepsilon\). The slack grows even faster, because \(\delta\) is multiplied by 12818.3 for a group of 10 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record. That hurts, since \(\delta\) was already chosen much smaller than one over the number of records. For example, a guarantee of \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) per record becomes \((5, 2.272\times10^{-3})\) for a user with 10 records.
So if you care about people, don’t patch a per-record guarantee with group privacy. Define neighbours as datasets that differ in one person’s records, and bound each person’s contribution, for example by capping how many records a user may add. Then prove DP at that level directly. Group privacy is the fallback for when you cannot, and for correlated records such as households.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Sequential composition
An analyst asks several queries of the same data, each answered with fresh noise, and an adversary sees all the answers together. Write \(M_i\) for the \(i\)-th of \(k\) mechanisms and \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) for its budget. Releasing all their outputs is then \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.3}\] This is basic composition. It holds because independent outputs have independent noise, so their privacy losses add. It needs every mechanism to use fresh coins and the same neighbouring relation.
The rule also covers adaptive composition, where each query is chosen after reading the earlier answers, as long as each budget is fixed in advance. For example, an eleventh query that runs only if the first ten look interesting is covered, provided its budget was fixed beforehand. Budgets chosen from the answers, as in “keep going until the estimate looks good”, are another matter. They need a privacy filter, a rule that decides when to stop as the budget is spent (Adaptive composition). Pure DP with basic composition is the exception, since stopping before a fixed total is exceeded is always safe there.
Basic composition is loose for many releases. Ten Gaussian counts at \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) each cost an exact \(\varepsilon\) of 1.504, where basic composition charges 5. So use the accountants of Advanced and optimal composition and Part 4 once releases number more than a handful.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.5 Parallel composition
A histogram counts people in disjoint bins, and per-region statistics use disjoint subsets of the data. If you split the data by region, each region can spend the full budget, because one person’s record falls in one region only. Split the possible records into disjoint parts by a public rule fixed in advance, so that each person lands in exactly one part. Then run a mechanism \(M_i\) with independent coins on the records in the \(i\)-th part. If each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove, the whole release is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{19.4}\]
This is why a histogram costs one \(\varepsilon\), not one per bin. With Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on every bin, the histogram is \(\varepsilon\)-DP however many bins it has. Under replace, a record can move from one bin to another, so two bins change and the cost doubles to \(2\varepsilon\). The cost goes back to the maximum when each part is a fixed slot that belongs to one person, as in local randomized response.
The rule fixed in advance is the condition that is easiest to break. A split into “the top 10% of earners and the rest” moves its boundary when one high earner is added, so records cross it and both parts change. The same goes for partitioning on the list of keys that happen to appear in the data, because the list itself reveals who is present. Use fixed bins or a public key list, or treat a data-dependent split as a mechanism of its own.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.6 Keeping a budget
Fix a total budget for a dataset before the first release, and charge every release against it. Suppose a dashboard over one patient table has a total of \((1, 10^{-5})\). A histogram of 20 diagnoses with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) on every bin costs only 0.5, by parallel composition. A mean age, released as a noisy sum and a noisy count at 0.125 each, costs 0.25 by sequential composition. A set of Gaussian counts at \((0.25, 10^{-5})\) uses the rest. Any further query must then be refused, or paid for from a new budget, and the snippet in Section 19.7 keeps exactly this ledger. Libraries keep the same ledger. OpenDP’s Context.compositor takes a total budget and a number of queries. Its context.query() then charges each one. diffprivlib’s BudgetAccountant tracks spending across its mechanisms, and Tumult Analytics sessions hold a total budget and evaluate each query against it.
Most real failures break a condition of the three properties, and the damage is usually total rather than a small loss. Table 19.1 lists the common cases.

Each release alone is 1-DP, but their difference cancels the noise and gives the exact number of smokers under 40, so the pair is not DP at all. In code, the bug hides in two mechanisms seeded with the same random seed and in a cached noise value re-added to a related query. It also hides in noise reused across the shards of a distributed system. Returning the same noisy answer to a repeated identical query is fine, because that is post-processing of one release.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.7 Code
The ledger below charges each release against a total fixed in advance, and refuses any release that would exceed it. It also computes group privacy, where hand calculations go wrong most often.
from math import exp


def group_privacy(eps: float, delta: float, k: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The guarantee for a group of k records, from an (eps, delta) guarantee per record."""
    return k * eps, delta * sum(exp(j * eps) for j in range(k))


class Ledger:
    """Basic composition for releases from one dataset, with a total fixed in advance."""

    def __init__(self, eps_total: float, delta_total: float) -> None:
        self.eps_total, self.delta_total = eps_total, delta_total
        self.eps_spent, self.delta_spent = 0.0, 0.0

    def charge(self, name: str, eps: float, delta: float = 0.0) -> None:
        if self.eps_spent + eps > self.eps_total or self.delta_spent + delta > self.delta_total:
            raise ValueError(f"{name}: over budget")
        self.eps_spent += eps
        self.delta_spent += delta

    def charge_parallel(self, name: str, budgets: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> None:
        """Mechanisms on disjoint parts of the data, under add/remove, cost the largest budget."""
        self.charge(name, max(e for e, _ in budgets), max(d for _, d in budgets))


ledger = Ledger(1.0, 1e-5)
ledger.charge_parallel("histogram, 20 bins", [(0.5, 0.0)] * 20)
ledger.charge("noisy sum", 0.125)
ledger.charge("noisy count", 0.125)
ledger.charge("Gaussian counts", 0.25, 1e-5)
print(ledger.eps_spent, ledger.delta_spent)  # 1.0 1e-05
try:
    ledger.charge("one more count", 0.1)
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)  # one more count: over budget
eps_k, delta_k = group_privacy(0.5, 1e-5, 10)
print(f"{eps_k:.1f} {delta_k:.3e}")  # 5.0 2.272e-03
print(f"{group_privacy(1.0, 1.0, 10)[1]:.1f}")  # 12818.3

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.1 Why this matters
Suppose you run a hospital database and want to publish how many patients have diabetes with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. The two mechanisms of this chapter are how almost every such release is built, up to the noisy gradients of private model training.
Both compute the exact answer of a query \(f\) on the dataset \(D\). They then add fresh random noise, written \(Z\), so that the mechanism publishes \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{20.1}\] Three decisions fix the whole mechanism. The sensitivity, how far one record can move the answer, sets the scale of the noise. The noise distribution sets the kind of guarantee, since Laplace noise gives pure DP while Gaussian noise needs a small slack \(\delta\). And a calibration formula sets the exact amount, through the privacy loss of The definition of differential privacy.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.2 Sensitivity
The noise must cover the largest change that one record can make to the answer. A query often returns a vector of \(d\) numbers, such as the bins of a histogram, so you need a size for a change to a vector. Laplace noise uses the \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of the absolute changes. Gaussian noise uses the \(\ell_2\) norm, the square root of the sum of the squared changes. Writing \(D \simeq D'\) for a pair of neighbours, the \(\ell_p\) sensitivity of the query is the largest change between their answers, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \simeq D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p, \qquad p \in \{1, 2\}. \tag{20.2}\] The two are never far apart, since \[\Delta_2f \le \Delta_1f \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2f. \tag{20.3}\] They are equal when one record moves a single coordinate.
The sensitivity also depends on the neighbouring relation. Under add/remove one dataset has one record more than the other, and under replace one record is swapped for another, so the size \(n\) is public. Write \(B\) for the largest value a record may take after clipping. Table 20.1 then gives the standard queries.

Compute the sensitivity from the domain, before you look at the data. A sensitivity read off the data, for example from the largest value present, makes the noise itself leak that value (Beyond global sensitivity). For unbounded data the sensitivity is infinite, so clip every value to a fixed range first. For example, take the mean age of 1,000 patients, with ages clipped to at most 100. Under replace its sensitivity is 0.1, since no patient can move the mean by more than a tenth of a year.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.3 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism (Dwork et al., 2006) adds independent noise from the Laplace distribution to each coordinate, a two-sided exponential peaked at 0. Its scale, written \(b\), sets its typical size. To be \(\varepsilon\)-DP at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\), the mechanism sets the scale to \[b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}. \tag{20.4}\]
The error of the mechanism is the noise itself. Each coordinate is off by \(b\) on average, and lands more than a distance \(t\) from the truth with probability \(e^{-t/b}\). To bound all \(d\) coordinates at once, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\), give each coordinate a share \(\beta/d\) of it. The width that results is \[\Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{20.5}\] Publish this width with the release, and read it backwards as an error budget. Fix a target width \(t\) for one number and solve for the privacy level, which gives \[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta_1f\,\ln(1/\beta)}{t}. \tag{20.6}\] For example, a count that must be within 10 of the truth, with probability 0.95, needs an \(\varepsilon\) of 0.2996.
At the hospital, 1,234 of the 10,000 patients have diabetes. A count has sensitivity 1 under add/remove, so at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\). Its 95% error bar is 29.96, a relative error of 0.0243.
The scale does not contain the size of the data, so the relative error of a count of size \(n\) is about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\). But the sensitivity must include every number one record can move. If one record can change all of 10 released counts, noise calibrated for one count gives only \(10\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.4 The Gaussian mechanism
The Gaussian mechanism adds independent normal noise with mean 0 to each coordinate, with a standard deviation written \(\sigma\). Its privacy loss is unbounded in the far tail, so it always carries a \(\delta\). In exchange, it is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) one. Only the ratio of the sensitivity to the noise matters, so write \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) for the number of noise standard deviations between the answers on two neighbours. Write \(\Phi\) for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution. The mechanism is then \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{20.7}\]
The formula is how you calibrate. As \(\mu\) grows, \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) rises steadily from 0 to 1, so exactly one value \(\mu^*\) hits your target \(\delta\). The smallest noise that works is then \[\sigma^* = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*}, \qquad \text{where } \delta_{\mu^*}(\varepsilon) = \delta, \tag{20.8}\] and bisection finds \(\mu^*\) in a few lines (Section 20.7). At the common setting of \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), this analytic calibration gives \(\sigma^* = 3.7306\,\Delta_2f\).
Many papers and libraries still use the classic calibration of Dwork and Roth (2014). For \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) both between 0 and 1, it sets \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{20.9}\] Table 20.2 compares the two at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

A Gaussian mechanism satisfies a whole curve of guarantees, one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\), and the accountants of Part 4 compose whole curves. So report \(\sigma/\Delta_2f\) with every Gaussian release, as well as the pair you chose. Accountants that work in zero-concentrated DP take the equivalent \(\rho = \Delta_2f^2/(2\sigma^2)\) (Concentrated differential privacy).
For the diabetes count at the same \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the 95% error bar is 1.96 standard deviations, or 60.27. Laplace noise gave 29.96 with no \(\delta\) at all, so for a single count it wins twice.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.5 Laplace or Gaussian?
The choice depends on how one record spreads its change across the coordinates, as the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of each released number shows. Write \(\sigma_1\) for the analytic noise level at unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. At the same \(\varepsilon\), the errors per coordinate are then \[\text{Laplace: } \frac{\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{Gaussian: } \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1. \tag{20.10}\]
In a sparse query, such as a histogram under add/remove, one record moves one coordinate. The two sensitivities are then equal, so at the common setting Laplace noise wins at every \(d\). In a dense query, by contrast, one record moves every coordinate. The Laplace error then grows like \(d\) while the Gaussian error grows only like \(\sqrt d\), so Laplace noise is more accurate only while \[d < \frac{(\varepsilon\sigma_1)^2}2. \tag{20.11}\] At the common setting, the unit noise level is 3.7306, so for threshold counts Gaussian noise wins from 7 counts on.
Gaussian noise also wins when releases are composed many times. Several Gaussian releases compose exactly into one Gaussian mechanism, whose \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is the square root of the sum of the squared sensitivities. Private training needs both advantages. One example’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model, so private training clips each gradient’s \(\ell_2\) norm and calibrates Gaussian noise to that clip.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.6 Calibrating a release
Every noisy release takes five steps.

Fix the neighbouring relation and the unit of privacy, usually one person under add/remove.
Clip every value to a range fixed in advance, and read the sensitivity off Table 20.1 or work it out from the worst record.
Choose Laplace noise for one number or a sparse vector, and Gaussian noise for a dense vector.
Set the scale with Equation 20.4 or Equation 20.7, and charge it to your budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Draw the noise with a vetted library, and publish the error bar and the noise parameters with the result.

A mean under add/remove has no simple sensitivity, because its denominator moves too. Release instead a noisy sum and a noisy count, each with half of the budget, and divide one by the other. Dividing is post-processing, so it costs nothing more. When you do not know the range to clip to, Private mean estimation shows how to find it privately.
In OpenDP, dp.t.make_clamp and dp.t.make_sum build the clipped query, and dp.m.make_laplace or dp.m.make_gaussian adds noise of a given scale. Its dp.binary_search_param then finds the scale for a target \(\varepsilon\). IBM’s diffprivlib has mechanisms.Laplace and mechanisms.GaussianAnalytic, whose .randomise(x) adds the noise, and tools.mean(x, epsilon=..., bounds=...) for a clipped mean. Plain numpy.random.laplace is for prototypes only, because textbook floating-point samplers can leak through the low-order bits of their output (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.1 Why this matters
A differentially private system rarely answers just one query. A dashboard refreshes a hundred counts, and a training run takes thousands of noisy gradient steps. Each step on its own satisfies differential privacy (DP), with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\), as in The definition of differential privacy. But what you report, and what you calibrate the noise to, is one guarantee for the whole run.
Post-processing, group privacy and composition gave the first answer, basic composition, which adds up the \(\varepsilon\) of the steps. A hundred queries at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) then cost 10. Yet if you allow the whole run a slack of \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the same hundred queries are \((4.31, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The gap exists because the privacy losses of the steps add up, and each loss is a random amount. Over \(k\) steps their total has a mean of only about \(k\varepsilon^2/2\) and a spread of about \(\sqrt k\,\varepsilon\), so it almost never reaches its maximum \(k\varepsilon\).

text:

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.3 Basic and advanced composition
Basic composition says that \(k\) steps that are each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP are together \((k\varepsilon, k\delta)\)-DP. It is the only rule that keeps \(\delta = 0\).
Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010) trades a little slack for a much smaller \(\varepsilon\). Pick an extra slack \(\delta'\) for the whole run. Then \(k\) steps that are each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP are together \((\varepsilon', k\delta + \delta')\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{21.1}\] The first term is the spread of the total privacy loss, and the second is its average, the drift. The original theorem has \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) in place of \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), which is about twice as large. Use the \(\tanh\) form. The original form is useless for large steps. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) per step its drift alone is \(1.7183k\), more than basic composition’s total \(k\).
For the hundred queries, the spread term is 4.80 and the drift adds 0.50, which gives 5.30. Advanced composition only helps once \(\sqrt k\) outgrows the factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the original form beats basic composition only from \(k = 29\) steps on (Table 21.2).
