title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
28.1 Why this matters
The mean is the statistic that private machine learning computes most often. Every step of private gradient descent clips per-example gradients, averages them and adds noise, and even a survey share is a mean of 0/1 answers. But what an analyst wants is usually the mean of the population the records came from. So the planning questions are how many records a private estimate needs, and how to choose a clipping range without looking at the data.
Differential privacy (DP) must hold for every dataset, including datasets your assumptions say cannot happen (The definition of differential privacy). So an assumption about the data, such as “the records are normal”, may make a mechanism more accurate, but it must never enter the privacy argument. Every mechanism below clips the data to a range, which keeps it private whatever the data are. Its noise is proportional to the width of that range, and the recipe of the chapter follows from it. Spend a small part of the budget finding where the data are, then clip there and spend the rest on the mean.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
section: 28.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
text:
28.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
Throughout the chapter, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and neighbours differ in one replaced record. An estimate is judged by its root-mean-square error (RMSE), the typical distance between the estimate and the population mean.
Start with records in a known interval, such as yes/no answers coded 0 and 1. Write \(w\) for the width of the interval and \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of a record. Release the average plus Laplace noise with scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\), which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record moves the average by at most \(w/n\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The RMSE then combines the sampling error and the noise: \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{28.1}\] To plan a study, set the RMSE equal to a target error \(\alpha\) and solve for \(n\). The snippet in the Code section does this exactly, and a simple upper bound is \[n \le \frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\sqrt2\,w}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{28.2}\]
So sampling needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2\) records whatever you do, and privacy adds at most about \(w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) more. For a yes/no survey in the worst case for sampling, a population that is half yes, an RMSE of 0.05 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs 108 people instead of 100.
But the privacy term grows like \(1/\varepsilon\), so it dominates at strong privacy and a coarse target. It also grows with the width \(w\), the most one record can move, which is why the rest of the chapter is about making the range narrow.
Report the error in its three parts, which are sampling, the bias that clipping causes and the noise. With a public range that holds every record the bias is zero. But the later sections clip into the data, and a confidence interval that ignores that bias is too narrow. The formulas also treat \(n\) as public, which holds when neighbours replace a record. If the dataset size is itself private, release a noisy sum and a noisy count and divide, with the budget split between them.
Libraries follow this pattern. In diffprivlib, tools.mean(x, epsilon=..., bounds=(lower, upper)) clips to the bounds and adds noise, and tools.var and tools.quantile do the same for variances and quantiles. If you leave out bounds, it computes them from the data and raises a PrivacyLeakWarning, because a range read off the observed minimum and maximum leaks them. Tumult Analytics’ QueryBuilder takes the bounds as arguments of average(column, low, high), and OpenDP likewise makes you declare the clamping bounds and the dataset size before it builds a mean.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
section: 28.3 The cost of an unknown range
text:
28.3 The cost of an unknown range
Now let the records be normal with variance 1, with a mean known only to lie between \(-R\) and \(R\). Normal records rarely stray far from their mean. For 1,000 records, all of them lie within a distance \(\tau\) of 4.604, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\) of 0.05.
The naive estimator clips every record to the widest place the data could be, \(R + \tau\) on either side of zero, and adds Laplace noise for that width. It is private, but its error grows in step with \(R\). With 1,000 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and a range of a million, its RMSE of 2828.44 is useless. That is the price of a clumsy mechanism, because Lower bounds shows that privacy forces a cost of only about \(\ln R/\varepsilon\) records for the range.
Coarse then fine (Karwa & Vadhan 2018) comes close to that floor. In the coarse step, cut the range into bins of width \(2\tau\), so that the records fill at most two bins. Pick one bin with the exponential mechanism, scoring each bin by the number of records in it, and spend part of the budget, \(\varepsilon_1\), on it. The fine step then clips every record to the chosen bin and its two neighbours, and it releases their average with Laplace noise for that window.
The fine step spends the rest of the budget, so the two steps together are \(\varepsilon\)-DP by composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Whether the result is accurate depends on the coarse step. Write \(m\) for the number of bins. Then the coarse step picks a full bin, except with probability \(\beta\), once \[n \ge \frac{4\ln(m/\beta)}{\varepsilon_1}. \tag{28.3}\] After that, the fine step’s error does not depend on \(R\) at all. With a quarter of the budget on the coarse step, the full edition’s 1,000 records give an RMSE of 0.0609 whether \(R\) is 10 or a million.
So choose by what you know. When the range is already narrow, the naive estimator wins, and with 1,000 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the crossover is at \(R = 13.81\). Beyond it, use coarse then fine. A private quantile, such as diffprivlib’s tools.quantile, can also do the locating. If you can accept approximate DP, with its small slack \(\delta\), you can drop \(R\) altogether. A stability-based histogram does the coarse step with about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records whatever the range (Beyond global sensitivity).
Two things go wrong. A budget split, bin width or \(\beta\) chosen after looking at the data leaks it. And a coarse step with too few records can pick an empty bin, so the fine step clips everything to the wrong place.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
28.4 Many dimensions: clip the norm
Vectors in \(d\) dimensions, such as embeddings or gradients, follow the same recipe with a different measure of size. Clip each record’s \(\ell_2\) norm, its length, to a radius \(C\), so that one replaced record moves the average by at most \(2C/n\). Then add Gaussian noise calibrated to that sensitivity (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). This is exactly the step of private gradient descent, which clips per-example gradients to a fixed norm (private training). With the radius close to the spread of the data, an error \(\alpha\) needs about \[n \approx \frac{d}{\alpha^2} + \frac{d\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}}{\alpha\varepsilon} \tag{28.4}\] records, and the fingerprinting lower bound shows that the privacy term cannot be avoided.
When you do not know where the mean is, the range problem returns, and a grid of bins would cost records in proportion to \(d\). The shrinking balls of CoinPress (Biswas, Dong, Kamath & Ullman 2020) avoid the grid. Over a few rounds, they clip to a ball around the current guess, release a noisy average and shrink the ball, for about \(\sqrt d\ln R/\varepsilon\) extra records. On 100,000 records in a thousand dimensions, the full edition’s script finds an RMSE of 0.1736 against 0.1000 without privacy, because the privacy noise grows like \(d\) while sampling grows like \(\sqrt d\). Fix the number of rounds and the budget split before seeing the data, because the rounds compose and too many of them eat the budget.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
section: 28.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
text:
28.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
Incomes, session lengths and per-example gradient norms have heavy tails. Suppose all you know is that the variance is at most \(\sigma^2\). Then a clipping range wide enough to touch no record is enormous. The way out is to clip into the data on purpose and accept a bias.
Clip every record to within a half-width \(\tau\) of a centre near the mean, found by a coarse step. With the centre at the mean, the bias is at most \(\sigma^2/\tau\), and the noise grows in proportion to \(\tau\). The bound on the total error is smallest at \[\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{n\varepsilon}{2\sqrt2}}, \tag{28.5}\] which uses only \(n\), \(\varepsilon\) and the variance bound. At that width, an error \(\alpha\) needs about \[n \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{8\sqrt2\,\sigma^2}{\alpha^2\varepsilon} \tag{28.6}\] records. So with heavy tails privacy is no longer a lower-order cost, because its term has the same power of \(\alpha\) as sampling. No \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism does better for every such distribution. A bound on a higher moment lowers the cost.
Table 28.1 shows the trade-off between bias and noise on Pareto records, a heavy-tailed distribution scaled to variance 1. The worst-case width \(\tau_b = 18.80\) cuts the error from 0.4012 to 0.0607, and the best width for this distribution does better still.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
A model trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), the method called DP-SGD, takes thousands of noisy steps, each on a random batch. The guarantee you report is a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\), the chance that the promise fails for a person (Numerical accounting defines it exactly). The composition theorems of Part 3 are far too loose for thousands of steps. An accountant does better, because it tracks a richer summary of each step’s privacy cost that composes tightly, and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end.
One DP-SGD run is the running example. Each step samples each example with probability 0.01 and adds noise with multiplier 1. After 10,000 steps, advanced composition certifies \(\varepsilon = 24{,}379.55\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). But a privacy loss distribution accountant certifies only 6.24 for the same run (Choosing an accountant). So an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing until you name the accountant that produced it, which is also why libraries and papers can disagree about the same run.
If you train with DP-SGD, read four chapters. Rényi differential privacy is the curve that most accountants track. Amplification by subsampling shows how much a random batch helps, provided the data loader samples the way the accountant assumes. Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions computes the tightest \(\varepsilon\) available, and Choosing an accountant turns the part into a decision guide.
The other chapters serve narrower needs. From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests explains the conversion behind every Rényi number. Concentrated differential privacy budgets analytics queries with one number. f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy reads a guarantee as a limit on attacks. Amplification by shuffling and by iteration and Adaptive composition cover shuffled pipelines and budgets decided during training.
The part uses the accountants of three libraries, Opacus, Google’s dp_accounting and Microsoft’s prv_accountant. Each chapter ends with a link to the full edition, which derives every result.
By the end, you will be able to account for a DP-SGD run with a library and check it against a second one. Above all, you will report \(\varepsilon\) with the accountant that produced it, so that someone else can reproduce it.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.1 Why this matters
Suppose you train a model with 1000 steps of full-batch noisy gradient descent. Each step adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20 to a quantity that one person’s record can move by at most 1. You want the differential privacy (DP) guarantee of the whole run, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) at a small slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The tools of Part 3 turn each step into one such pair and then apply advanced composition (Composition). They give \(\varepsilon = 68.01\), while the true answer is 7.51, so you would pay for a bound nine times too large in noise or in accuracy.
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) fixes this by keeping a whole curve for each step instead of one point. The curves of the steps simply add, with no \(\delta\) spent along the way, and you convert the total into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. For the same 1000 steps, this gives \(\varepsilon = 8.84\), only 18% above the truth. It is what the RDP accountants of Opacus and Google’s dp_accounting library track.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.2 The RDP curve
Call \(P\) and \(Q\) the output distributions of a mechanism on two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. The Rényi divergence of Divergences measures how far apart they are. It has a parameter called the order, written \(\alpha\), which is any number above 1. Writing \(p\) and \(q\) for the densities of the two distributions, it is \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy. \tag{29.1}\] A larger order weighs more heavily the outputs that are much likelier under \(P\) than under \(Q\). So a small order looks at the typical case, and a large order at the worst case.
A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP if this divergence is at most \(\varepsilon\) for every pair of neighbours. The smallest such \(\varepsilon\), as a function of the order, is the mechanism’s RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and a higher curve means less privacy. Each point of it bounds one exponential moment of the privacy loss, the logarithm of \(p/q\), and Numerical accounting works with that loss directly.
The curve never decreases with the order. Its two ends tie it to familiar quantities. As the order falls towards 1, it tends to at least the Kullback–Leibler divergence between neighbours, the average privacy loss. At order infinity it is the largest privacy loss of any output, so an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP at every order. Accountants store the whole curve on a grid of orders. This part uses a grid of 154 orders, the default list of Opacus with 128, 256 and 512 added.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
29.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
To account for a mechanism you need its curve, and the three basic mechanisms have one in closed form (Mironov 2017). Each formula below assumes sensitivity 1, the most one record can move the answer. For the Gaussian mechanism, write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier, the noise standard deviation in units of the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Its curve is the straight line \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{29.2}\] The Laplace mechanism adds noise whose typical size is its scale \(b\), and its curve is \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)/b} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha/b}\right). \tag{29.3}\] Randomized response, which reports a bit truthfully with probability \(p\) and flips it otherwise, has a closed-form curve too, given in the full edition. Table 29.1 gives the three curves at a few orders.

These curves are for steps that use the whole dataset. A private step of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, works on a random batch and has a much smaller curve, which Amplification by subsampling computes. You rarely type these formulas in, because libraries hold them. The rdp_bank module of autodp, for example, has RDP_gaussian, RDP_laplace and RDP_randresponse, which return the curve at one order.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.4 Composition adds curves
Training runs thousands of mechanisms in sequence, and each may depend on what the earlier ones released, as a gradient step depends on the current model. RDP composes by adding curves order by order. Write \(\varepsilon_i\) for the curve of step \(i\), and \(\varepsilon_M\) for the curve of a whole run of \(k\) steps. Then \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every order } \alpha. \tag{29.4}\] The sum is exact when the steps are independent. Different mechanisms mix freely, because you only add numbers at the same order.
A pipeline that mixes mechanisms, such as a Gaussian count, a Laplace histogram and a randomized-response survey, is accounted the same way. In dp_accounting you wrap the events in a ComposedDpEvent, wrap a repeated one in a SelfComposedDpEvent, and compose the result. All the curves you add must describe the same notion of neighbours and the same unit of privacy, though. In dp_accounting 0.6.0, for example, the RDP accountant refuses a RandomizedResponseDpEvent under its default add-or-remove neighboring_relation, which a PoissonSampledDpEvent needs (Amplification by subsampling explains the relations).
The condition that matters is that each step’s curve is fixed in advance. Steps may adapt to earlier outputs, but the noise level and the number of steps must not be chosen from the data during the run. If they are, for example by stopping when a validation metric looks good, you need Adaptive composition.
For Gaussian steps the sum has a useful shortcut, because adding \(k\) copies of the straight line gives the curve of a single Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). The shortcut also shows why DP-SGD needs subsampling. If this part’s running example, 10,000 steps with noise multiplier 1, used the full dataset at every step, it would act like one step with noise multiplier 0.01. Its exact \(\varepsilon\) would be 5425.5, which is no guarantee at all.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.5 Post-processing and group privacy
Post-processing is free in RDP. If you apply any randomized map \(g\) to the output without looking at the data again, the curve of the result is no larger at any order: \[\varepsilon_{g\circ M}(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\alpha). \tag{29.5}\] So releasing the trained model or its predictions costs nothing beyond the training run, as long as \(g\) never reads the data.
Groups are harder. When one user contributes \(m\) records, you need a guarantee for all of them at once. RDP has a generic group rule, Mironov’s, under which each doubling of the group halves the order and triples \(\varepsilon\). It is loose, and for the Gaussian mechanism it overstates the exact value 1.5 times for two records and 3.375 times for eight.
So for Gaussian noise, skip the generic rule and use the group’s sensitivity. A group of \(m\) records moves the answer by at most \(m\) times as much as one record, so the curve becomes \[\varepsilon_{\text{group}}(\alpha) = \frac{m^2\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{29.6}\] which is \(m^2\) times the single-record curve. Better still, clip per user and account at the user level (User-level privacy).

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.6 Convert once, at the end
After composing, you hold a curve, but you report an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair. A conversion tries every order of the grid and keeps the one that gives the smallest \(\varepsilon\), which libraries report as the best order. From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests gives the formulas. The workflow is what matters here, because you compose the curves of all steps first and convert once, at the end.
The moments accountant of the original DP-SGD paper (Abadi et al. 2016) is this same workflow with different bookkeeping. It tracks \(\lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1)\), the logarithm of the moment generating function of the privacy loss, and its conversion is Mironov’s, the original RDP conversion. So read an older paper’s moments-accountant \(\varepsilon\) as an RDP number. Similarly, compute_dp_sgd_privacy_statement in TensorFlow Privacy 0.9.0 uses the RDP accountant of dp_accounting by default.
Table 29.2 shows what composing curves gains for runs of \(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\). It compares advanced composition with RDP, converted by Mironov’s conversion, and with the exact value from the Gaussian’s privacy curve (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy).

A best order on the edge of the grid means that the true optimum lies outside it, and the reported \(\varepsilon\) is too large.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.7 Accounting with a library
In production, you describe each step to a library and let it compose and convert. Google’s dp_accounting describes each mechanism as an event, so a DP-SGD step is a GaussianDpEvent inside a PoissonSampledDpEvent, and an RdpAccountant composes the events and converts the total. For example, these lines account for the running example in version 0.6.0.
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(
    sampling_probability=0.01,
    event=dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=1.0),
)
accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()       # or RdpAccountant(orders=[...])
accountant.compose(step, count=10_000)
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(target_delta=1e-5)
Opacus works differently, because its accountant is attached to the optimizer. There, PrivacyEngine(accountant="rdp") selects the class opacus.accountants.RDPAccountant, which records each update through step(noise_multiplier=..., sample_rate=...). Its method get_privacy_spent(delta=...) then returns \(\varepsilon\) with the best order. Outside training, the functions compute_rdp and get_privacy_spent of opacus.accountants.analysis.rdp do the same in two calls. Ask for RDP explicitly when you want these numbers, since the default accountant of Opacus 1.6.0 is a numerical one.
Three checks catch most mistakes. First, if the best order the library returns sits at either end of the grid, pass a longer list of orders. Second, make sure the event matches the sampler your data loader runs, because a Poisson event for a shuffled fixed-size batch is a different mechanism (Amplification by subsampling). Third, count each step once. In Opacus the optimizer already steps the accountant after every update, so a manual call to step on top of it charges each update twice.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.1 Why this matters
An accountant that tracks Rényi differential privacy (RDP) ends a training run holding a curve, with one value for each order \(\alpha\) above 1 (Rényi differential privacy). Nobody reports the curve, though. A paper, a model card or a regulator asks for a differential privacy (DP) guarantee, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). So every RDP analysis ends with a conversion, and the conversion decides the number you publish.
The short answer is to use the improved conversion, which every maintained library already uses, and to check that the best order is inside the grid. For the Gaussian mechanism it still sits 5 to 10% above the exact \(\varepsilon\), and only a different kind of accountant removes that slack.
crumbs: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 30.2 What δ means for your users
text:
30.2 What δ means for your users
An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee says that one person’s record changes the chance of any outcome by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), except for an extra probability \(\delta\). Strictly, \(\delta\) is an average over the privacy loss of each output, defined in Numerical accounting. In practice, treat \(\delta\) as the chance that the guarantee fails for a person, possibly badly. Write \(n\) for the number of people in the data. Then \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\), which is why The definition of differential privacy recommends a value such as \(1/n^{1.5}\).
crumbs: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.3 Mironov’s and the improved conversion
The original conversion is Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017). For a mechanism with RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) and any order \(\alpha\), it says that the mechanism is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.1}\] You minimize it over the grid of orders. The result is valid but loose, because the conversion charges every output whose privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\) with its whole probability, and then bounds that tail with Markov’s inequality.
The improved conversion recovers most of that loss. Balle and coauthors, Canonne, Kamath and Steinke, and Asoodeh and coauthors found it independently in 2020. A mechanism with RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP, at every order, with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.2}\] You again minimize over the grid, and if the result comes out negative, you report 0, since a guarantee at a negative \(\varepsilon\) also holds at 0. At any fixed order the improved value is lower by an amount that depends only on the order, 0.3612 at order 10, and more at smaller orders.
For a worked example, release the mean of a bounded statistic once with the Gaussian mechanism at noise multiplier 1, so that its curve is \(\alpha/2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), Mironov’s conversion gives 5.299. The improved conversion gives 4.729, against an exact value of 4.377 (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy).
This explains why your library’s \(\varepsilon\) can be lower than an older paper’s for the same settings, since older papers and code used Mironov’s conversion. Their numbers are loose, not wrong. So if two RDP accountants report values about 0.4 apart for the same run, with a best order near 10, one of them uses Mironov’s conversion. On this part’s running example, private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, Mironov’s conversion gives 7.43 and the improved one 6.71.
crumbs: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.4 Which conversion your library uses
Both widely used libraries use the improved conversion, as of Opacus 1.6.0 and dp_accounting 0.6.0. In Opacus, RDPAccountant calls the function get_privacy_spent(orders=..., rdp=..., delta=...) of opacus.accountants.analysis.rdp, and in dp_accounting, RdpAccountant.get_epsilon(target_delta) calls compute_epsilon. But their default grids of orders differ, and the grid matters as much as the formula. The Opacus list RDPAccountant.DEFAULT_ALPHAS stops at order 63, while the DEFAULT_RDP_ORDERS of dp_accounting go on to 1024.
So set the orders yourself when the default does not fit. In Opacus, pass alphas=[...] to the accountant’s get_privacy_spent or get_epsilon. In dp_accounting, pass orders=[...] to the RdpAccountant and read the best order from get_epsilon_and_optimal_order. Opacus warns when the best order is at an end of its list, but dp_accounting does not, so there you compare the returned order with the ends of the list yourself.
One composed curve gives a guarantee at every \(\delta\), so you can report several pairs at no extra privacy cost. In dp_accounting, call get_epsilon(target_delta) once per \(\delta\), or get_delta(target_epsilon) for the reverse question. For the single release above, the improved conversion gives 4.729 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and 6.086 at \(10^{-8}\), as the snippet at the end prints.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.5 Choosing the order
For a run of \(k\) Gaussian steps with noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the composed curve is a straight line in the order. Its slope, written \(\rho\), is \(k/(2\sigma^2)\). Then the improved conversion’s best order is close to \[\alpha^* - 1 \approx \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\rho}} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{k}}. \tag{30.3}\] More steps or less noise make the curve steeper, so they push the best order towards 1. But a smaller \(\delta\) pushes it up only through the square root of a logarithm, so \(\delta\) matters little. Table 30.1 shows the range a grid must cover.

No cleverer formula closes the gap between 4.729 and the exact 4.377 for the single release, because the curve itself lacks the information. Subsampled DP-SGD steps have curves that are not straight lines, and the gap can be much larger (Choosing an accountant measures it for the running example). title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.7 RDP, attacks and other guarantees
An RDP curve also limits attacks. Each order bounds the power of any test that tries to tell whether your record was used. Write \(a\) for the test’s false-positive rate. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair only caps the power at \(e^\varepsilon a + \delta\), while at low false-positive rates the whole curve caps it far more tightly. So read attack risk from the curve, or better from a trade-off function (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy). Then compare it with what an audit measures (Auditing private training).
Mixing RDP with other guarantees works in one direction only. A pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP component has a curve, which Concentrated differential privacy gives. But an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) component with \(\delta\) above 0 has none, because a mechanism that publishes your record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP yet has infinite Rényi divergence. So never feed an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair into an RDP accountant, and take the curve from the mechanism behind it instead.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.1 Why this matters
Suppose you run a pipeline of Gaussian releases, such as noisy counts or the noisy marginals behind a synthetic dataset. You would like to keep its differential privacy (DP) budget as a single number that you add to after each release. Rényi DP describes each mechanism by a whole curve, its Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve, with one value for each order of the Rényi divergence. The Gaussian mechanism’s curve is a straight line through the origin, so one number, its slope, carries all of it.
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) is the bookkeeping built on that number, and it is the most widely used form of concentrated differential privacy (CDP). It is the right ledger for releases built from Gaussian noise on the full data. It is the wrong ledger for training on subsampled minibatches, because it throws away almost all of the privacy that subsampling buys.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.2 The zCDP ledger
A mechanism is zCDP when its RDP curve lies under a line through the origin. To state it, write \(D_\alpha\) for the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\), and call two datasets neighbours when they differ in one person’s record. Then a mechanism \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP if, for all neighbouring datasets and all orders above 1, \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\alpha. \tag{31.1}\] Two properties make this a ledger. Composition adds the slopes, even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, and processing an output never raises its \(\rho\).
The Gaussian mechanism is the case the definition was built for. Write \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of its noise and \(\Delta\) for the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the most one record can move the query’s value. Its RDP curve is exactly a line, so one step costs \[\rho = \frac{\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{31.2}\] With the noise multiplier convention, which measures \(\sigma\) in units of the sensitivity, a step with \(\sigma = 1\) costs \(0.5\). Doubling the noise multiplier cuts the cost to a quarter.
The best-known user is the 2020 United States Census TopDown algorithm (Abowd et al. 2022). It answers many queries with the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), which keeps counts as integers. Among libraries, Tumult Analytics offers a RhoZCDPBudget. In OpenDP, dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP turns a zCDP measurement into one with a privacy profile, and dp.c.make_fix_delta then fixes the slack so that you can read off the privacy level.
The Census example carries two warnings. First, \(\rho\) is not the privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\) of an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee, where \(\delta\) is the slack. A \(0.5\)-zCDP step converts to about \(\varepsilon = 4.7\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (Section 31.4), so a reader who mistakes one for the other badly overrates the protection. Second, \(\rho\) covers only what passed through the noise. The Census Bureau released some statistics exactly, as a matter of policy, and these invariants sit outside the guarantee. A report should list such exact releases next to the budget.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.3 Charging other kinds of step
A real pipeline mixes mechanisms, and Table 31.1 gives the charge in \(\rho\) for the common ones.

A pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP step, such as a Laplace count or a randomized-response bit, changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours. The sharp charge \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) is the smallest that holds for all such steps, because randomized response is the worst case, and at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is 0.4621. The exponential mechanism’s charge of \(\varepsilon^2/8\) is due to Cesar and Rogers (2021).
The general rule breaks down for large \(\varepsilon\). A pure DP step’s RDP curve never rises above \(\varepsilon\), while the line keeps climbing and passes that cap at order \(2/\varepsilon\). So a \(5\)-DP step charged \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 12.5\) sits above its own cap at every order. Converting that charge back gives a worse \(\varepsilon\) than the 5 you started with, so keep such steps in RDP, where an accountant can charge them the exact curve of randomized response.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.4 From ρ to (ε, δ)
You always report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) in the end. Write \(\ell\) for \(\ln(1/\delta)\). Applying Mironov’s conversion to a line gives the simple conversion of Bun and Steinke (2016). It says that a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\,\ell}. \tag{31.3}\] The improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) adds two negative correction terms at each order. It has no closed form, so you minimize it numerically, as the code below does. For the Gaussian the true \(\varepsilon\) is also known, from its privacy profile in f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy. Table 31.2 compares the three.

At \(\rho = 0.5\), the simple formula overshoots the truth by 21%, and the improved one by 8%. So use the improved conversion, or the exact Gaussian profile when every step is Gaussian.
For calibration you run the conversion backwards, from a target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) to the largest total \(\rho\) that meets it. Solving the simple conversion for \(\rho\) shows that the target is met by any \[\rho \le \Big(\sqrt{\varepsilon + \ell} - \sqrt{\ell}\Big)^2. \tag{31.4}\] Then split \(\rho\) over the queries. If query number \(i\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_i\) and spends \(\rho_i\), its noise needs the standard deviation \[\sigma_i = \frac{\Delta_i}{\sqrt{2\rho_i}}. \tag{31.5}\] For example, a release that must be \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP may spend at most \(\rho = 0.02082\). A single query of sensitivity 1 then needs \(\sigma = 4.901\). If you split the same budget equally over four queries, each gets a quarter of \(\rho\) and so needs twice the noise, 9.801.
That recipe works because the split happens in \(\rho\), which adds, and never in \(\varepsilon\), which does not. Suppose you have a budget of \(\rho = 1\) and have spent half of it. Each half alone converts to 4.728, and two of those are far more than the whole run’s 7.077, because the conversion grows like the square root of \(\rho\). So keep budgets in \(\rho\), subtract in \(\rho\), and convert once, at the end. In OpenDP, dp.binary_search_param does the last step of calibration for you, by searching for the noise scale that meets a target. Use the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity here, because the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of a vector query is never smaller and so overpays in noise.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.5 Groups and approximate zCDP
A household, a user with many records or a hospital contributes several records, so you may need the guarantee for a group. Take a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism \(M\) and two datasets that differ in \(m\) records. Bun and Steinke (2016) show that \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le m^2\rho\,\alpha. \tag{31.6}\] The square is exact for the Gaussian, since a group shifts the query \(m\) times as far. For example, a user with 4 records in a \(0.1\)-zCDP release is protected at \(\rho = 1.6\). Plain RDP’s group bound is much weaker (Rényi DP).
Some useful mechanisms, such as propose-test-release and stability-based histograms, are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but cannot be zCDP at all. Approximate zCDP keeps them in the ledger by adding a second column. Each such step adds \(\varepsilon^2/2\) to \(\rho\) and its slack to the second column, and at the end the second column’s total is added to the \(\delta\) of the conversion.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
section: 31.6 Subsampled steps: keep them out of zCDP
text:
31.6 Subsampled steps: keep them out of zCDP
Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD for short, runs each step on a Poisson sample of the data. Each record enters the batch independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, and this makes a step far more private than the Gaussian mechanism inside it (Amplification by subsampling). But zCDP cannot see the gain. The subsampled step’s RDP curve is tiny at small orders and bends up towards the unsubsampled line at large ones. A line that covers the whole curve must therefore have slope \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), whatever the sampling rate.
The cost of ignoring this is enormous. On this part’s running example of 10,000 steps with \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), zCDP reports \(\varepsilon = 5475.8\). RDP accounting of the same run gives 6.719, because the conversion only uses the small orders where the curve is still tiny.
Truncated concentrated differential privacy (tCDP) asks for the line only on low orders, so it sees some of the amplification. It is rarely used, because it does no better than RDP.
So if a pipeline mixes Gaussian releases with a DP-SGD run, keep all of it in RDP. A \(\rho\)-zCDP step is just the RDP line \(\rho\alpha\), so it joins an RDP ledger without loss. In Google’s dp_accounting library, for example, you add it to an RdpAccountant as a GaussianDpEvent with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\). The training steps go in next to it as a PoissonSampledDpEvent.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.7 Code
The whole zCDP ledger is a few lines of code. You charge each Gaussian step its \(\rho\), add the charges, and convert once, and the last line splits a budget over four queries.
from math import log, sqrt


def zcdp_gaussian(sigma: float, sensitivity: float = 1.0) -> float:
    return sensitivity**2 / (2 * sigma**2)


def zcdp_to_eps_improved(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Minimized over 20,001 log-spaced orders, the full edition's fine grid."""
    best = float("inf")
    for i in range(20001):
        alpha = 1 + 10 ** (-4 + 8 * i / 20000)
        eps = rho * alpha + log(1 / delta) / (alpha - 1) + log(1 - 1 / alpha) - log(alpha) / (alpha - 1)
        best = min(best, eps)
    return best


def rho_for_target(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest rho whose simple conversion stays within eps at delta."""
    return (sqrt(eps + log(1 / delta)) - sqrt(log(1 / delta))) ** 2


def sigma_for_rho(rho: float) -> float:
    return 1 / sqrt(2 * rho)


rho = 10 * zcdp_gaussian(sigma=1.0)  # ten Gaussian steps with sigma = 1
print(f"{rho:.1f}")  # 5.0
print(f"{zcdp_to_eps_improved(rho, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 19.047
budget = rho_for_target(1.0, 1e-5)  # the whole release must be (1, 1e-5)-DP
print(f"{budget:.5f} {sigma_for_rho(budget):.3f}")  # 0.02082 4.901
print(f"{sigma_for_rho(budget / 4):.3f}")  # 9.801

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.1 Why this matters
Every privacy guarantee bounds how well an attacker can tell from a mechanism’s output whether it ran on a dataset \(D\) or on a neighbour \(D'\) that differs in one record. Differential privacy (DP) answers with two numbers, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) with a curve of divergences. Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) answers with one number. All three summarize a more complete answer, the attacker’s best error rates, and this chapter works with that answer directly.
It pays off for two reasons. First, Gaussian noise gives a family of answers called Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). Its one parameter, written \(\mu\), reads directly as the best success rate of a membership attack. Gaussian steps compose within the family, so a Gaussian pipeline has an exact guarantee in one number. Second, a central limit theorem (CLT) gives a quick estimate of \(\mu\) for training with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. That estimate can understate the true privacy loss, so it must never be the number you report.
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.2 Trade-off curves and f-DP
The attacker’s decision is a hypothesis test (Hypothesis testing), and a test can make two kinds of mistake. Write \(a\) for its type I error, how often it claims \(D'\) when the data was \(D\). Write \(b\) for its type II error, how often it makes the reverse mistake. In a membership attack, where \(D'\) contains the target’s record, \(a\) is the false positive rate and \(1 - b\) the true positive rate. The trade-off function of a mechanism gives, at each \(a\), the smallest \(b\) that any test can reach.
A guarantee is a floor under that curve. Write \(T\big(M(D), M(D')\big)\) for the trade-off function of a mechanism \(M\) on two datasets. Dong, Roth and Su (2022) call the mechanism \(f\)-differentially private (\(f\)-DP) if, for all neighbours, \[T\big(M(D), M(D')\big) \ge f. \tag{32.1}\]
The familiar guarantee with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a slack \(\delta\) is the special case whose floor is two straight lines, \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(a) = \max\big(0,\; 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a,\; e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - a)\big). \tag{32.2}\] Two straight lines make a crude floor. Randomized response and the Laplace mechanism both carry the label “\(\varepsilon = 1\)”, but only randomized response sits on \(f_{1,0}\), while the Laplace curve lies above it in the middle. So when you compare mechanisms, or audit one, compare curves.
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.3 μ-GDP, read as an attack
The Gaussian mechanism’s curve has a simple form. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier, the standard deviation of the noise in units of the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Every Gaussian mechanism then reduces to telling a standard normal draw from one shifted by a distance \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function, so that \(\Phi(t)\) is the chance that a standard normal draw is at most \(t\). The best test’s type II error at type I error \(a\) is \[G_\mu(a) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu\big). \tag{32.3}\] A mechanism is \(\mu\)-Gaussian differentially private (\(\mu\)-GDP) if \(G_\mu\) is a floor for it. For the Gaussian mechanism this floor is the exact curve, so nothing is lost.
The parameter \(\mu\) reads directly as an attack. Take a count released with \(\sigma = 1\), so 1-GDP. At a 1% false positive rate, and whatever the attacker knows about the rest of the data, it detects the target’s record at most 9.24% of the time. Table 32.1 gives this best true positive rate for three values of \(\mu\), next to the \(\varepsilon\) that each converts to.

It is also the ceiling that a membership inference attack can reach, and that a privacy audit tests against, usually at low false positive rates. As a rough guide, Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and that \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing.

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.4 Converting μ to (ε, δ)
To report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), you turn the curve into pairs. Its privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest slack that goes with each privacy level. For a curve that is unchanged when you swap \(D\) and \(D'\), the whole profile loses nothing, because together its pairs rebuild the curve. For \(\mu\)-GDP the profile has a closed form (Dong et al., Corollary 2.13): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{32.4}\] This is also the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) curve of the Gaussian mechanism, the analytic calibration of The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms (Balle & Wang 2018).
You use it in both directions, with any root finder, such as scipy.optimize.brentq on scipy.stats.norm.cdf, or the bisection in the code below. To report, fix \(\delta\) and solve Equation 32.4 for \(\varepsilon\) by bisection, which works because the profile falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows. For example, 1-GDP is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP. To calibrate, fix the target pair, bisect for the largest \(\mu\) that meets it, and set the noise multiplier to \(1/\mu\). For example, a single \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release needs \(\sigma = 3.7306\).
One pair, on its own, loses a lot. At a type I error of 0.1, for example, the pair for 1-GDP allows a type II error as low as 0.0113. The curve \(G_1\) itself requires 0.6109.
Do not calibrate with the classical formula instead, which sets the noise for a query of sensitivity \(\Delta\) to \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{32.5}\] It is valid only for \(\varepsilon < 1\), and even there it adds more noise than the exact curve requires. For a numerical accountant, dp_accounting.pld.privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism builds the same exact curve as a privacy loss distribution.
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.5 Composition: μ² adds
Dong et al. show that composing \(f_i\)-DP steps gives a curve that depends only on the \(f_i\), even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs. For Gaussian curves it stays Gaussian (Dong et al., Corollary 3.3): \[G_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes G_{\mu_k} = G_\mu, \qquad \mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}. \tag{32.6}\] Here \(\otimes\) stands for composition, and the quantity that adds up is \(\mu^2\). So full-batch noisy gradient descent is \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP after a number \(k\) of steps. Since that is the exact curve, no accountant can improve on it. The same holds for every pipeline of Gaussian noise without subsampling, such as analytics queries, the noisy vote counts of private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) and matrix mechanisms.
The zCDP ledger does the same arithmetic, where \(\rho\), the zCDP parameter, equals \(\mu^2/2\). But its conversion loses some of the curve, while Equation 32.4 loses none.
Composing curves rather than pairs matters in practice. Four 1-GDP releases compose to 2-GDP, which is \((9.9973, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Suppose you instead turn each release into a pair with a quarter of the \(\delta\) budget, \((4.6902, 2.5\times10^{-6})\), and add the pairs by basic composition. You get \(\varepsilon = 18.7607\), almost twice as much. So for a pipeline of Gaussian releases without subsampling, keep a ledger of \(\mu^2\) and convert once. Curves that are not Gaussian leave their family when composed, so for them you need a numerical accountant.
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.6 The CLT estimate for DP-SGD
Most mechanisms are not Gaussian. But a central limit theorem for \(f\)-DP says that many steps that each leak little compose to nearly a Gaussian curve (Dong et al. 2022). DP-SGD is such a run.
Each step of DP-SGD samples a batch by Poisson sampling, which includes each record independently with a sampling rate \(q\). It then clips each gradient and adds Gaussian noise (Amplification by subsampling). With add/remove neighbours, Bu et al. (2020) show that \(k\) such steps are approximately \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = q\sqrt{k\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}. \tag{32.7}\] It shows that the parameter grows in proportion to the sampling rate and to the square root of the number of steps, and steeply as the noise falls.
The formula is an approximation, not a bound, and it errs on the unsafe side. A CLT controls the bulk of a distribution much better than its tails, where small values of \(\delta\) are decided. After the 10,000 steps of this part’s running example, the CLT gives \(\varepsilon = 6.0071\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). A numerical accountant proves that the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377, so the CLT number would be false (Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz 2021). Opacus offers this accountant as accountant="gdp", implemented by opacus.accountants.GaussianAccountant, and it warns that the GDP accountant is experimental and can underestimate the privacy spent. For anything you report, use its default "prv" accountant or "rdp" (Choosing an accountant). The formula also assumes Poisson sampling with add/remove neighbours (Amplification by subsampling).
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
section: 32.7 RDP forgets part of the curve
text:
32.7 RDP forgets part of the curve
An RDP curve is a summary of the trade-off curve, and it forgets part of it even for the Gaussian. For 1-GDP the exact \(\delta(1)\) is 0.1269. By any conversion, its RDP curve certifies no better than 0.2149. So for Gaussian noise without subsampling, account in GDP.
crumbs: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.8 Code
A GDP accountant needs only the normal distribution, which Python’s statistics.NormalDist provides. The snippet computes the attack reading of \(\mu\), the conversions in both directions and the CLT estimate.
from math import exp, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

N = NormalDist()


def gdp_power(mu: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """Best true positive rate of any attack on mu-GDP at a given false positive rate."""
    return 1 - N.cdf(N.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - mu)


def gdp_delta(eps: float, mu: float) -> float:
    """The exact delta(eps) of mu-GDP."""
    return N.cdf(-eps / mu + mu / 2) - exp(eps) * N.cdf(-eps / mu - mu / 2)


def gdp_eps(mu: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The eps at which mu-GDP reaches delta, by bisection."""
    lo, hi = 0.0, 500.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if gdp_delta(mid, mu) > delta else (lo, mid)
    return hi


def gdp_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The largest mu that meets (eps, delta), by bisection."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 100.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if gdp_delta(eps, mid) < delta else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def clt_mu_dpsgd(q: float, sigma: float, steps: int) -> float:
    """CLT estimate of mu for Poisson-subsampled DP-SGD; not a bound."""
    return q * sqrt(steps * (exp(1 / sigma**2) - 1))


print(" ".join(f"{gdp_power(m, 0.001):.4f}" for m in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0)))  # 0.0048 0.0183 0.1378
print(f"{gdp_eps(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 4.3772
mu = gdp_mu(1.0, 1e-5)  # calibrate one release to (1, 1e-5)
print(f"{mu:.4f} {1 / mu:.4f}")  # 0.2681 3.7306
mu = clt_mu_dpsgd(q=0.01, sigma=1.0, steps=10_000)
print(f"{mu:.4f} {gdp_eps(mu, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 1.3108 6.0071

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.1 Why this matters
Most private models are trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made to satisfy differential privacy (DP), a method called DP-SGD. Each step clips every example’s gradient, sums the clipped gradients and adds Gaussian noise, whose standard deviation is the clipping norm times the noise multiplier \(\sigma\). Suppose every record paid the full cost of a Gaussian mechanism at every step. With \(\sigma = 1\), ten thousand steps would then cost a privacy level of \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) (Rényi DP).
DP-SGD escapes this cost because each step looks only at a small random batch. Write \(q\) for the sampling rate, the probability that a given record lands in the batch. An attacker must then first guess whether the record was used at all, and that uncertainty is worth a lot. This effect is called amplification by subsampling. It depends on exactly how the batch was drawn, so the accountant, the code that adds up a run’s privacy cost, must assume the sampler the training code actually runs. Getting that wrong is the largest single error in DP-SGD accounting.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.2 One step under Poisson sampling
The simplest sampler is Poisson sampling, in which each record enters the batch by its own coin flip, with probability \(q\), independently of every other record. Pair it with add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record being present or absent. Balle, Barthe and Gaboardi (2018) give the tight result. If a step is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP on its own, where \(\delta\) is the slack, then the same step run on a Poisson sample is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{33.1}\]
The formula behaves very differently for small and large \(\varepsilon\). For small \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \(q\varepsilon\), so a 1% sample makes a step about a hundred times cheaper. With that sample, for example, a 1-DP step costs 0.0170. But for large \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \[\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q), \tag{33.2}\] so sampling only subtracts a fixed amount. With the same sample, a 10-DP step still costs 5.3993. The switch happens where \(\varepsilon\) is near \(\ln(1/q)\).
The result has two conditions. Each record’s coin must be independent of the others, so that the record is drawn with probability exactly \(q\) whatever else is in the batch. And the batch must stay secret, because an attacker who sees the list of records drawn knows whether the target was used. The rule applies to any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step, not only to the Gaussian. So a pure DP or randomized-response release run on a secret Poisson sample is amplified too. For example, 1-DP randomized response on a 10% sample costs 0.1586. Per-step pairs compose badly over thousands of steps, though (Section 33.4).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
section: 33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
text:
33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
Most training code does not draw Poisson batches. Some draws a fresh random batch of a fixed size, written \(m\), from the \(n\) records at each step. Much more code shuffles the data once per epoch and cuts the list into consecutive batches, which is called shuffle and partition. Each sampler pairs naturally with a neighbouring relation, and Table 33.1 gives what to account for under each pairing.



Table 33.1: What to account for under each combination of sampling scheme and neighbouring relation.










Sampling
Neighbours
What to account for




Poisson, rate \(q\)
add/remove

Fixed size \(m\) of \(n\)
add/remove
A Poisson accountant with rate \(m/n\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\) (Lebeda et al. 2024)


Fixed size \(m\) of \(n\)
replace-one
Per step, Equation 33.1 with \(q = m/n\) and \(\sigma/2\); no Poisson shortcut


Poisson, rate \(q\)
replace-one
About twice the add/remove cost for pure DP at small \(\varepsilon\)

zero-out
No amplification formula; the Poisson number can be far too small






The factor of two in the noise comes from the gradient sum. Adding or removing a record moves the clipped sum by at most the clipping norm. But a record that enters a fixed-size batch pushes another one out, so the sum can move by twice as much. Twice the shift with the same noise is the same as the original shift with half the noise multiplier, and that is not a small change. This part’s running example takes ten thousand steps with \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the Poisson accountant gives it \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). With fixed-size batches under add/remove it must be run at \(\sigma = 0.5\), and it then gives 47.42, about seven times more.
Shuffle and partition is worse, because the source of amplification is missing. Within an epoch the record is in exactly one batch and is never absent, so the attacker only has to find which batch held it. Chua et al. (2024) build a dataset where the target’s batch stands out, under zero-out neighbours, which set the target’s gradient to 0. A test on it proves that one shuffled epoch of the running example has \(\varepsilon\) of at least 4.06, while a Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21. So a Poisson number reported for shuffled training can be provably false.
So read the data loader before you trust a reported \(\varepsilon\). A PyTorch DataLoader with shuffle=True and a batch_size is shuffle and partition, and a tf.data pipeline that shuffles and then batches is not Poisson sampling either. Opacus replaces the loader with a Poisson one by default: PrivacyEngine.make_private takes poisson_sampling=True unless you turn it off, and opacus.data_loader.DPDataLoader.from_data_loader converts a loader by hand. A Poisson loader gives batches of varying size, which is a quick check that it is in use. When the largest batches do not fit in memory, Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits them into physical batches without changing the accounting (Private stochastic gradient descent). If you cannot use Poisson sampling, report under the matching row of Table 33.1, or say plainly that \(\varepsilon\) assumes a sampler you did not run.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.4 The accountant for DP-SGD
Accountants for DP-SGD work in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), which describes a mechanism by a curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) over orders \(\alpha > 1\) (Rényi DP). Curves add over steps, even adaptive ones. So a run of \(k\) steps has the curve \(k\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\), which is converted to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once.
Mironov, Talwar and Zhang (2019) show that one Poisson-subsampled Gaussian step has, at integer orders, the curve \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\ln A_\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \qquad A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{33.3}\] Here the index \(j\) counts the imagined copies of the run that used the record, and accountants compute fractional orders by numerical integration. On the running example the curve is tiny at low orders. At order 2, for example, it is \(1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\), against 1 without sampling. Table 33.2 shows what the accountant gives over a run, against the per-step route that amplifies each step with Equation 33.1 and then composes the pairs.

The per-step route fails because each step keeps a tiny share of \(\delta\), which forces a large per-step \(\varepsilon\) that sampling barely reduces. So never compose per-step pairs for DP-SGD. The best order also falls as the run grows, to about 4 at ten thousand steps. So make sure the accountant’s grid includes small and fractional orders, because a missing order can only raise \(\varepsilon\).
In practice you use a library. Opacus’s RDPAccountant and Google’s dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant both compute Equation 33.3, and in dp_accounting you describe a step as PoissonSampledDpEvent(sampling_probability, GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier)). For fixed-size batches it has a SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent for the replace-one relation, while Microsoft’s prv_accountant describes the same step as a PoissonSubsampledGaussianMechanism. The value 6.71 is still an upper bound, and numerical accounting computes the tight value.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
section: 33.5 Small q and the design of a run
text:
33.5 Small q and the design of a run
For small \(q\) the curve has a simple leading term, which is what makes the trade-offs between batch size, noise and epochs visible: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{\alpha q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}{2} \approx \frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\ \text{for large } \sigma. \tag{33.4}\] The per-step cost is quadratic in \(q\), while a run of \(E\) epochs takes \(E/q\) steps. So the total RDP is about \[\frac{E\,q\,\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{33.5}\] At a fixed number of epochs, smaller batches are therefore cheaper in privacy.
That gives the recipe for planning a run. Fix the batch size \(B\) and the number of epochs \(E\) that your accuracy needs. Then the sampling rate is \(q = B/n\) and the number of steps is \(k = En/B\), where \(n\) is the size of the dataset you actually train on, after any filtering. A wrong \(n\) gives a wrong \(q\), and so a wrong \(\varepsilon\). Let the accountant solve for the noise multiplier that meets the target. Opacus does this with get_noise_multiplier(target_epsilon=..., target_delta=..., sample_rate=..., epochs=...), or in one call with make_private_with_epsilon. Then check the result with a second accountant (Choosing an accountant).
Use Equation 33.4 for planning only, never inside an accountant, because at high orders it is far too small. The closed-form bound of the original moments accountant (Abadi et al. 2016) has the same shape and is outdated.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.6 Other mechanisms
For RDP, unlike for Equation 33.1, no rule returns every mechanism’s subsampled curve exactly. General bounds for other mechanisms exist (Zhu & Wang 2019), but they are looser, so use the exact sum for the Gaussian.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.7 Code
The accountant below handles Poisson sampling and add/remove neighbours. It computes Equation 33.3 in log space at integer orders only, so its value for the running example is a little above the 6.71 of fractional orders.
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def subsampled_gaussian_rdp(alpha: int, q: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """RDP at integer order alpha of one Poisson-subsampled Gaussian step (sensitivity 1)."""
    logs = [
        lgamma(alpha + 1) - lgamma(j + 1) - lgamma(alpha - j + 1)
        + (alpha - j) * log(1 - q) + j * log(q) + (j * j - j) / (2 * sigma**2)
        for j in range(alpha + 1)
    ]
    top = max(logs)
    log_a = top + log(sum(exp(t - top) for t in logs))  # log-sum-exp avoids overflow
    return log_a / (alpha - 1)


def dpsgd_eps(q: float, sigma: float, steps: int, delta: float) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """Compose over the steps, convert with the improved conversion at the best integer order."""
    best = (float("inf"), 0)
    for alpha in range(2, 64):
        rdp = steps * subsampled_gaussian_rdp(alpha, q, sigma)
        eps = rdp + log((alpha - 1) / alpha) - (log(delta) + log(alpha)) / (alpha - 1)
        best = min(best, (eps, alpha))
    return best


print(f"{subsampled_gaussian_rdp(2, 0.01, 1.0):.4e}")  # 1.7181e-04
print("%.3f %d" % dpsgd_eps(0.01, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5))  # 6.719 4

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.1 Why this matters
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP), using the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) called DP-SGD. The run took 10,000 steps, with sampling rate 0.01 and noise multiplier 1, and now you need the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which the whole run is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) gives an upper bound that may be loose by an amount you cannot see (Rényi DP). The central limit theorem (CLT) of f-DP and Gaussian DP gives an approximation that may land on either side of the truth.
A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes the answer itself. It returns an upper bound and a lower bound, and you know in advance how far apart they can be. On this run it brackets the true \(\varepsilon\) between 6.1377 and 6.2377, while RDP says 6.7127.
crumbs: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.2 The privacy loss distribution
Call your dataset \(D\) and a neighbouring dataset \(D'\). The mechanism’s output then has a distribution \(P\) on the first and \(Q\) on the second. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the logarithm of how much likelier it is on \(D\), \[L(y) = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}. \tag{34.1}\] The loss is positive when the output favours \(D\) and negative when it favours \(D'\). The output is random, so its loss is too, and the distribution of the loss of an output drawn from \(P\) is the PLD.
The PLD is all you need to compute the slack \(\delta\). The definition of DP lets each output be up to \(e^\varepsilon\) times likelier under \(D\) for free, and \(\delta\) pays for the excess (The definition of differential privacy). Write \((x)_+\) for \(x\) when it is positive and 0 otherwise. Then for every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = P[L > \varepsilon] - e^{\varepsilon}\,Q[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{34.2}\] In words, \(\delta\) averages a weight over the losses. The weight is zero for losses up to \(\varepsilon\) and rises towards 1 above it, so \(\delta\) reads only the upper tail of the PLD.
For the Gaussian mechanism the PLD has a closed form, which makes it the check for any accountant. Write \(\mu\) for the query’s sensitivity divided by the noise standard deviation, which is the shift in units of the noise. The PLD is then the normal distribution with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\). Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function. Putting the two normal tails into Equation 34.2 gives \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{34.3}\] This is the exact \(\delta\) of the Gaussian mechanism, and the privacy curve of \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). Since \(\delta\) falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows, you solve it for \(\varepsilon\) by bisection, as the snippet in the Code section does.
crumbs: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.3 Composition is convolution
When steps run independently, the privacy loss of the whole run is the sum of the per-step losses, as Composition showed. The distribution of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their distributions. So the PLD of \(k\) steps is the \(k\)-fold convolution of the per-step PLDs, and this step loses nothing. So all the error of a PLD accountant comes from computing the convolution on a machine.
Gaussian steps give reference values that every accountant must reproduce. The means and the variances of normal losses add, so \(k\) Gaussian steps with shift \(\mu\) act like one step with shift \(\sqrt k\,\mu\). Ten steps with \(\mu = 1\) are therefore \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and an accountant that misses this value should not be trusted on DP-SGD.
DP-SGD steps are not independent, because each gradient depends on the model that earlier outputs produced. The fix is a dominating pair, a fixed pair of distributions that is at least as easy to tell apart as the step, whatever happened before. Zhu, Dong and Wang (2022) prove that convolving the PLDs of dominating pairs gives a valid \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for the adaptive run. For the Gaussian and the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian, the pairs that libraries use lose nothing. You need a filter instead if the noise level or the number of steps is chosen from the outputs (Adaptive composition).
crumbs: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.4 Pessimistic and optimistic discretization
A computer puts the losses on a grid, the multiples of a spacing \(h\). Rounding changes \(\delta\), but the weight in Equation 34.2 never decreases as the loss grows, so the direction of the rounding fixes the direction of the error. The pessimistic discretization rounds every loss up, and the optimistic one rounds every loss down. The order survives any number of convolutions, so for \(k\) steps and every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta_{\text{optimistic}}(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta_{\text{pessimistic}}(\varepsilon). \tag{34.4}\]
The width of this sandwich is known before you run anything. Each step’s two roundings are at most one grid step apart, so after \(k\) steps the two values of \(\varepsilon\) at your target \(\delta\) are at most \(kh\) apart. For a smooth PLD the width is almost exactly \(kh\), so the error grows linearly in the number of steps.
The two sides are not equally strong. The rounded-up PLD still belongs to a real pair of distributions, which dominates the original, so the pessimistic value is a guarantee even for adaptive runs. The optimistic value is only a lower bound on what the mechanism costs, so it is an error bar and a referee, never a number to report. The midpoint of the two sides, or rounding each loss to the nearest grid point, is a good estimate but is not a bound in either direction.
crumbs: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.5 Composition by FFT
Production accountants convolve with the fast Fourier transform (FFT), padding each convolution so that no mass wraps around the window. If you write your own, pad too, because a wrapped result can err in either direction and is then no bound at all.
Two refinements of the grid are in use. The privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant of Gopi, Lee and Wutschitz (2021) rounds each loss to the nearest grid point, after shifting the grid to keep the true mean. Its rounding errors then partly cancel, growing like \(\sqrt k\,h\) instead of \(kh\), and it still proves error bounds on \(\varepsilon\). Connect the dots (Doroshenko et al. 2022), which Google’s dp_accounting uses by default, builds the best pessimistic PLD on a given grid, so it allows coarser grids.
crumbs: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.6 The subsampled Gaussian and DP-SGD
A DP-SGD step with Poisson sampling reduces to a one-dimensional pair (Amplification by subsampling). In units of the clipping norm, the output without the record is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), normal noise centred at 0 whose standard deviation is the noise multiplier \(\sigma\). When the dataset holds the record, it is drawn with the sampling rate \(q\), and when drawn it shifts the centre by 1. So with the record the output follows the mixture \((1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). A guarantee for adding or removing one record must cover both orders of this pair. The remove direction puts the mixture in the role of \(P\), and the add direction swaps the two.
The two directions behave very differently. A rare large output betrays that the record was used, so the remove direction’s loss has a long right tail, while the add direction’s loss stays below \(-\ln(1 - q)\). So one step at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) costs 0.1995 in the remove direction and only 0.0091 in the add direction. Neither direction is the larger in general, so compose both and report the larger. This pair also assumes Poisson sampling, and a loader that forms batches another way needs a different accountant (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.7 Running it with a library
A maintained library should land inside Table 34.1’s bracket. In Google’s dp_accounting, the function from_gaussian_mechanism of the module dp_accounting.pld.privacy_loss_distribution builds the subsampled Gaussian. Its grid spacing is value_discretization_interval, whose default is \(10^{-4}\). Its argument pessimistic_estimate chooses the side of the rounding. Its default neighbouring relation is adding or removing one record, so it covers both directions and reports the larger. Then self_compose composes the steps and get_epsilon_for_delta reads off \(\varepsilon\):
from dp_accounting.pld import privacy_loss_distribution as pld_lib

step = pld_lib.from_gaussian_mechanism(standard_deviation=1.0, sampling_prob=0.01,
    value_discretization_interval=1e-5, pessimistic_estimate=True)
upper = step.self_compose(10_000).get_epsilon_for_delta(1e-5)
Run it again with pessimistic_estimate=False for the lower bound.
Its event interface, dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant, composes a PoissonSampledDpEvent that wraps a GaussianDpEvent, and get_epsilon(target_delta) returns the pessimistic value. Microsoft’s prv_accountant package takes the error you accept instead of a grid spacing. Its PRVAccountant takes a list of mechanisms, such as PoissonSubsampledGaussianMechanism, with max_self_compositions, eps_error and delta_error. Then compute_epsilon(delta, num_self_compositions) returns a lower bound, an estimate and an upper bound, and you report the upper one. The accountant is set up for at most max_self_compositions steps of each mechanism, so make that at least the number of steps you will run. Opacus uses the same accountant by default, through PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv"). If two libraries’ brackets fail to overlap, one of them has a bug (Choosing an accountant).
A numerical accountant is slower than RDP, but one run of it is cheap next to training. The cost adds up when you calibrate the noise, because a search evaluates the accountant at many noise levels. So search with RDP, then confirm the final noise level with the PLD.

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.1 Why this matters
Uncertainty is worth privacy, as subsampling showed, and two other kinds of it matter in practice. The first is about which report is yours. In the shuffle model (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models), each of \(n\) users randomizes their own data, and a shuffler strips identities and mixes the order. Each report satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at a level \(\varepsilon_0\) that is usually large. But your report hides among the others, so the bag of reports satisfies central DP with an \(\varepsilon\) that falls like \(1/\sqrt n\).
The second is uncertainty about what happened inside training. If only the final model is released, later noise also covers a record used early, and on a convex loss the privacy loss can even stop growing. Of the two, shuffling is a deployable tool with a computable guarantee, used for example in Prochlo (Bittau et al. 2017). Hidden-state amplification, by contrast, rarely applies to deep learning. All results use replace-one neighbours, two datasets of the same size that differ in the value of one record.
crumbs: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.2 Shuffled binary randomized response, exactly
For the simplest local randomizer, the shuffled guarantee can be computed exactly. Each user holds a bit and sends it through binary randomized response (The definition of differential privacy). The user reports the true bit with probability \(\theta = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\) and the flipped bit otherwise. After shuffling, the analyst learns only how many reports are 1, and your report moves that count by at most one.
So the guarantee is the privacy of a pair of count distributions. Let your bit be 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\), and suppose the other users all hold 0. Each of them reports 1 with probability \(1 - \theta\), so the number of their 1-reports is binomial, and we write \(b(y)\) for its chance of being \(y\). The count is then distributed as \[P(y) = \theta\,b(y) + (1 - \theta)\,b(y - 1), \qquad Q(y) = (1 - \theta)\,b(y) + \theta\,b(y - 1), \tag{35.1}\] when you hold 0 and when you hold 1. Its exact privacy curve is a sum over the possible counts, the same sum as in Numerical accounting. You compute it in both directions and keep the larger, which the snippet in Section 35.7 does in a few seconds. Other values for the other users change it by less than \(10^{-4}\) in the full edition’s checks.
For intuition, the count is close to normal, and your report shifts its mean against a spread that grows like \(\sqrt n\). So the shuffled count approximately satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) (f-DP and Gaussian DP), with a shift in standard deviations of \[\mu \approx \frac{2\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt n}. \tag{35.2}\] Don’t deploy with this approximation, because it fails when the others send few 1-reports. For example, with 1000 users at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), it gives 0.9667 where the exact value is 1.6910.
Shuffling never improves pure DP, the guarantee whose slack \(\delta\) is zero. An all-zero count is still \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times likelier when you hold 0, however many users there are, and shuffling only makes it rare. So any shuffled guarantee below \(\varepsilon_0\) needs \(\delta > 0\).
crumbs: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 35.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
text:
35.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
Real deployments send histograms, categories or noisy vectors, so you need a bound for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer, the randomized map from one user’s data to their report. The bound to use is that of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021). Its idea is that each other user is, with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), a clone whose report looks exactly like one of your two possible reports.
That reduction gives a small pair of count distributions, whose exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the numeric clone bound. It holds for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer, even one chosen adaptively, as when each user randomizes their own gradient in shuffled stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The same paper also gives a closed form, which needs enough clones to hide among, \[\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{35.3}\] When that holds, the shuffled output is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right). \tag{35.4}\] For large \(n\) its leading term gives the shape to remember, because the central \(\varepsilon\) falls like \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/n}\) with a constant that grows like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). Where the condition fails, though, the closed form says nothing.

The closed form is 3.10 to 4.75 times the numeric bound where it applies. So use the closed form to reason about scaling, and compute the numeric bound to deploy.
