title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 35.4 Choosing ε₀ and deploying a shuffler
text:
35.4 Choosing ε₀ and deploying a shuffler
The practical question runs backwards, because you want the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) that meets a target central guarantee, which means the least noise per report. So compute the bound for a few candidate values of \(\varepsilon_0\) and keep the largest that meets the target. The choice of bound can decide feasibility, and a larger \(\varepsilon_0\) buys accuracy. Take 100,000 users and a target of 0.2 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Among the values in Table 35.1, the closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0\) up to 2, while the numeric clone bound allows 4.
Before you report a shuffled \(\varepsilon\), check that the deployment meets the assumptions of the bound.

The order is uniformly random and hidden. With a fixed or leaked order, or metadata such as arrival time or network address, the analyst knows which report is yours, and the guarantee falls back to \(\varepsilon_0\).
The shuffler is trusted not to collude with the analyst. If they collude, again only \(\varepsilon_0\) remains.
The other users are honest. Users who collude with the analyst reveal their own reports, so count only honest users in \(n\).
The computation uses the number of reports actually shuffled. The bound gets worse as \(n\) falls, so use the smallest batch you will release, not the number of users enrolled.
Each user sends one report per batch. Otherwise the reports compose like any other releases.
crumbs: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.5 Amplification by iteration
Suppose projected noisy SGD makes one pass over \(n\) records and releases only the final model. Then the noise of every later step protects a record used early (Feldman et al. 2018). The guarantee needs every step to be a contraction, a map that never pushes two models further apart. Write \(\beta\) for the smoothness of the loss, the most its gradient changes per unit of distance. A gradient step on a convex loss is then a contraction when the step size is at most \(2/\beta\). A projection onto a convex set is one too. With Lipschitz losses as well, the record used at the \(t\)-th step gets one Gaussian step’s Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve. That curve is divided by the \(n - t + 1\) noisy steps from \(t\) to the end.
So the guarantee depends on the position, and a report must state the worst one. For a pass over 10,000 records with noise multiplier 1, the last record gets \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), converted as in RDP conversions. That is a single Gaussian step, with no amplification at all, while the record in the middle gets 0.0707.
crumbs: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 35.6 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
text:
35.6 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
Full-batch noisy gradient descent (GD) uses every record at every step, so composition charges in proportion to the number of steps. On a bounded convex set, though, the runs on \(D\) and \(D'\) can never drift further apart than the set’s diameter \(d_K\), the largest distance between two of its points. Altschuler & Talwar (2022) prove that the privacy loss of the last iterate then stops growing. Write \(s\) for the per-step shift between the runs and \(\sigma\) for the per-step noise, both in parameter units. When \(d_K/s\) is an integer, the RDP of the last iterate stays below \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \frac{2\alpha d_Ks}{\sigma^2} \tag{35.5}\] however long you train.
For example, on the unit interval with \(s = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\), the bound stops at 4.0000 at order 2, while composition charges 20.0000 for 2000 steps. Strong convexity gives a plateau without a bounded set, because each step then shrinks the gap between the runs. The plateau arrives after about as many steps as the loss’s condition number (Chourasia, Ye & Shokri 2021).
These results need two conditions, and deep learning breaks both. No mainstream library, Opacus or dp_accounting included, offers last-iterate accounting. The first is that only the last iterate is released. Checkpoints, logged models or picking the best checkpoint put you back to composition. The second is that every step is a contraction, which requires a convex loss. Annamalai (2024) constructs a non-convex loss for which the last iterate of differentially private SGD (DP-SGD) leaks as much as all iterates together. So never report a hidden-state \(\varepsilon\) for non-convex training, and account for it with the ordinary DP-SGD composition instead. Use it for convex models, such as private logistic regression, that release only their final weights.
crumbs: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.7 Code
This snippet computes the exact central \(\varepsilon\) of shuffled binary randomized response from Equation 35.1, so you can use it to choose \(\varepsilon_0\). With SciPy, scipy.stats.binom.pmf gives the binomial probabilities directly.
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def log_binom_pmf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    return lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(p) + (n - k) * log(1 - p)


def shuffled_rr_pair(n: int, eps0: float) -> tuple[list[float], list[float]]:
    theta = exp(eps0) / (1 + exp(eps0))
    b = [exp(log_binom_pmf(y, n - 1, 1 - theta)) for y in range(n)] + [0.0]
    P = [theta * b[y] + (1 - theta) * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    Q = [(1 - theta) * b[y] + theta * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    return P, Q


def hockey_stick(P: list[float], Q: list[float], eps: float) -> float:
    return sum(max(p - exp(eps) * q, 0.0) for p, q in zip(P, Q))


def shuffled_rr_epsilon(n: int, eps0: float, delta: float) -> float:
    P, Q = shuffled_rr_pair(n, eps0)
    lo, hi = 0.0, eps0  # shuffling never does worse than the local eps0
    for _ in range(50):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        worst = max(hockey_stick(P, Q, mid), hockey_stick(Q, P, mid))
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if worst > delta else (lo, mid)
    return hi


print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(10_000, 2.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0870
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(100_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0847
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(1_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 1.6910

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.1 Why this matters
Every composition theorem so far assumes that each step’s privacy parameter, and the number of steps, are fixed before the run (Advanced and optimal composition). Real training breaks this whenever you stop on the validation loss or lower the noise as training stalls. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD, adds a third case, since a record with a small gradient costs less than the worst case. Plugging the values that occurred into a fixed-parameter theorem gives a report that can be wrong several times as often as it claims.
Fixed-step DP-SGD with a schedule chosen in advance needs none of this. Otherwise, which tool you need depends on what you fixed in advance. If only the stopping time adapts within a planned maximum, report \(\varepsilon\) for the maximum. If you fixed a budget and want to spend it adaptively, a privacy filter decides before each step whether it still fits. If you fixed nothing, a privacy odometer reports what you have spent so far, at a small extra price.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
section: 36.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
text:
36.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
Advanced composition bounds the total privacy loss of a run (Numerical accounting), except with a failure probability \(\delta\), when the number of steps is fixed in advance. Applying it ex post, at a stopping time chosen from the outputs, is a different claim that Rogers et al. (2016) showed to be invalid.
A simple rule breaks it. Run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) on one person’s bit, step after step, so that the total loss is a random walk. The plug-in bound is correct at every fixed step, but an analyst may stop the first time the walk crosses it and report the bound at that step. At \(\delta = 0.01\), the full edition finds this report wrong with probability 0.0318 within 10,000 steps, over three times its claim. Given enough steps, the walk crosses the bound with probability 1.
Two kinds of report escape the problem. For pure DP, basic composition, the plain sum of the per-step parameters, bounds the loss of every output, so it is valid however you stop. And a filter escapes, because it fixes its budget in advance and makes no running claim that a stopping rule could catch out.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
section: 36.3 Early stopping within a planned maximum
text:
36.3 Early stopping within a planned maximum
The commonest adaptive run needs no new theory. You fix the noise, the sampling rate and a maximum number of steps before training, and you stop early when the validation loss stops improving. Then report the \(\varepsilon\) of the planned maximum, not of the steps you ran. The run that stopped early releases a prefix of the full planned run. Anything computed from that prefix, including the decision to stop, is post-processing of the full run, so the full run’s guarantee covers it.
For example, plan 100 full-batch Gaussian steps whose noise multiplier is 10. That run is \((5.299, 10^{-5})\)-DP, so if you stop at step 60, you still report 5.299.
The rule has three conditions. First, the stopping decision must look only at released outputs, or at data you account for separately, because a decision that reads the private data leaks through the stopping time. Second, the maximum, the noise and the sampling rate must really be fixed. If you might extend training past the plan, you need a filter or an odometer. Third, report with the same accountant and \(\delta\) you calibrated with. Choosing hyperparameters from several runs is a separate cost, which Hyperparameter tuning accounts for.
Library accountants are not odometers. In Opacus, PrivacyEngine.make_private_with_epsilon calibrates the noise for a target \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) over a planned number of epochs. Its get_epsilon(delta), like the one in Google’s dp_accounting, composes the steps taken so far and converts them once. That is valid only at a time fixed in advance, so call it at the planned end, or report the target you calibrated for.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.4 The Rényi filter
When the noise itself changes during training, use a Rényi filter. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) measures each step by a curve over orders \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP). Fix one order and an RDP budget \(B\) before the run. Each step then has a spend, its RDP at that order, which may depend on earlier outputs but must be known before the step runs, so it is called predictable. Write \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) for the spend of the \(t\)-th step. The filter runs that step only if the spends so far, its own included, fit in the budget, \[\sum_{j \le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha) \le B. \tag{36.1}\] Then the stopped run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP, as if the spends had been fixed in advance (Feldman and Zrnic 2021).
Each condition matters, because a spend that depended on its own step’s output could be small exactly where the output reveals the most. The budget must also hold on every path, not on average. And the order must be fixed before the run, although you may track several and stop when any one runs out.
To aim at a DP target, write \(\varepsilon_g\) for the global privacy level you want. Then set the budget from the conversion of RDP conversions, run backwards, \[B = \varepsilon_g - \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{36.2}\] For example, a target of \((5.299, 10^{-5})\) at order 5.8 gives \(B = 2.900\). A full-batch Gaussian step spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma_t^2)\), where \(\sigma_t\) is its noise multiplier, so with \(\sigma_t\) at 10 the budget lasts 100 steps. Now suppose training plateaus at step 60 and you halve the noise. Each later step then costs four times as much, so the filter allows 10 more steps. Either way the run is \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP, whatever rule decided the switch, provided that rule looks only at released outputs.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.5 Filters for pure differential privacy
Interactive query systems give each query a pure-DP parameter \(\varepsilon_t\), chosen from earlier answers. The basic filter of Rogers et al. (2016) continues while they sum to at most the global \(\varepsilon_g\). It is exact, but its budget grows like the number of steps.
For square-root growth, use the Whitehouse filter of Whitehouse et al. (2023). It continues while \[\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2} + \tfrac12\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \varepsilon_g, \tag{36.3}\] summing over the steps so far and the one about to run, and its stopped run is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP. It reads like advanced composition because it is the Rényi filter applied to zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated DP), so adaptivity costs essentially nothing.
For example, a budget of 1 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) lets the Whitehouse filter run 349 steps of 0.01. That is slightly more than advanced composition allows with the number of steps fixed in advance. So use the Whitehouse form, checked before each step with that step’s parameter included.
For an analytics service, use a library that enforces the budget for you. OpenDP’s make_privacy_filter wraps an odometer built with make_fully_adaptive_composition and rejects any query that would push the total past its bound. Tumult Analytics tracks a Session’s remaining budget, such as a RhoZCDPBudget, and exposes it as Session.remaining_privacy_budget.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.6 Odometers
Open-ended analyses and training to a target accuracy have no budget to stop at. They need a running answer to “how much have I spent?” that holds at every step at once. The Ville odometer gives one. Fix a grid \(\Lambda\) of orders before the run, with \(|\Lambda|\) orders in it, and write \(S_t(\alpha)\) for the RDP spend so far at order \(\alpha\). With probability at least \(1 - \delta\), simultaneously for every step \(t\), the loss so far is at most \[U_t = \min_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\Big[S_t(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{36.4}\] This is the usual RDP conversion at the best order of the grid, with \(\delta\) replaced by \(\delta/|\Lambda|\), and that replacement is the whole price. So keep the grid small.
Over the part’s grid of orders, the price for full-batch Gaussian steps is 15 to 19%. For example, the 100-step run above gets 6.253 instead of 5.299. Lécuyer (2021) builds a slightly looser odometer from doubling Rényi filters.
An odometer is a tail bound, not a DP guarantee. To turn it into an \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP guarantee, stop by a rule that keeps the running bound at most \(\varepsilon_g\). If you have a budget anyway, a Rényi filter at one order fixed in advance is cheaper, because it needs no union over orders.
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.7 Individual privacy accounting in DP-SGD
A DP-SGD step clips each record’s gradient to a norm of at most the clipping norm \(C\), and adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\). The usual analysis charges every record as if its clipped gradient always had norm \(C\), but a record that the model fits moves the noisy sum less. Write \(\bar g_{i,t}\) for the clipped gradient of record \(i\) at step \(t\). With full-batch steps, that record’s spend is \[\varepsilon_{i,t}(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha\|\bar g_{i,t}\|^2}{2\sigma^2C^2} \le \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{36.5}\] This spend is predictable, because the gradient depends only on the record and the current model. So the individual filter of Feldman and Zrnic (2021) runs one Rényi filter per record and drops a record once its own spend would pass \(B\). Every record then has the guarantee of the worst-case run, while records with small gradients keep training long after.
In the full edition’s simulation with the order and budget above, the median typical record has an individual \(\varepsilon\) of 3.17 after 100 steps, against 5.299 for the worst case.
Read the per-record numbers with care. A per-record \(\varepsilon\) from the realized spend is an estimate, not a guarantee, because it is a fixed-time bound at a random quantity. It is also sensitive, since a small spend says that the model fits that record well, so show it only to the record’s owner. There is a fairness cost too, because the records the model serves poorly are dropped first, and these often come from under-represented groups (Yu et al. 2023; Disparate impact). Under Poisson subsampling, it needs every record’s gradient norm at every step, sampled or not (Koskela et al. 2023).
crumbs: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.8 Code
A filter or an odometer is a sum of spends and a test. This snippet codes the Rényi filter for a noise schedule, and prints the numbers of the example above.
from math import log


def renyi_filter(sigmas: list[float], alpha: float, budget: float) -> int:
    """Steps of a full-batch Gaussian noise schedule that a Renyi filter lets through."""
    spent, steps = 0.0, 0
    for sigma in sigmas:
        cost = alpha / (2 * sigma**2)
        if spent + cost > budget + 1e-12:  # tolerance for floating-point sums
            break
        spent, steps = spent + cost, steps + 1
    return steps


alpha, budget = 5.8, 2.9
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 1000, alpha, budget))  # 100
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 60 + [5.0] * 1000, alpha, budget) - 60)  # 10
print(f"{budget + log(1 / 1e-5) / (alpha - 1):.3f}")  # 5.299

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.1 Why this matters
You have trained a model with differential privacy (DP), using private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD (Amplification by subsampling). Each record joined each batch with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, here 0.01, and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) was 1. After 10,000 steps, a number this chapter writes \(k\), you must state the \(\varepsilon\) at which the model is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP, in a paper or a model card.
A procedure that bounds or estimates the true \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant, and on this run the accountants disagree by a factor of over a thousand. That is because they make different kinds of statement. An upper bound comes with a proof, so the run really is as private as it reports, while an approximation has none and may land below the truth. A certified lower bound is no guarantee, but it exposes any reported \(\varepsilon\) that is too small. So the rule of this chapter is short. Report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, and report enough that someone else can recompute it.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.2 Every accountant on one run
Accountants differ in how much of each step’s privacy they keep, filling in the rest with a worst case. From least to most, they are per-step composition and Rényi differential privacy (RDP), the central limit theorem (CLT) of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP), and the privacy loss distribution (PLD).

The proofs put the RDP bounds in a fixed order. With the optimal conversion, the smallest valid value for the curve, at the end, \[\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, Mironov}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, improved}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{true}}. \tag{37.1}\] Per-step composition, basic or advanced, is useless beyond a handful of steps, off by a factor of over a thousand after the full run. RDP is safe, and with the improved conversion it is 7.6% above the PLD at 10,000 steps, but far more on short runs. The CLT falls below the certified lower bound at every \(k\), so a paper that quotes it, such as 1.62 after 1,000 steps, claims a guarantee the run does not have.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
37.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
Practitioners usually fix the budget, the steps and the batch size, and then ask how much noise they need. For an accountant \(A\), write \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma)\) for the value it reports at noise multiplier \(\sigma\). The noise it requires for a target \(\varepsilon^*\) is then \[\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*) = \min\{\sigma > 0 : \varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\}. \tag{37.2}\] More noise never raises a correct accountant’s \(\varepsilon\), so a bisection finds it. Return the end of the bracket where the target was checked, because that end is safe.
A loose accountant turns its slack directly into extra noise. For a target of 3 over 10,000 steps, the pessimistic PLD needs \(\sigma = 1.584\), while RDP with the improved conversion needs 1.662. Across targets, the improved conversion costs up to 4.9% more noise than the PLD, and Mironov’s conversion far more. The CLT asks for less noise than the PLD, which at a target of 8 is provably too little. So calibrate \(\sigma\) with the accountant you will report.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.4 Where each accountant is tight
An accountant is tight only when its summary describes the mechanism exactly, so work through these questions in order.

Does the code match the accountant’s assumptions? Check this first (Section 37.5), because a mismatch costs more than any choice of accountant.
Are any parameters chosen during training? If only the stopping time adapts within a planned maximum, account for the maximum. If the noise or budget adapts, use a Rényi filter (Adaptive composition).
Is it the Gaussian mechanism without subsampling? Then the composed pair is exactly Gaussian, and GDP gives the exact \(\varepsilon\). RDP with the improved conversion is 8.0% above it on a hundred releases at \(\sigma = 10\), and zCDP gives the same as RDP here.
Is it DP-SGD, the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian? Then use the pessimistic PLD or a privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, with the optimistic value as the error bar. Avoid zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), because its single slope cannot express amplification by subsampling.
Are the steps pure DP, such as randomized response or the Laplace mechanism? The PLD is exact when the loss takes few values. A hundred randomized-response steps at 0.1 give 4.3068, against 4.6154 from RDP.
Do local reports pass through a shuffler, or is only the last model released? See Amplification by shuffling and by iteration.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.5 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
37.5 Matching the accountant to the code
Every number in Table 37.1 assumes a model of the training run that the accountant cannot check against your code. Many papers reported the Poisson-sampling number while training with shuffled fixed-size batches, a statement about a different algorithm (Ponomareva et al. 2023). So check each item of Table 37.2 before you report.

Fixed-size random batches: account with \(\sigma/2\). Shuffle and partition: report the unamplified guarantee


Neighbouring relation
Add or remove one record
Which relation does the claim state?
Replace-one costs more per step


Privacy unit
One example
Can one person contribute several examples?
Clip and sample per user, or pay for group privacy


Tuning and adaptivity
Settings fixed in advance
Tuning on private data, early stopping, noise schedules?
Account for the tuning runs; planned maximum, or a filter


Steps counted
Every step on private data
Warm-up runs, restarts, evaluation passes that release results?
Count them all


Noise scale
Noise standard deviation \(\sigma C\)
Is \(\sigma\) measured against the clipping norm actually used?
Recompute \(\sigma\) from the noise added






The sampler is the most expensive item. Lebeda et al. (2024) show that such a run is covered by the Poisson accountant at noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\). After the full run, the PLD upper bound rises from 6.24 to 43.42. That factor of 6.96 dwarfs any choice of accountant. Shuffle and partition is worse, because no amplification theorem covers it. What remains certain is one Gaussian step per epoch for zero-out neighbours, which gives \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\) over a hundred epochs at \(\sigma = 1\).
In a code review, a data loader with shuffle=True and a fixed batch_size is shuffle and partition, whatever sample_rate the accountant was given. Opacus samples by the Poisson scheme by default (poisson_sampling=True), so keep that default.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.6 What to report
An \(\varepsilon\) without its assumptions cannot be checked or compared, so Ponomareva et al. (2023) and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ask for the items below. Choose the slack \(\delta\) with care, because with \(n\) records, publishing one random record in full meets a \(\delta\) of about \(1/n\). So Ponomareva et al. ask for a \(\delta\) much smaller than \(1/n\), and NIST gives \(1/n^2\) as a common recommendation.
Reading \(\varepsilon\) off the composed PLD at another \(\delta\) is cheap, so report several values, not a single point. For the running example with 50,000 records, the pessimistic PLD gives 9.0502 at \(1/n^2\), against 6.2377 at \(10^{-5}\). Round upper bounds up, never to the nearest value, so 9.0502 becomes 9.06. A filled-in statement for the running example reads as follows.

Setting. DP-SGD in the central model. It covers every checkpoint and the final model.
Unit and neighbours. One training example per person, with neighbours that add or remove one example.
Training. Poisson sampling at rate 0.01 over 50,000 examples for 100 epochs, with clipping norm 1 and noise multiplier 1.
Accountant. The pessimistic PLD on the grid \(10^{-5}\), in both directions, with the library and its version.
Guarantee. The model is \((6.24, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((9.06, 4.0\times10^{-10})\)-DP. The optimistic values, 6.1377 and 8.9378, bound the accountant’s own error.
Not covered. Say what the guarantee leaves out, such as hyperparameters tuned on a public proxy dataset, pretraining on public data, or preprocessing statistics computed from the private data.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.7 Checking your accountant
An accountant is code, and code has bugs, so run checks whose answers you know. First, set \(q = 1\), which makes each step a plain Gaussian mechanism. Ten steps at \(\sigma = 1\) are then exactly \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and every upper bound must lie above it, as RDP’s 19.0536 does. Second, the PLD bracket on plain Gaussian steps must contain the exact value, which the calculator in Numerical accounting gives. Third, the order of Equation 37.1 must hold, with no upper bound below the optimistic PLD. Fourth, \(\varepsilon\) must never decrease as the number of steps grows, and never increase as the noise grows.
Then compare two maintained libraries, and pin their versions in your report. The full edition’s numbers agree with Opacus 1.6.0, dp_accounting 0.6.0 and prv_accountant 0.2.0. Disagreements usually have one of three causes. If two RDP accountants differ at each order by a fixed amount, 0.3612 at order 10, one of them uses Mironov’s conversion. Fractional orders are a weak spot of dp_accounting 0.6.0, where it returns a loose bound, so compare at integer orders. And if two PLD or PRV brackets fail to overlap, one library has a bug.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.8 Code
In Google’s dp_accounting, you describe the run as an event and compose it into an accountant. Restricting RDP to integer orders avoids the fractional-order weakness.
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(
    sampling_probability=0.01, event=dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=1.0))
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(event=step, count=10_000)

pld = dp_accounting.PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-5)
pld.compose(run)
eps_pld = pld.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5)       # should lie in [6.1377, 6.2377]
rdp = dp_accounting.RdpAccountant(orders=list(range(2, 65)))   # same compose / get_epsilon
For the inverse problem, dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism searches for the noise multiplier that meets a target \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). Opacus has opacus.accountants.utils.get_noise_multiplier, whose accountant argument defaults to "rdp", so pass "prv" to match the default of PrivacyEngine. Opacus’s "gdp" accountant uses the CLT, so never report it as a guarantee. For a cross-check, Microsoft’s prv_accountant installs a command-line tool that prints a lower bound, an estimate and an upper bound.
compute-dp-epsilon --sampling-probability 0.01 --noise-multiplier 1.0 --delta 1e-5 --num-compositions 10000

Rules of thumb

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
This part is for anyone who trains, ships or reviews a model under differential privacy (DP). It needs the Gaussian mechanism and composition from Part 3 and an accountant from Part 4. Audits also reuse the membership-inference attack of Part 2.
Every private training method has two halves. The privacy half is computed. The main algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. Its accountant derives \(\varepsilon\) from the noise multiplier, the sampling rate and the number of steps alone. The utility half, accuracy, is measured, not proved. So each chapter asks two questions: is the \(\varepsilon\) correct, and is the accuracy at that \(\varepsilon\) good enough?
The chapters follow the decisions of a project, and their order matters. First choose the privacy unit, a record or a person, as User-level differential privacy explains. Then fix the budget, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\), with Choosing ε. Only then choose the method. That is usually DP-SGD, or for a convex model one of the methods of Private empirical risk minimization. Sometimes it is better to answer queries privately, as in Private prediction, or to fine-tune a public model, as in Public data and private fine-tuning. When batches cannot be sampled at random, follow the regularized leader (FTRL) with correlated noise takes over, in DP-FTRL and matrix factorization.
Next, pay for the search over settings with Hyperparameter tuning and private selection. Finally, check which groups lose accuracy with Disparate impact, and test the model with planted records in Auditing private training. The two commonest mistakes are picking the method before the unit and the budget, and treating the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) as the end of the work.
Adaptive data analysis stands apart. It uses the same noise to keep a reused validation or test set honest, which protects conclusions rather than people.
The tools are Opacus for PyTorch, TensorFlow Privacy, and JAX Privacy, with Google’s dp_accounting or Microsoft’s prv_accountant for accounting. The running examples, a logistic regression and a small neural network, come with scripts that reproduce every number. By the end, you will be able to train a private model, defend its settings and its \(\varepsilon\), and audit it before you ship it.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.1 Why this matters
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM), which chooses the weights that minimize the average training loss, usually plus a penalty that keeps them short. The trained weights can give records away (Membership inference). Differential privacy (DP) bounds how much replacing one record can change what you release, through a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\). So randomness has to enter somewhere between the data and the released weights.
There are three places to put it, and each gives a classic algorithm. Output perturbation trains as usual and adds noise to the final weights, while objective perturbation adds a random term to the training objective and minimizes it exactly. Gradient perturbation goes furthest back and adds noise to every gradient step. Each one hides with noise how far one record can move some quantity, its sensitivity. For a convex model with a ridge penalty, objective perturbation is usually the most accurate. For anything else only gradient perturbation works, and with clipping and random batches it becomes stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with noise, DP-SGD.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.2 The setting and the noise
A training set \(D\) holds a number \(n\) of records, each with \(d\) features and a label of plus or minus one. Write \(\ell(w, z)\) for the loss of the weights \(w\) on a record \(z\). With a ridge of strength \(\lambda\), training minimizes the objective \(J\), \[J(w; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w, z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2, \tag{38.1}\] and its minimizer is written \(w^*\). Two datasets are neighbours here when one replaces a record of the other. Every sensitivity is built from one more number \(L\), a bound on the length of each record’s loss gradient. For logistic regression with features of length at most 1, \(L = 1\). A private release \(\tilde w\) is judged by its excess risk, the amount by which its objective exceeds the smallest possible value.
The running example is logistic regression with ten features and a ridge of 0.01, at a target of \((1, 10^{-5})\). Every Gaussian method here calibrates its noise exactly (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). For this target the noise must be 3.7306 times the sensitivity, and the classic formula asks for 30% more. The snippet in Section 38.10 computes the factor for any target.
For pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, with no slack, the noise vector instead has a density that falls exponentially with its length, with a scale equal to the sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\).
The guarantee holds only if your pipeline enforces the bounds it assumes. Clip or normalize every feature vector to length at most 1, with a bound fixed from public knowledge, because a norm computed from the private data leaks. Keep logistic labels at plus or minus one, and clip the labels of a linear regression to a public range, because \(L\) grows with them. Fix \(\lambda\) in advance, since choosing it by validation on private data is a search that must be paid for (Hyperparameter tuning). Finally, the ridge must cover every weight, the intercept included. Scikit-learn’s default solver leaves the intercept unpenalized, so drop it and append a constant feature instead, counted in the norm bound.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.3 Output perturbation
Output perturbation treats training as a black box (Chaudhuri & Monteleoni 2008). When the loss is convex, the ridge makes the objective strongly convex, and that pins down how far one record can move the minimizer, \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{38.2}\] Write \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest safe ratio of sensitivity to noise, which is 0.2681 for the running example’s target. The release adds to the minimizer a Gaussian vector \(Z\), with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) on each coordinate, \[\tilde w = w^*(D) + Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N\big(0, \sigma^2I\big), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{\lambda n\,\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{38.3}\] With ten thousand records the sensitivity is 0.02, and the noise is 0.07461 per coordinate.
What goes wrong is the solver. The bound holds for the exact minimizer, and an optimizer that stops where the gradient has length \(g\) adds \(2g/\lambda\) to the sensitivity. In the running example, a tolerance of \(10^{-3}\) raises the sensitivity to 0.22, eleven times the exact value. So stop on a gradient length below \(L/n\), checked at the end, never on a fixed step count.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.4 Objective perturbation
Objective perturbation (Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate 2011) adds a random linear term to the objective and minimizes the result exactly. All of the objective’s curvature resists that term, so data that add curvature also reduce the damage.
It needs a loss of a particular form. The loss must depend on the weights only through the margin, the label times the inner product of the weights and the features. Its slope must be at most 1, its curvature between 0 and a known constant \(c\), and the features of length at most 1. Logistic regression qualifies with \(c = \frac14\). A small share of the budget pays for the curvature, and the noise gets what is left, \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big). \tag{38.4}\] The noise \(b\) is the pure-DP noise with scale \(2/\varepsilon'\), and the release is \[\tilde w = \arg\min_w\Big[J(w; D) + \frac1n\langle b, w\rangle\Big]. \tag{38.5}\] This is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. If \(\varepsilon'\) comes out zero or negative, raise the ridge until the curvature share takes at most half of the budget. With ten thousand records in the running example, the noise keeps 0.9950 of the budget.
When the data’s curvature near the minimizer is about \(h\) in every direction, objective perturbation beats output perturbation by a factor of about \((h/\lambda)^2\). In the running example \(h\) is about three times the ridge, and the excess risk is ten times smaller.
The price is exact minimization, which no solver delivers, and floating-point rounding can itself leak (Discrete mechanisms). The loss must also be smooth, so a hinge loss must be smoothed first.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.5 Gradient perturbation: noisy gradient descent
The third method makes each training step private and composes the steps. Its simplest form is full-batch gradient descent from zero weights, with a step size \(\eta\) and a fixed number of steps, written \(T\). At every step \(t\), fresh Gaussian noise, written \(\xi_t\), is added to the gradient, so the update is \[w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta\big(\nabla J(w_t; D) + \xi_t\big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{38.6}\] Releasing every iterate is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any loss whose per-record gradients have length at most \(L\), convex or not. The noise grows like \(\sqrt T\) because Gaussian steps compose exactly, by the rules of Gaussian differential privacy.
So the step count is a privacy parameter. Too few steps leave optimization error, and too many drown the solution in noise. For a strongly convex objective you can choose \(T\) from public quantities only, such as the largest curvature the logistic loss allows, and with ten thousand records this rule picks 218 steps. Choosing \(T\) by its validation score instead is a computation on the data that must be paid for.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.6 Noisy gradient descent without a ridge
text:
38.6 Noisy gradient descent without a ridge
Many convex models have no useful ridge. Then keep the weights in a ball whose radius \(R\) is fixed in advance from public knowledge. Shrink them back onto it after each noisy step, and release the average of the iterates. The noise is the same as in Equation 38.6, and the excess risk falls like \(RL\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\), which is optimal up to logarithms. The cost is computation, since ten thousand records already need 179,629 full passes, so practice runs the same idea on random minibatches.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.7 How the three compare
For strongly convex objectives, the best excess risk that any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm can guarantee is of order \[\frac{L^2\,d}{\lambda\,n^2\varepsilon^2}, \tag{38.7}\] up to logarithms. So a model with more parameters loses more accuracy at the same privacy level. And \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\) appear only as their product, so halving \(\varepsilon\) costs the same accuracy as halving the data. On the running example, objective perturbation has the lowest excess risk at every dataset size.
Pure-DP noise also beats Gaussian noise there, but only because the dimension is small, since its mean squared length grows like \(d^2\) rather than \(d\), so prefer Gaussian noise for large models.
How much data do you need before the noise stops hurting? Predictions are more forgiving than excess risk. With a thousand records, objective perturbation lowers held-out accuracy from 0.747 to 0.736, and output perturbation lowers it to 0.681. With ten thousand records, all four releases come within 0.002 of non-private accuracy, so a low-dimensional convex model can be made private almost for free. As a rule, privacy adds little to the sampling error once the number of records is well above \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\) (Bassily et al. 2019).

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.8 When the model is not convex
text:
38.8 When the model is not convex
A neural network’s loss is not convex, and that breaks output and objective perturbation, which both need a unique minimizer that moves little. Gradient perturbation keeps its guarantee, because its proof used only the gradient bound. But a network’s gradients have no bound, so you clip each record’s gradient to a length \(C\) (Beyond global sensitivity), which biases what is optimized. Clipping, noise, random minibatches and an accountant together make DP-SGD.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.9 Libraries
For a linear model you rarely need to write any of this. IBM’s diffprivlib offers LogisticRegression(epsilon=..., data_norm=...), modelled on scikit-learn’s, which implements objective perturbation. Set data_norm, the largest feature-vector length, yourself and clip to it, because if you leave it unset diffprivlib computes it from the data and warns that this leaks. Its LinearRegression takes epsilon with bounds_X and bounds_y, the public ranges of the features and labels. Both stop an iterative solver at a tolerance, so the exact-minimizer condition holds only approximately.
Output perturbation needs only an ordinary solver and a noise draw. Scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression minimizes \(C\) times the summed loss plus half the squared weights, so \(C = 1/(\lambda n)\) gives the objective of this chapter.
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf = LogisticRegression(C=1 / (lam * n), fit_intercept=False, tol=tol, max_iter=max_iter)
clf.fit(X, y)                                     # rows of X with length <= 1
sigma = 2 * L / (lam * n * mu)                    # mu from the snippet below
w = clf.coef_.ravel() + np.random.default_rng().normal(0, sigma, X.shape[1])
Choose tol well below \(L/n\) and check the final gradient length, since the default tolerance voids the sensitivity bound. For a model trained by gradient steps, use Opacus as in DP-SGD. Its accountant assumes add/remove neighbours rather than replacement, so state the relation next to each \(\varepsilon\).

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.10 Code
The snippet finds the largest safe Gaussian ratio by bisection and sizes the noise of output perturbation for the running example.
from math import erfc, exp, sqrt


def phi(x: float) -> float:
    """Standard normal cumulative distribution function."""
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest sensitivity-to-noise ratio mu for which the Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 50.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        d = phi(mid / 2 - eps / mid) - exp(eps) * phi(-mid / 2 - eps / mid)
        lo, hi = (lo, mid) if d > delta else (mid, hi)
    return lo


mu = gaussian_mu(1.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{mu:.4f} {1 / mu:.4f}")  # 0.2681 3.7306
print(f"{2 / (0.01 * 10_000) / mu:.5f}")  # 0.07461

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.1 Why this matters
Nearly every deep-learning system that satisfies differential privacy (DP) runs one algorithm. It is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with each example’s gradient clipped to a fixed length and Gaussian noise added to every step, called DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016). Clipping bounds one record’s influence for any model (Private empirical risk minimization). An accountant then adds up the cost of every step into one privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\).
The privacy analysis never looks inside the model, so the settings split in two. The noise, the sampling rate and the number of steps decide \(\varepsilon\), while the clipping norm and the step size are free to be tuned for accuracy. Most failures come from code that silently breaks the proof, so a checklist matters as much as the settings.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.2 The algorithm and its guarantee
A training set holds \(n\) records, and the gradient of one record’s loss is its per-example gradient, written \(g_i\) for record \(i\). DP-SGD repeats five operations at every step.

Sample a batch. Each record enters independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, which is called Poisson sampling.
Compute the per-example gradient of each record in the batch.
Clip each gradient longer than the clipping norm \(C\) to length \(C\).
Add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate of the sum, where the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) measures the noise in units of \(C\).
Divide by the expected batch size, the fixed number \(B = qn\), and step against the result, scaled by the step size \(\eta\).

Write \(w_t\) for the weights at step \(t\) and \(S_t\) for its batch. Then the update, with fresh Gaussian noise \(\xi_t\), is \[w_{t+1} = w_t - \frac{\eta}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big) + \xi_t\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I). \tag{39.1}\] Releasing every intermediate set of weights is then \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ because one has a record the other lacks. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant computes \(\varepsilon\) from the sampling rate, the noise multiplier and the number of steps alone (Amplification by subsampling).
This part’s running example takes 10,000 steps with \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), which costs \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). To pick \(\sigma\) for a target, fix the rate and the number of steps and let the accountant solve for it. With the same settings, \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs a noise multiplier of 4.13.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.3 The implementation checklist
The guarantee rests on four conditions, each a property of your code that a reviewer can check. Code that breaks one still trains and reports as before.
First, one record must move the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Batch normalization breaks this, because its statistics let one record change every other record’s gradient, so private models use group or layer normalization instead. The clipping norm must also be fixed in advance, since a \(C\) set from the current batch makes the noise depend on the data.
Second, the accountant must assume the sampler the code actually runs (Amplification by subsampling). Many data loaders shuffle once per epoch and cut the data into fixed batches. A record is then never absent from an epoch, and the true \(\varepsilon\) can be far above the Poisson number. Fixed-size batches drawn afresh at every step are covered under add/remove if you give a Poisson accountant the batch’s fraction of the data as its rate and half your noise multiplier.
Third, divide the noisy sum by the public number \(B\), never by the actual batch size, because the actual size changes when the target record is added.
Fourth, the accountant must count every step that touched the data, including those of runs discarded during tuning.
Beyond the proof, state the neighbouring relation next to every \(\varepsilon\), since under replacement one record can move the sum by \(2C\). Preprocessing that looks at the data, such as normalizing by the mean, must itself be private. And a person with many records needs user-level privacy.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.4 Clipping and the step size
The clipping norm leaves privacy alone but controls both of its costs. A small \(C\) clips more gradients, so records with large gradients count for less, and they are often rare examples (Disparate impact). A large \(C\) instead means more noise, since the noise is \(\sigma C\).
When every gradient is clipped, only the product \(\eta C\) of the step size and the clipping norm matters. So the practical recipe is to clip hard and tune one number. On the running example, holding \(\eta C\) at 0.25 keeps test accuracy at 0.9599 or above for every \(C\) up to 0.3. With the step size held fixed instead, a clipping norm of 10 drops accuracy to 0.8347.
What goes wrong is that gradient norms drift. The median per-example gradient norm of the running example falls from 3.592 to 0.006 in a thousand steps, so a \(C\) that clips everything early clips only a minority later. Adaptive clipping, which tracks a quantile of the norms privately, follows the drift for a small share of the budget, and Opacus offers it as clipping="adaptive".

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
39.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
Suppose the privacy budget and the number of epochs, passes over the data, are fixed. Should you take many small steps or a few large ones? For a small sampling rate and a noise multiplier well above 1, the noise multiplier must grow like \(\sqrt q\). Since \(q\) is \(B/n\), the noise on the averaged gradient falls with the batch size, \[\sigma \propto \sqrt{\frac Bn}, \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}. \tag{39.2}\] Small batches are even worse than this law says, because they need a noise multiplier near or below 1, where each step costs more than the law assumes. For example, take a budget of \(\varepsilon = 4\) over 100 epochs. Going from a batch of 10 to one of 1,000 then cuts the noise per averaged gradient by a factor of 18.6, where the law predicts 10.
Fewer steps are the price, and a larger step size pays it. At scale, De et al. (2022) and Anil et al. (2022) report that very large batches are a main ingredient of accurate models. So choose the largest batch that your hardware and your epoch count allow, and scale the step size up with it.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.6 Making it fast
Computed one record at a time, DP-SGD can run up to two orders of magnitude slower than ordinary training. Of the three fixes, two are free. Vectorized per-example gradients, through torch.func.vmap with grad, JAX’s vmap or Opacus’s backward hooks, compute exactly the same clipped sum in parallel, so they change only the running time. Ghost clipping saves memory as well. A dense layer’s per-example gradient is the outer product of the layer’s input and the error flowing back into it. Its length is therefore the product of their lengths, so the norms come without forming the gradients.
Microbatching is the costly fix. It averages fixed groups of records and clips the averages, but one record can then flip its group’s clipped average, so the sensitivity doubles to \(2C\). Write \(m\) for the number of records per group. The noise on each coordinate of the averaged update then becomes \[2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B} \tag{39.3}\] at the same \(\varepsilon\). On the running example, groups of 4 cut test accuracy from 0.9589 to 0.9336, so use it only as a last resort, and check that your library charges for it.

So the best private model is often smaller than the best non-private one, unless public pretraining does most of the work.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.8 The Opacus workflow
To make a PyTorch training loop private, Opacus wraps an ordinary model, optimizer and data loader. First, ModuleValidator.fix(model) replaces batch normalization with group normalization. A PrivacyEngine then returns private versions of all three. Its make_private_with_epsilon picks the noise multiplier for a target \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and number of epochs, while make_private takes noise_multiplier directly. Both take max_grad_norm, the clipping norm, and by default replace the loader with one that draws Poisson batches (poisson_sampling=True). The engine’s default accountant is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, "prv", and accountant="rdp" selects the Rényi one.
from opacus import PrivacyEngine
from opacus.validators import ModuleValidator

model = ModuleValidator.fix(model)               # BatchNorm -> GroupNorm
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
engine = PrivacyEngine()                         # accountant="prv" by default
model, optimizer, loader = engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=optimizer, data_loader=loader,
    target_epsilon=4.0, target_delta=1e-5, epochs=epochs, max_grad_norm=C)
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for x, y in loader:                          # Poisson batches
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        criterion(model(x), y).backward()        # per-example gradients
        optimizer.step()                         # clip, add noise, step
print(engine.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5))
To size the noise before training, opacus.accountants.utils.get_noise_multiplier(target_epsilon=..., target_delta=..., sample_rate=..., epochs=...) solves for \(\sigma\). When a large batch does not fit in memory, BatchMemoryManager from opacus.utils.batch_memory_manager splits it into smaller physical batches but still steps once per logical batch, so the accounting is unchanged. Passing grad_sample_mode="ghost" turns on ghost clipping, and make_private then also returns a wrapped loss function. In TensorFlow, TensorFlow Privacy’s DPKerasSGDOptimizer takes l2_norm_clip, noise_multiplier and num_microbatches, and the last should equal the batch size.
Tune in a fixed order. First fix \(\varepsilon\), a \(\delta\) below \(1/n\) and the number of epochs, since they are the contract. Then choose a large batch, thousands of examples if you can, and let the accountant set the noise multiplier. Finally, set \(C\) near or below the median per-example gradient norm, measured on public or proxy data, and search the step size, which now stands for \(\eta C\). Count that search as Hyperparameter tuning explains.
When a private model is much worse than its non-private twin, the noise is too long for the signal. Change the batch size first, then train fewer weights, for instance by starting from a public model. If training diverges, lower \(\eta C\). And if \(\varepsilon\) looks too good, look for a shuffling loader, a microbatch setting or uncounted tuning runs.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise satisfies differential privacy (DP) at the level its accountant reports for one run, and is called DP-SGD. But nobody trains once. You try a grid of step sizes, score each model on a validation set and ship the best, and every run and every score touched private data. So the search leaks, and you must pay for it honestly.
The answer depends on one choice. With a fixed number of runs, releasing the best can cost as much as releasing all of them. For example, one run of this part’s running example costs a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 6.71, but a grid of 10 runs costs 27.23. Now draw the number of runs at random, from a distribution fixed in advance. The same expected number of runs then costs between 10.08 and 13.67.
crumbs: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.2 The procedure and the report
First, spend private runs only where you must, because the cheapest tuning is tuning you don’t do on private data. Runs on public or proxy data cost nothing, and so do published DP-SGD settings for similar tasks. Fix a large batch, the number of epochs and a small clipping norm in advance. Below the typical gradient norm only the clipping norm’s product with the step size matters, so that product is often the only thing left to search (DP-SGD). Use tuners such as Optuna or Ray Tune on private data only for random search, with the number of runs drawn first.
Second, fix the search before you touch the private data. Write down the candidate set, the distribution of the number of runs, the score and the validation set. Deciding to “try a few more”, or restarting a search whose result disappoints, makes the search depend on the data, and no theorem covers that.
Third, make the score private, with a disjoint validation set and noise on each count of correct predictions (Section 40.6). Fourth, account for the whole search. For two or three candidates, charge for every run by composition (Section 40.4). For more, use random search with a random number of runs (Section 40.5). Count every run that touched the private data, including crashed runs, debugging runs and evaluations used for early stopping.
Log the candidate set, the drawn number of runs, and each run’s hyperparameters, accounting settings and noisy score. Opacus’s get_epsilon reports one run only, so compose the runs in an accountant yourself. If you trained 50 configurations at \(\varepsilon = 2\) each, the honest answer is not 2 but the composition of all 50, which grows almost linearly at large \(\varepsilon\) (Table 40.1).
Finally, report two numbers. The \(\varepsilon\) of the released run says what the model alone would leak, while the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure is what the release actually guarantees. For the Poisson search of Section 40.7, a complete report reads as follows.

DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate 0.01, clipping norm 0.5, noise multiplier 1.53 and 1,000 steps. One run satisfies \((0.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The step size was selected by random search over \(\{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\), with a Poisson number of runs with mean 8. Each run was scored by its correct predictions on a disjoint validation set of 5,000 records, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20. The whole procedure satisfies \((1.99, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022, Theorem 6), for add/remove neighbours at the record level.

An audit tests only the released model, so it cannot catch a missing tuning charge.
crumbs: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.3 The best of k runs can cost k runs
text:
40.3 The best of k runs can cost k runs
A common argument says that choosing among eight step sizes reveals at most three bits. It is wrong, because the release is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. If each run is a randomized response that comes out “good” or “bad”, the best of \(k\) runs is bad only if every run is bad. The evidence from that event multiplies across runs, so the best of \(k\) runs is exactly \(k\varepsilon\)-DP.
Tuning without privacy and then training once privately does not escape this. Even a single chosen regularization weight can reveal whether a few outliers were in the training set (membership inference).
crumbs: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.4 Paying by composition
The safe answer is to charge for every run. The best run is computed from the runs’ outputs alone, so it costs at most what releasing all of them costs (Properties of DP). Rényi differential privacy (RDP) describes each run by a curve \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\) over orders \(\lambda\) (Rényi DP). The curves of \(k\) runs add, so the whole search has a curve \(\varepsilon_A\) of at most \[\varepsilon_A(\lambda) \le k\,\varepsilon(\lambda). \tag{40.1}\] For DP-SGD this is simple, because \(k\) runs of a number of steps \(T\) cost exactly as much as one run of \(kT\) steps.
In the running example, ten runs cost 4.06 times one run, because the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\) pays its fixed cost only once. To keep ten runs at the budget of one, each run needs a noise multiplier of 2.45, which costs accuracy.
crumbs: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.5 A random number of runs
The way past the \(k\varepsilon\) barrier is to draw the number of runs at random, independently of the data. Then “every run was bad” is mostly explained by the search stopping early. Liu & Talwar (2019) showed this first for random stopping, which stops after each run with a fixed probability and costs \(3\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\)-DP runs.
For DP-SGD, use the version of Papernot & Steinke (2022), which works with RDP curves. First fix the candidate set and a distribution for the number of runs \(K\). It is either Poisson or truncated negative binomial, a family with a shape parameter \(\eta\). Then draw \(K\) and run that many candidates drawn at random from the set. Release the best by a noisy score. The whole search then costs about one run, plus a term that grows only with the logarithm of the expected number of runs, \[\varepsilon_A(\lambda) \le \varepsilon(\lambda) + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\lambda - 1} + (\text{a term set by the shape of } K). \tag{40.2}\] For pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP runs it tends to \((2 + \eta)\varepsilon\), so the logarithmic distribution (\(\eta = 0\)) gives \(2\varepsilon\) and the geometric (\(\eta = 1\)) gives \(3\varepsilon\). Google’s dp_accounting computes it, by composing in an RdpAccountant a RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(event, mean, shape) that wraps one run’s event. Its shape is infinite for Poisson, 1 for geometric and 0 for logarithmic.
import dp_accounting
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(
    dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
search = dp_accounting.dp_event.RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(run, mean=8, shape=float("inf"))
acc = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
acc.compose(search)
print(acc.get_epsilon(1e-5))

A smaller \(\eta\) gives a cheaper bound but more often stops after a single run, and the Poisson bound suits runs that are already very private. A random number of runs may also miss the best candidate. On a grid of 8 with 8 runs on average, it never tries the best one with probability 0.4667.
The theorems have three conditions, and each is easy to break. First, each run must draw its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, which is random search. So Bayesian optimization, which picks each candidate from earlier scores, is not covered and needs adaptive composition. Second, the number of runs must be drawn independently of the data. Third, the score that ranks the runs must be part of each run’s private output.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.6 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
40.6 Selecting by a noisy validation score
When the candidates are fixed, such as public pretrained checkpoints, only the choice among them uses private data. That is a pure selection problem, which Selection solved. Score each candidate by its number of correct predictions on a private validation set. One record changes such a count by at most 1, while an accuracy divides by a size that is itself private. Then the exponential mechanism at a budget \(\varepsilon\) picks a candidate whose expected shortfall from the best count is at most \[\frac{2}{\varepsilon}(\ln k + 1) \tag{40.3}\] correct predictions, among \(k\) candidates. On a validation set of \(m\) records, that is an accuracy gap of at most \(2(\ln k + 1)/(\varepsilon m)\). For example, choosing among eight trained models on 5,000 validation records costs about a tenth of a point of accuracy at a budget of 0.1.
With disjoint training and validation sets, each record sits in one of them, so a search over trained candidates costs the larger of the training cost and the selection cost, not their sum.
The random-number bounds need a private score too. An exact validation accuracy leaves the validation records unprotected, so add Gaussian noise to each run’s count of correct predictions. With noise of standard deviation 20, one noisy count costs 0.182. Eight of them stay below the training runs’ cost at every order the conversion uses, so they add nothing to the total.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), the DP-SGD of this part, owes much of its accuracy to Poisson sampling. Many pipelines cannot honestly claim that sampling, because they cut fixed batches, read data in arrival order or take whichever phones check in. Using the Poisson accountant anyway can understate the privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) considerably (Amplification by subsampling).
Giving up amplification honestly is expensive. On this part’s running example, five passes at \(\varepsilon = 2\) on a fixed order need a noise multiplier of 4.458 instead of 0.928, and test accuracy falls from 0.9460 to 0.8941. This chapter wins that loss back by correlating the noise across steps. The first such method used the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer and is called DP-FTRL. Its modern form, the matrix factorization mechanism, closes nearly all of the gap.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.2 The matrix mechanism
Plain gradient descent subtracts each step’s noisy sum of clipped gradients, scaled by the step size \(\eta\) over the batch size \(B\), from the starting weights \(w_0\): \[w_{t+1} = w_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t, \qquad \hat S_t = \hat x_1 + \dots + \hat x_t, \tag{41.1}\] where \(\hat x_t\) is the noisy gradient sum of step \(t\). A training run is therefore a release of prefix sums, and momentum or a learning-rate schedule only changes the fixed weights with which they are combined. Every model is computed from them, so it is post-processing and inherits their privacy (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Stack the true gradient sums as the rows of a matrix \(x\). The prefix sums are then \(Ax\), where \(A\) has ones on and below the diagonal. The matrix mechanism splits \(A\) into an encoder \(R\) and a decoder \(L\) with \(A = LR\). It adds Gaussian noise \(z\) to the encoded gradients and decodes the result: \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz. \tag{41.2}\] Each entry of the noise \(z\) has standard deviation \(sC\), where \(C\) is the clipping norm and the noise scale \(s\) plays the role of DP-SGD’s noise multiplier.
Privacy depends only on the columns of the encoder. A record used at one step shifts \(Rx\) by that step’s column of \(R\) times its clipped gradient. So the encoder’s sensitivity, in units of \(C\), is the length of its longest column \(r_j\). The mechanism is then a Gaussian mechanism whose ratio of sensitivity to noise is \[\mu = \frac{\operatorname{sens}(R)}{s}, \qquad \operatorname{sens}(R) = \max_j\|r_j\|. \tag{41.3}\] To calibrate, look up the largest ratio that meets your target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), written \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), with the exact Gaussian calibration of f-DP and Gaussian DP. Then set \(s = \operatorname{sens}(R)/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). This chapter uses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout, and at \(\varepsilon = 2\) the ratio is 0.502.
Accuracy depends on the rows of the decoder. Write \(\ell_t\) for the row that produces the \(t\)-th prefix sum. Each coordinate of its error has standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_t\|\), which is \(C/\mu\) times the error per unit of privacy \[e_t = \operatorname{sens}(R)\,\|\ell_t\|. \tag{41.4}\]
Two conditions make all this valid during training. First, both factors must be lower-triangular, so that each step’s release uses only gradients that already exist. Second, a record’s slot in the data order must be fixed in advance, independently of the data. The sensitivity above also assumes neighbours that add or remove a record. If they replace a record instead, its gradient can change by \(2C\), and every sensitivity in this chapter doubles.
In code, the mechanism is noisy SGD that adds the correlated noise \(R^{-1}z\) to the gradient sums. You keep a buffer of past noise draws and never form a large matrix.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.3 Choosing a factorization
For a single pass, each factorization trades the encoder’s column length against the decoder’s row length. The numbers below are for one epoch of \(T = 100\) steps.
Independent noise, the identity encoder, is DP-SGD without amplification. Its prefix-sum noise is a random walk, with a final error per unit of privacy of 10.
The binary tree, the encoder of the original DP-FTRL (Kairouz et al. 2021), adds noise to the sum over every node of a binary tree over the steps. Its error grows like \(\log T\), with a largest error of 6.93 over one epoch.
The square-root factorization uses the same lower-triangular matrix for both factors, a square root of \(A\). You can compute it with scipy.linalg.sqrtm on the prefix-sum matrix, or from the closed-form coefficients in the snippet below, which are constant along each diagonal. Over one epoch its sensitivity is 1.591, and its final error is 2.53, a quarter of independent noise’s.
Optimized factorizations exist in research code (Denisov et al. 2022), but they cost time cubic in \(T\) and gain little, so the free square root is the default.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.4 Several passes: banding and the data order
text:
41.4 Several passes: banding and the data order
Over \(k\) passes a record enters the encoder through \(k\) columns. When no two columns have a negative inner product, as for the identity, the tree and the square root, the worst case is a record that contributes the same full-length gradient each time. The sensitivity is the length of the sum of its columns, maximized over the participation patterns that the data order allows: \[\operatorname{sens}(R) = \max_{\text{patterns}}\Big\|\sum_{i=1}^kr_{\tau_i}\Big\|, \tag{41.5}\] where \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_k\) are the steps of one pattern.
Repeated participation costs correlated noise more, because the square root’s columns for nearby steps overlap, so its sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt k\). Banding fixes this by keeping only the first \(b\) diagonals of the square root. Suppose every two participations of a record are at least \(b\) steps apart, a condition called \(b\)-min-separation. Then the columns no longer overlap, and the sensitivity is at most \(\sqrt k\) times the longest column, as for independent noise. Its decoder rows are longer, so banding pays only when participations repeat.
The running example reuses one public random permutation every epoch, so each record takes part exactly 100 steps apart, which is the band used below.

So the data order is part of the mechanism, and a permutation kept for every epoch guarantees a separation of exactly one epoch. Reshuffling every epoch can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, one step apart, and that breaks the banded bound.

Three patterns guide the choice. Independent noise without amplification is a poor option, trailing DP-SGD by 8.5 points at \(\varepsilon = 2\) and ten epochs, while the banded square root comes within 0.02 points. At large \(\varepsilon\) and few epochs, amplification gains little, so correlated noise can even beat DP-SGD. At small \(\varepsilon\) over many epochs, DP-SGD keeps its lead, and only banding keeps up.
You can choose before training anything, by computing each candidate’s noise in the final prefix sum, \(sC\) times the length of the decoder’s last row. On the running example, the method with the least of it was the most accurate, or nearly so, in every configuration.
Federated learning is the main use, because the server cannot sample devices at a known rate. If a device contributes at most once every \(b\) rounds, a banded mechanism with band at most \(b\) gives a provable guarantee, and Google trained its Gboard keyboard language models this way with DP-FTRL (Xu et al. 2023).
You rarely write the mechanism yourself. Google’s JAX Privacy library implements matrix-factorization noise for JAX training, including banded factorizations. TensorFlow Federated provides tree-aggregation noise for federated training through tff.aggregators.DifferentiallyPrivateFactory.tree_aggregation. Opacus assumes Poisson sampling, so it is the wrong tool here. Whatever the library, check that its sensitivity uses the participation pattern and the neighbouring relation you actually have.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.6 Code
To check a library’s configuration, the snippet computes a banded square root’s sensitivity for your separation and number of epochs.
from math import sqrt


def sqrt_coeffs(t: int) -> list[float]:
    r = [1.0]
    for k in range(1, t):
        r.append(r[-1] * (2 * k - 1) / (2 * k))
    return r


def toeplitz_sensitivity(c: list[float], t: int, sep: int, epochs: int) -> float:
    best = 0.0
    for offset in range(sep):
        steps = range(offset, t, sep)[:epochs]
        col = [sum(c[i - p] for p in steps if 0 <= i - p < len(c)) for i in range(t)]
        best = max(best, sqrt(sum(v * v for v in col)))
    return best


T = 100  # steps per epoch
band = sqrt_coeffs(T)  # the banded encoder keeps the first T coefficients
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(band, T * 20, T, 20):.3f}")  # 7.115
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(band, T * 10, T, 10):.3f}")  # 5.031
Divide the sensitivity by \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) to get the noise scale.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Training a model with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD), as DP-SGD does, makes every later query free, but you must own the training loop. The model may be a large language model (LLM) that you can prompt but not train, or one that answers only a few dozen questions in its life. In those cases you can train ordinary models, keep them secret, and make each answer private instead.
The idea is “one record, one vote”. You split the private records into \(k\) disjoint shards, train one model, a teacher, on each, and release a noisy winner of their vote. Because a record lives in one shard, it can change only one vote. This chapter says when such answers beat a private model, how private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) turns them into a free-to-use model, and how the vote protects an LLM’s prompt.
crumbs: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.2 The noisy vote: GNMax
Assign records to shards by a fixed rule chosen before looking at the data, such as a hash of a record identifier, or of a user identifier if the privacy unit is a user. Adding or removing a record then changes one teacher, which can move one vote from one label to another. The list of vote counts, the vote histogram, therefore moves by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean length. The fixed rule is a condition, because if you cut shards by position in a file, inserting one record shifts every later record and can change every teacher. Likewise, if one person’s records land in several shards, that person moves several votes.
GNMax (Papernot et al. 2018) adds Gaussian noise to each count and releases only the label with the largest noisy count. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise’s standard deviation. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) describes a mechanism by its privacy loss \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) at each order \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP). In those terms each answer costs a straight line: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{\sigma^2}. \tag{42.1}\] The lines of \(Q\) answers add up, even when each query is chosen after seeing the earlier answers. Now write \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest slope whose line still converts to your target, a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) with slack \(\delta\) (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)). The noise that \(Q\) answers need is then \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{42.2}\] This chapter uses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout. A budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) then allows a slope of 0.0306, and \(\varepsilon = 4\) allows 0.3731.



Table 42.1: Noise per count for \(Q\) answers at \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\), from the RDP accountant.

Two facts follow from Equation 42.2. The noise grows like the square root of the number of answers, and it does not depend on the teachers at all. So a teacher can be any model, or even a human annotator who saw one shard. The original PATE used LNMax, with Laplace noise. It needs less noise for a single answer, but about twice as much from 100 answers on, so use GNMax for anything beyond one or two answers.
Publishing the noisy counts as well as the label releases a whole vector, which the analysis does not cover. And since a gap can never exceed the number of teachers, the noise for 10,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\) swamps any ensemble with fewer than a few thousand teachers.
