title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.3 How accurate a noisy vote is
text:
42.3 How accurate a noisy vote is
On two labels, the noisy vote returns the plurality label unless the difference of the two noises exceeds the gap \(g\) between the two counts. That difference is Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sqrt2\sigma\), so the plurality wins with probability \[\Pr[\text{plurality}] = \Phi\Big(\frac{g}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}\Big), \tag{42.3}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. The noiseless plurality is a ceiling, because noise can only pull an answer toward a coin flip.
Take this part’s running example from DP-SGD, whose 10,000 private records have two labels, and split them among 100 teachers. With the noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\), a lopsided vote of 98 to 2 returns the plurality with probability 0.9051. But a close vote of 52 to 48 does so with probability 0.5218, barely better than a coin.
More teachers mean smaller shards and weaker teachers, so the right number is found by measuring. On the running example, shrinking the shards to 20 records cuts a teacher’s accuracy to 0.6459. Yet the noiseless plurality stays between 0.9336 and 0.9403, because weak teachers err nearly independently. The gaps therefore grow with the number of teachers, and 500 teachers did best. So add teachers as long as the median gap keeps growing, and measure the noiseless vote first, since no budget gets you above it.
crumbs: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.4 Private answers or a private model
text:
42.4 Private answers or a private model
The same budget can train a private model, whose answers are free, or pay for answers one at a time. A private model’s accuracy does not depend on the number of queries, while the vote’s falls as answers accumulate. So private answers are at least as accurate up to a break-even number of queries \(Q^*(\varepsilon)\), and the private model wins beyond it.

To decide for your task, estimate the private model’s accuracy at your budget, and compute the vote’s expected accuracy from Equation 42.3 and the teachers’ gaps on held-out queries. title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.5 PATE: from private answers to a private model
text:
42.5 PATE: from private answers to a private model
PATE spends the budget once. It labels \(Q\) public, unlabelled inputs with GNMax answers and trains a new model, the student, on them. The student is released and the teachers never are. Its weights and predictions cost exactly what the \(Q\) answers cost.
The recipe has four conditions. You need public inputs from the same distribution as the private data, which is easy for images or text and impossible for most medical records. The pool must really be public, because nothing protects an input that is someone’s private record. The number of labels needs tuning, since more labels mean more noise on each. And the teachers stay on a server you trust, because they are non-private models open to every attack of Part 2.
On the running example, PATE loses to DP-SGD at every budget measured. At \(\varepsilon = 4\), the best student of 250 teachers reaches 0.8898, against 0.9573 for DP-SGD. The weak teachers often disagree, and PATE wins only where teachers agree on most inputs and the student also learns from unlabelled inputs. On handwritten digits, Papernot et al. (2018) report a student within one point of the non-private accuracy.
crumbs: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.6 Data-dependent accounting and Confident-GNMax
The cost \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) is a worst case over all vote histograms. But when nearly all teachers agree, one record almost never changes the answer, and a data-dependent analysis (Papernot et al. 2018) charges such a query far less. On tasks where teachers are nearly unanimous, as on digits, \(\varepsilon\) falls by a large factor. On the running example the saving is only about 20%, because few queries have large gaps.
The trap is that a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes, so publishing it leaks information about the data. Papernot et al. release it with noise scaled to its smooth sensitivity (Beyond global sensitivity) and pay for that release. Until it is released privately, a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is a measurement, not a guarantee.
Two refinements exist. Confident-GNMax answers only the queries on which a noisy check finds the teachers in agreement, which gave a student of 0.8894 on the running example, a small gain over plain GNMax. Stable aggregation (Bassily, Thakkar & Thakurta 2018) releases the exact plurality of lopsided votes, but it is mainly a tool for proofs.
crumbs: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.7 Private in-context learning
An LLM can learn a task from labelled examples placed in its prompt, called exemplars. If the exemplars are private, the answers leak them. Duan et al. (2023) show that GPT-3, prompted with one private example, favours that example’s correct label enough for a membership inference attack.
The fix is private prediction with prompts as teachers (Duan et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2024). You split the private exemplars into disjoint groups by a fixed rule such as a hash, prompt the model once per group with the query, and release the GNMax label of the answers. So each answer costs \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) as before, whatever the LLM computes.
Wu et al. also draw a fresh Poisson sample of the exemplars for each query, at a sampling rate \(r\), and split only the sample into groups. So each answer costs the subsampled Gaussian of Amplification by subsampling, whose noise multiplier here is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\). If \(\varepsilon_{r,s}(\alpha)\) is that curve at rate \(r\) and multiplier \(s\), then \(Q\) answers cost \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = Q\,\varepsilon_{r,\,\sigma/\sqrt2}(\alpha). \tag{42.4}\] Within one query the groups must still be disjoint, or one record would move two votes. Subsampling cuts the noise sharply, from 181 to 7.39 in the full edition’s simulation of 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\).
In-context learning is where private prediction is strongest, because prompted LLMs agree with each other far more than small models do. Wu et al. report 91.97% sentiment accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 1\), about as good as one non-private prompt. PromptPATE (Duan et al.) goes one step further, as PATE does. It labels a few public inputs privately and uses them as the exemplars of one public prompt, which then answers any number of queries at no further cost. Check whether a reported \(\varepsilon\) for it is data-dependent before treating it as a guarantee.
crumbs: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.8 Code
The vote itself is a few lines of NumPy: count each label, add Gaussian noise to the counts and take the largest. Account for the answers with a maintained library rather than by hand. In Google’s dp_accounting, one GNMax answer is a GaussianDpEvent whose noise multiplier is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\). Compose \(Q\) of them with SelfComposedDpEvent, or wrap each in a PoissonSampledDpEvent for subsampled in-context learning. Then read \(\varepsilon\) off an RdpAccountant or a PLDAccountant. The full edition’s script private_prediction.py reproduces this chapter’s numbers.

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.1 Why this matters
Training from random weights with the differential privacy (DP) version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, loses a great deal of accuracy at a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 1 and below. The most accurate private models are built differently. They start from a model pretrained without privacy on a large public dataset, and only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data. Such models are far more accurate than those trained privately from scratch, as Tramèr & Boneh (2021) and later work report.
Fine-tuning only a small part of the model, such as the last layer or a low-rank update to each matrix, often helps further. That is because DP-SGD adds noise to every weight it trains, while the useful signal is bounded by clipping and usually lies in a few directions. This chapter gives the order in which to try the options and what public data does not protect.
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.2 How many weights to train
The privacy argument of DP-SGD needs only that one record changes the clipped gradient sum by at most the clipping norm \(C\), whichever weights are trained. So the choice of trainable weights leaves \(\varepsilon\) unchanged and changes only how much noise lands on the model. Public data are free for a related reason, because anything computed from public data alone, such as the starting weights, is a fixed input as far as the private data are concerned. The condition is that nothing in it was chosen by looking at the private data. That includes normalization statistics and tokenizers, which are fine when fitted on public data and a leak when fitted on private data.
The noise grows with the number \(k\) of trainable weights. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier and \(B\) for the expected batch size. Then the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt k}{B}. \tag{43.1}\] The signal, the average clipped gradient, is at most \(C\) long whatever \(k\) is, and it can even grow when fewer weights are trained, because shorter gradients are clipped less.
This part’s running example is a small network with 3,329 weights, pretrained on a related public task and then fine-tuned on 10,000 private records. It trains for 10,000 steps with a clipping norm of 0.5 and a batch size of 100, at a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise multiplier is 4.13, and the noise length is 1.191 for all weights against 0.166 for the 65 weights of the last layer.
Measured against the signal, the noise is 92.0 times larger for all weights but only 6.7 times for the last layer. So the signal needs about 8,455 steps to show through the noise for all weights, and only 44 for the last layer.
Counting weights overstates the cost, though. Noise hurts only in directions in which the loss is curved enough to notice it within the run (Li, Liu et al. 2022). Write \(h_j\) for the curvature of the loss in its \(j\)-th principal direction. With step size \(\eta\), the number of directions the noise has time to fill is the effective dimension \[d_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{j=1}^k\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big), \tag{43.2}\] and the noise raises the loss in proportion to it. On the running example, full fine-tuning has an effective dimension of 451 out of 3,329 weights. So its noise is 51 times larger in squared length than the last layer’s, but it costs only about 7.5 times more. A larger step size or a longer run fills more flat directions with noise, which is why private fine-tuning wants smaller step sizes than training from scratch.
Freezing weights has a cost too, a bias, because no amount of private data can move the model along a frozen direction that the task needs.
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.3 Linear probing first
The simplest option freezes everything but the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the frozen features, which is linear probing. Tramèr & Boneh (2021) showed that it beats end-to-end private training on standard image benchmarks at moderate budgets. It turns private deep learning back into the convex problem of Private empirical risk minimization, so it is the safe first baseline.
Its accuracy is capped by the features. The error of a private probe is the privacy cost of convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) in \(k\) dimensions plus the feature gap. That gap is how far the best linear model on the features falls short of the best model of any kind, and it does not shrink with more records or a larger \(\varepsilon\). The best possible probe reaches 0.9536, against 0.9606 for a network trained non-privately from scratch. The private probe stays within 0.006 of its ceiling at every budget, but it can never pass it. So measure the probe’s non-private ceiling first, and if it already meets your target, stop there. To train the probe privately, feed the frozen features to diffprivlib.models.LogisticRegression, or run DP-SGD on the one layer.
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.4 Low-rank adapters and full fine-tuning
When the features are not quite right, the probe stops at its ceiling, and you need to change the earlier layers. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) freezes each pretrained matrix \(W_0\) and learns a correction \(UV^\top\) whose rank, the number \(r\) of columns of the two factors, is small. For a matrix with \(d_{\text{in}}\) inputs and \(d_{\text{out}}\) outputs, that is \[k = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \tag{43.3}\] trainable weights instead of \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\).
Training starts with the factor \(U\) at zero, so the model begins exactly at the pretrained one, and with the factor \(V\) random. That random draw must be independent of the private data. The adapter’s per-example gradients are outer products, so the ghost clipping of DP-SGD applies and no per-example matrix is ever formed. Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning, at a fraction of the cost.
Full fine-tuning is not ruled out. Li, Tramèr et al. (2022) matched or beat the adapters by fine-tuning all the weights of language models, with large batches, a step size tuned for private training, and a fine-tuning objective that resembles the pretraining one. The evidence on accuracy goes both ways, but the adapter is cheaper to store, compute and clip.
In PyTorch, the usual stack is Hugging Face’s peft library for the adapter and Opacus for DP-SGD. Build a LoraConfig(r=..., target_modules=...) and wrap the base model with get_peft_model(model, config), so that only the adapter’s weights require gradients. Then pass the model, its optimizer and data loader to the make_private method of Opacus’s PrivacyEngine, which computes per-sample gradients only for the trainable parameters. For large language models, the private-transformers package of Li et al. and Microsoft’s dp-transformers wrap this setup, with ghost clipping to save memory.
A third option projects each private gradient onto a subspace estimated from public gradients and adds noise only there (Zhou, Wu & Banerjee 2021). It keeps the same \(\varepsilon\) and trades noise for the bias of the signal it projects away.

On this task, pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\), since the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\).
Which weights to train depends on the budget. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best, because its noise is 7.2 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s and its ceiling is not yet binding. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, it is stuck near that ceiling, while the adapter and full fine-tuning keep improving. Their best step size is 2.5 times smaller than the one for training from scratch. The adapter’s rank, by contrast, is cheap to get roughly right, since ranks from 1 to 16 differ by less than the run-to-run spread.

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.6 What public data does not buy
text:
43.6 What public data does not buy
The guarantee is exactly this. For every fixed public dataset, the map from the private dataset to the fine-tuned model is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. With respect to the public dataset, there is no guarantee of any kind. Non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and training-data extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode (Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini 2024).
This matters most for a person whose record is in both datasets, because only the private copy is protected, and a membership attack against the pretrained model (Membership inference) has no bound at all. Web-scale “public” datasets contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so a private set of medical notes or emails may well overlap with them.
Before you train and when you report, go through this checklist.

Deduplicate the private set against the public data. That protects copies, not people, because exact matching misses paraphrases and records about the same person.
Check that the public data resemble the private task, because benchmarks with a “private” set close to curated public data overstate what you will get on genuinely sensitive data.
Choose the public model, the step size, the adapter rank and the architecture on public data, or pay for every private run. Keeping the best of three privately fine-tuned models spends the budget of all three runs, unless you use a private selection procedure (Hyperparameter tuning).
Say what the public data are, how they were obtained and whether overlap was checked, and state that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.7 Code
Before choosing what to fine-tune, compare the candidates’ noise lengths at the noise multiplier your accountant gives.
from math import sqrt


def noise_length(sigma: float, clip: float, batch: float, trainable: int) -> float:
    return sigma * clip * sqrt(trainable) / batch


def lora_weights(rank: int, d_in: int, d_out: int) -> int:
    return rank * (d_in + d_out)


adapter = lora_weights(4, 51, 64) + 65  # first-layer adapter plus the 65-weight last layer
print(adapter)  # 525
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 3329):.3f}")  # 1.191
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, adapter):.3f}")  # 0.473
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 65):.3f}")  # 0.166
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. On the running example, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and noise, the DP-SGD of this part, reaches a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 6.71 per record. But people do not contribute one record each. A messaging user contributes hundreds of messages and a patient dozens of visits, and together a person’s records can reveal far more than any one of them.
The fix rests on one idea: the neighbouring relation is the privacy unit. Whatever differs between two neighbouring datasets is what the guarantee protects. So to protect people, make neighbours differ in all of one person’s records, bound how far one person can move the computation, and account with that bound. This chapter shows what a record-level \(\varepsilon\) means for a person, and three ways to train with a guarantee for the person instead. To make it concrete, the running example’s 10,000 records are spread very unevenly over 1,000 users, so that the largest holds 348.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.2 The privacy unit
Take a mechanism \(M\), and two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) that differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. The mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if, for every such pair and every set \(S\) of outputs, \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{44.1}\] Example-level DP is the same inequality for datasets that differ in one record. User-level DP is therefore not a new notion, and every property and accountant of Part 4 holds for it unchanged. Only the sensitivity changes. The right unit, whether a record, a user, a household or a device, answers the question “whose participation do I want to hide?” Report it with every \(\varepsilon\) (Choosing an accountant).
The textbook answer for a person with \(k\) records is group privacy (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). An example-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is user-level \((k\varepsilon, \delta_k)\)-DP for users with at most \(k\) records, where the person’s slack is \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{44.2}\] Ten records protected at \(\varepsilon = 1\) each give their owner \(\varepsilon = 10\), and the slack is worse, because it multiplies the per-record \(\delta\) by up to \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\). On the running example, even with the per-record \(\delta\) tuned so that the user’s slack is \(10^{-5}\), a user with two records gets \(\varepsilon = 18.61\), and a user with ten gets no guarantee at all.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
section: 44.3 What an example-level model gives a user
text:
44.3 What an example-level model gives a user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, but you know exactly how a user’s records enter each step. Each step includes every record independently with the sampling rate \(q\). For a user with \(k\) records, what matters is the chance that some record of theirs is in the batch. While \(kq\) is small, a user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled at rate \(kq\). So you can screen a user’s exposure by rerunning the record-level accountant at the rate \(kq\). The user’s \(\varepsilon\) then grows roughly linearly in their number of records. An exact accountant for a user with \(k\) records also exists (Charles et al. 2024), and it is a little worse than the screen.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.4 User-level DP-SGD
The better route makes the user the unit that DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for (McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang 2018). Starting from weights chosen without looking at the data, each step does five things.

Sample users. Put each user in the batch independently with probability \(q\), now the user sampling rate.
Compute one vector per user. From each sampled user’s records alone, compute their average gradient, or the change in weights after a few local SGD steps.
Clip per user. Rescale that vector to length at most the clipping norm \(C\).
Add noise. Sum the clipped vectors and add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) per coordinate, where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier.
Step. Divide by the expected number of sampled users and take a gradient step.

Because one user moves the sum by at most \(C\), however many records they have, the guarantee is user-level DP with exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD. A common variant clips each record instead and keeps at most \(k\) records per user. It has the guarantee of DP-SGD with noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), so it needs \(k\) times more noise.
Changing the unit has two consequences. First, you pay for the number of units. On the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 units, sampling records needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\). Sampling users must use a rate ten times higher, and then it needs \(\sigma = 3.78\). Second, records inside a user are free. They can be averaged, used for several local steps or subsampled without changing \(\varepsilon\). More records make each user’s vector a better estimate, so the signal improves while the noise stays fixed (Levy et al. 2021).
The data plumbing comes first. Carry a user identifier through the pipeline, and shard and sample by it. Per-example libraries such as Opacus clip each row of a batch, so with them you write a data loader that yields users and compute each sampled user’s clipped vector yourself. Federated frameworks are built around this pattern, for example TensorFlow Federated’s tff.learning.dp_aggregator, with a device as the user. Whatever the implementation, three things break the proof:

A user’s vector depends on other users’ data, for example through normalization by population statistics.
One person is spread over several accounts, so the unit is the account and the person is again a group.
Users are iterated in a fixed shuffled order instead of Poisson-sampled, which is a different mechanism (Matrix factorization).

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.5 Contribution bounding
If your pipeline is built around records, you can keep it and still protect users. Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, the cap, and runs example-level DP-SGD on what remains. The result is user-level DP with the \(\varepsilon\) that the user accountant gives for \(k\) records, and users with fewer records are covered too. The condition is that each user’s kept records are chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random. Otherwise adding one user could change which records others keep. Analytics libraries apply the same bound to queries, for example PipelineDP’s max_partitions_contributed and max_contributions_per_partition parameters, and Tumult Analytics’ MaxRowsPerID truncation.
Choosing the cap trades noise against bias (Amin et al. 2019). A larger cap keeps more data but needs more noise, while a smaller cap discards records and reweights the data toward light users. On the running example at a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), raising the cap from 1 to 50 multiplies the noise by 5.8. Accuracy then falls from 0.8917 to 0.6401. The best cap depends on the data, so take it from public knowledge of the population or choose it privately (Hyperparameter tuning). Trying caps on test accuracy spends privacy that the accountant does not see.
The two techniques also combine. You can cap each user’s records only to bound the compute, and still clip one vector per user. The cap then costs data but no noise.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.6 Heterogeneous users
User-level training changes the objective, not only the noise. Example-level training weights each user by their number of records, while user-level training with averaged vectors weights users equally. For a keyboard model, weighting people equally keeps a few very active users from defining everyone’s suggestions. For a model meant to fit the overall distribution of records, it under-weights heavy users, and a per-user cap discards their extra records outright (Disparate impact).
If heavy users should count for more, sum a user’s gradients instead of averaging them before clipping. Their influence then rises with their records until the sum reaches \(C\). Both choices stay inside the per-user computation, so \(\varepsilon\) does not change.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.8 Code
The rate-\(kq\) screen needs only a record-level accountant. In Google’s dp_accounting, it is one subsampled Gaussian step composed over the run:
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(
    sampling_probability=k * q,
    event=dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=sigma),
)
accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, steps))
print(accountant.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5))
With \(k = 1\) and \(q\) the user sampling rate, the same code accounts for user-level DP-SGD. The script user_level.py builds the user population, implements the exact user accountant and trains the three strategies.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.1 Why this matters
Training the part’s running example with differential privacy (DP) at a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) of 4 costs less than one point of test accuracy (private gradient descent). The private model reaches 0.9548, against 0.9610 without privacy. That number is an average over the whole test set, so it says nothing about who loses the point. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) studied networks trained with the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. They found that the lost accuracy falls mostly on the classes and subgroups that are under-represented in the training data, and called this the disparate impact of DP on model accuracy.
So a model that is “less than a point worse” on average can be ten points worse for one group of people. Those groups are often the ones a privacy guarantee is meant to protect, such as small populations, people with rare conditions and records that are unusual in other ways.

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.2 Evaluating a private model per group
text:
45.2 Evaluating a private model per group
Before you look at any results, decide which groups matter, and give each group its own test records. Then train a non-private baseline with the same data and recipe. A gap between groups may already exist without privacy, so the quantity that DP is responsible for compares each group with itself.
Write \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) for a model’s accuracy on the test records of group \(g\). The privacy cost \(\pi_g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the same training is made private, \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big]. \tag{45.1}\] The average runs over training runs, because private training is random. DP has disparate impact when different groups have different privacy costs, and the difference between two groups’ costs is the privacy cost gap.
Every accuracy needs an interval. Each test record is either classified correctly or not, so a group’s accuracy is a binomial proportion, and the exact Clopper–Pearson interval covers it (Hypothesis testing). In SciPy, scipy.stats.binomtest(correct, m).proportion_ci(method="exact") returns it, and in statsmodels proportion_confint(correct, m, alpha=0.05, method="beta") does. The gap between two groups needs its own interval. Write \(\hat p_g\) for a group’s measured accuracy and \(m_g\) for its number of test records. For a first group \(a\) and a second group \(b\), measured on disjoint test records with large counts, an approximate 95% interval for the gap is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}. \tag{45.2}\]
These intervals are wider than most people expect. Suppose a 2,000-record test split holds a 5% minority, so only 100 of its records come from the minority. On one model trained at \(\varepsilon = 4\), 88 of them were correct, which gives an interval 13.6 points wide. Against the majority’s 1,812 out of 1,900, the measured gap of 0.074 has the interval \([0.010, 0.138]\) by Equation 45.2. So the gap is real, but it could be anywhere from one point to fourteen. The width falls only like one over the square root of the number of records. So a 5-point gap shows only with a few hundred test records from the group, and a 1-point gap only with thousands.
A larger test set does nothing about the second source of variation, which is training itself. The next run gives another model, and a small group’s accuracy varies far more between runs. In the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), the minority’s run-to-run standard deviation is almost six times the majority’s. So a comparison of two recipes on one run each can easily reverse for the small group, and you should train three or more times.
fairlearn.metrics.MetricFrame, given a sensitive_features column, computes any metric per group in its by_group table, without intervals. The evaluation can also leak. Per-group accuracies on private test data are statistics of that data, so publishing them needs its own privacy analysis (Choosing ε).

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
text:
45.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
Both causes, clipping and noise, are blind to groups. The clipping row of Table 45.1 adds no noise, so it gives no privacy at all. Yet the minority already loses 4.04 points there while the majority gains 0.51, so clipping alone is disparate.
Clipping caps every record’s pull on the update at the clipping norm \(C\), so it cuts back hardest the groups whose gradients are long. Gradients are long where the model fits a group badly, as for rare patterns, and where the group’s inputs are large, as for outlying records. A small group that has not been learned yet has both, so training gives it less weight than its share of the data.
The noise is the same for every group, while a group’s signal grows with its size. So a small group’s signal is the weakest against the noise, and its privacy cost grows roughly like one over its share of the training records. The two causes also compound, since a group whose gradients clipping halves pays like a group half its size.
What you need from this is a diagnosis. Log the median per-example gradient norm and the fraction of records clipped, per group, during training. In Opacus, each parameter’s p.grad_sample holds the per-example gradients after the backward pass, so their norms can be grouped by a label you keep beside the batch.

The fixes that work






Oversampling raises a group’s pull but costs that group’s privacy, because a record’s guarantee depends on its own chance of being sampled (Amplification by subsampling). The rule must be fixed in advance, with the accountant at the highest rate. Sampling the 5% minority four times as often, at \(\varepsilon = 4\) for its records, raises the noise multiplier from 1.36 to 4.71. Without the higher noise, the minority would silently get \(\varepsilon = 20.96\), the weakest privacy for the group already worst served. With it, the gap narrows from 9.93 points to 3.99, but by levelling down. Both groups lose accuracy, the majority 8.01 points.
Some of the cost cannot be avoided by any algorithm, because learning a small group’s own rule is private estimation on its few records (Lower bounds). So the reliable fixes are more data from the group, or a starting point that already serves it, such as a public pretrained model (Public data and private fine-tuning).

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.6 Code
This function computes the interval for the accuracy gap, Equation 45.2, and prints the one quoted above.
from math import sqrt


def gap_interval(pa: float, ma: int, pb: float, mb: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Approximate 95% interval for the accuracy gap pa - pb, measured on disjoint test sets."""
    se = sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / ma + pb * (1 - pb) / mb)
    return pa - pb - 1.96 * se, pa - pb + 1.96 * se


print("%.3f %.3f" % gap_interval(0.954, 1_900, 0.880, 100))  # 0.010 0.138
The full edition’s script trains the running example with a minority and computes every number in this chapter:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/disparate_impact.py

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\). The chapter on private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, measured what each budget costs in accuracy. That is half of the choice, and the other half is what each budget means for the people in the data. Without it, \(\varepsilon\) gets chosen by habit (“everyone uses 8”), and the choice does not survive a reviewer who asks what the number promises.
The answer reads privacy as a test. An attacker who wants to know whether a record was used for training runs a membership test, and every test has two error rates. The budget \(\varepsilon\), together with its small slack \(\delta\), caps one rate in terms of the other. But the training algorithm has its own curve of the best rates an attacker can reach, which is usually much lower. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) well means computing that curve, reading it where your threat lives, and writing down what it says.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.2 Justifying a choice
A defensible choice fixes the claim before the number, in six steps.

Unit and neighbours. Say whether the privacy unit is a record, a user or a device, and whether neighbours add or remove a unit or replace it. Say over what period the budget is spent, counting every run and search that touched the data (Hyperparameter tuning).
Threat. Say whether the concern is membership, reconstruction or attribute inference, what the attacker knows beforehand, and what it sees, because this decides where you read the curve.
Whole guarantee. Compute the trade-off curve with a tight accountant (Section 46.3), choose \(\delta\) small (Section 46.5), and read the curve at the threat’s operating points.
Evidence. The curve is a theorem about an algorithm, not about your code. So run an empirical audit whose lower bound is consistent with the claim (Auditing private training).
Utility. Plot accuracy against \(\varepsilon\) next to the risk, and pick the smallest budget past the bend where accuracy stops rising steeply.
Comparison. Only now compare with deployments (Section 46.6) and with the tiers of Ponomareva et al. (2023) in the rules of thumb.

On the running example, measure the risk in step 5 as the largest true positive rate (TPR) of a membership test at a false positive rate (FPR) of 1%. The first two doublings of the budget, from 1 to 4, raise test accuracy by 2.66 and then 1.07 points, while that TPR stays below 0.0724. But the next doubling gains only 0.56 points, and it nearly triples the TPR, to 0.2092. So past \(\varepsilon = 4\), each point of accuracy is bought with a much larger worst-case risk.
A team that chooses the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run can then write the statement in Table 46.1, a template for any model card.

title: 46  Choosing ε
section: 46.3 The pair and the whole curve
text:
46.3 The pair and the whole curve
A membership test says “member” or “non-member” about one target record. Its TPR is the chance that it says “member” when the target was in the training set. Its FPR is the chance that it says so when the target was not. Every test against an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{46.1}\] Attacks are judged at a low FPR, because an attack that rarely flags a non-member identifies people with confidence (Membership inference). Yet at \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair caps the TPR at 0.9997, which constrains almost nothing.
A real training run satisfies DP for a whole range of pairs, with one \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for each \(\varepsilon\). The best TPR an attacker can reach at a given FPR is the lowest of all their lines, which is called the trade-off curve: \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \min_{\varepsilon}\big(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big). \tag{46.2}\] For DP-SGD, a PLD accountant computes this curve, and its two roundings bracket the truth (Numerical accounting). At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the curve of the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run allows a TPR of at most 0.0589, far below the pair’s cap. So a budget of 8 means little as a bare pair, but something real for DP-SGD once you report its curve.
Use the PLD bracket to certify, while an RDP accountant also gives a valid but looser curve. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation in the snippet below is a quick check, not a bound, since at \(\varepsilon = 16\) it reports 0.3234, above the exact value. With Google’s dp_accounting, build the run’s PLD and read the curve through Equation 46.2, passing a grid of \(\varepsilon\) to get_delta_for_epsilon:
from dp_accounting.pld import privacy_loss_distribution as pld
import numpy as np

run = pld.from_gaussian_mechanism(1.36, sampling_prob=0.01).self_compose(10_000)
eps = np.linspace(0.0, 20.0, 2001)
tpr = np.min(np.exp(eps) * 1e-3 + run.get_delta_for_epsilon(eps))  # TPR at FPR 1e-3
For \(\varepsilon\) alone, dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant and Opacus’s default accountant="prv" give the same kind of tight answer (Numerical accounting). The curve describes a strong attacker who sees every intermediate model, and a typical record attacked through the final model is much safer.
The same curve bounds reconstruction (Reconstruction attacks). Suppose an attacker knows the target is one of a number \(m\) of equally likely records. It then succeeds with probability at most the curve read at an FPR of \(1/m\), so at most 0.0589 for a thousand candidates at \(\varepsilon = 8\).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.4 What an attacker can believe
Most people ask how sure someone can become that they were in the data. Write \(p\) for the attacker’s prior, its probability of “member” before it sees the model. If no output has a privacy loss above \(\varepsilon\), its belief afterwards is at most \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{output}] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{46.3}\] So DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief itself. At \(\varepsilon = 4\), an attacker who starts at 1% can end at 35.55%. That is the worst output, though, and in DP-SGD the realized loss is usually far below \(\varepsilon\).
Base rates matter as much as the loss. An attacker who acts on a flag is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{46.4}\] Suppose an attacker with a 1% prior flags at an FPR of \(10^{-2}\), against the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run. Its flags are then right with probability at most 0.1744, so five out of six are false. A statement about beliefs must therefore name the attacker, because an insider with a prior of 0.5 starts much closer to certainty.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.5 How small δ must be
A deliberately bad mechanism shows what \(\delta\) permits. It publishes each of \(n\) records in full, independently with probability \(\delta\), and it is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. Yet it publishes at least one record with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{46.5}\] For the running example’s 10,000 records at \(\delta = 1/n\), that is 0.6321. So \(n\delta\) must be much smaller than 1. Here \(n\) counts privacy units, which means people when one person has many records (User-level differential privacy). NIST SP 800-226 reports the common recommendation that \(\delta\) be at most \(1/n^2\), and calls values above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious.
For DP-SGD a smaller \(\delta\) is cheap, because its privacy loss has a light tail. Moving the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run to \(\delta = 1/n^2\) raises its budget only to 5.209.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Comparing with deployed values
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” hides what every \(\varepsilon\) needs, its privacy unit and the period over which it is spent. The Census Bureau’s 2020 redistricting data used zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), whose guarantee is a single number \(\rho\). It spent \(\rho = 2.56\) on persons, reported as \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), with one person’s record replaced as the unit. Google’s Gboard language models, trained privately in federated learning, had device-level guarantees for a whole training run, from about 1 to 14 at the same \(\delta\). Apple’s local DP is stated per donation, with QuickType at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and two donations a day, so up to 16 a day.
So convert both budgets to the same unit, neighbouring relation and \(\delta\) before comparing. A zCDP parameter \(\rho\) converts to a pair by \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{46.6}\] An add/remove guarantee \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) implies only the replace-one guarantee \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\). A budget per day adds up over time, to 365 a year at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per day.
So the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run is not “less than half the Census budget”, because at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) it is at 11.627, and a replacement can double that.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.7 Code
This snippet turns a claimed pair into the TPR it allows, and approximates DP-SGD’s curve with GDP.
from math import exp, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist


def pair_tpr_cap(eps: float, delta: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """The largest TPR any test can reach at a given FPR, from the pair (eps, delta) alone."""
    return min(1.0, exp(eps) * fpr + delta, 1 - exp(-eps) * (1 - delta - fpr))


def gdp_tpr(q: float, steps: int, sigma: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """GDP estimate of DP-SGD's TPR at an FPR (sampling rate q, noise multiplier sigma); not a bound."""
    mu = q * sqrt(steps * (exp(1 / sigma**2) - 1))
    return NormalDist().cdf(NormalDist().inv_cdf(fpr) + mu)


print(f"{pair_tpr_cap(4, 1e-5, 1e-3):.5f}")  # 0.05461
print(f"{gdp_tpr(0.01, 10_000, 1.36, 1e-3):.5f}")  # 0.01244

Rules of thumb

Report the curve, not just the pair, as the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2}\).

Never quote \(\varepsilon\) without its unit, \(\delta\) and period, and never compare a daily budget with a lifetime one.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.1 Why this matters
The running example trains a network with differential privacy (DP), using the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) called DP-SGD. Its noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the noise’s standard deviation in units of the clipping norm, is 1. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant turns its configuration into a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 6.71 at a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\). That number is a proof about an algorithm, while what ships is code, and a bug in the noise or the sampling barely changes the accuracy.
An audit checks the code by attacking it. It plants records called canaries, trains with and without them, and counts how often a membership test guesses right. DP caps how often any test can be right, so a test that is right too often proves that the code is less private than claimed. The reverse never holds, because a weak attack also fails against a leaky model.

text:

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.3 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
text:
47.3 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
Read the code for each bug below, since an audit catches only some of them.

Variance passed where a standard deviation is expected. With the running example’s clipping norm of 0.5, this halves the noise. A per-step audit catches it.
Noise scaled for the mean but added to the sum, which makes it too small by the batch size. A per-step audit catches it at once.
Clipping applied after averaging, or noise from a weak seed with only 100 possible values. Nasr et al. (2023) found both in real code with per-step audits.
The accountant told the wrong numbers, such as 20,000 records instead of 10,000 because augmented copies were counted. The noise is right, so only an end-to-end audit can catch it, and only if the error is large.
Batches shuffled but accounted as Poisson sampling, which can make the true \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one (Amplification by subsampling). No cheap audit exercises the sampling, so read that code yourself.

The per-step audit puts a Dirac canary (Section 47.5) into every step of one run and leaves it out of another. Each step’s noisy value on the canary’s coordinate, in units of the clipping norm, is one trial, and for correct code it follows \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}. \tag{47.1}\] The audit bounds the separation \(\mu\) of these two distributions from below with Equation 47.5, and correct code has \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). On the running example, two runs of 10,000 steps bound \(\mu\) by 0.886 for the correct code, against the claimed 1, while the variance bug gives 1.745 and is refuted.
Audits catch errors only in the unsafe direction, so code that adds too much noise passes every audit.

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.4 From an attack to a lower bound
text:
47.4 From an attack to a lower bound
A trial is one training run with or without the canary, and the attack says “in” when a score, such as minus the canary’s loss, is above a threshold. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the chance that it says “in” when the canary was trained on. Its false positive rate (FPR) is the chance that it says “in” when the canary was left out. DP requires, for every test, \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{47.2}\]
The rates are measured from \(n\) trials with the canary and \(n\) without, so the bound must use their pessimistic ends. Write \(\bar\alpha\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR (Hypothesis testing). Write \(\underline\tau\) for the lower bound on the TPR, both at level \(\beta/2\), where \(\beta\) is the chance that the audit is wrong. For a count of k events in n trials, SciPy gives the upper bound as scipy.stats.beta.ppf(1 - beta / 2, k + 1, n - k), and statsmodels’ proportion_confint(..., method="beta") gives the same interval. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the code is then not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any level below \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline\tau - \delta}{\bar\alpha},\ \ln\frac{1 - \bar\alpha - \delta}{1 - \underline\tau}\Big\}. \tag{47.3}\] The bound needs independent trials and a threshold chosen without looking at the counted trials. So choose the threshold on half of the trials, and count on the other half.
Suppose 1,000 runs with the canary give 500 true positives, and 1,000 without give one false positive. The point estimate is 6.21, but confidence is expensive, and the certified bound is only 4.43. Even a perfect attack hits a ceiling. With \(n\) trials per hypothesis, it can certify at most about \[\varepsilon_{\max}(n) \approx \ln\frac{n}{\ln(2/\beta)}. \tag{47.4}\] So each extra unit of \(\varepsilon\) costs a factor of \(e\) in trials. At 95% confidence, 1,000 trials per hypothesis certify at most 5.60, and 10,000 at most 7.90. Certifying the running example’s 6.71 takes at least 3,038, so no feasible end-to-end audit can confirm that a large claim is tight.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.5 Canaries and threat models
An input-space canary is a record designed to stand out, such as a mislabeled example. A gradient-space canary has a gradient that the auditor writes directly. The strongest is the Dirac canary of Nasr et al. (2023). Its gradient has length exactly the clipping norm, all on one coordinate that no other record’s gradient touches.
The threat model says what the attacker sees. In the black-box model it sees only the final model. In the white-box model it sees every intermediate model, and so it can recover each step’s noisy gradient sum. Against a Dirac canary seen white-box, the most powerful test thresholds a likelihood-ratio statistic built from those sums, which the full edition derives. A simpler score that adds up the canary coordinate’s total change is weaker, lowering the most the audit can certify on the running example from 6.01 to 4.35.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.6 Tight audits of the mechanism
An end-to-end white-box audit with Dirac canaries faces the accountant’s own worst case, but it still falls far short of the claim, because at small \(\delta\) the level is decided at a tiny FPR. For the running example that rate is \(8.1\times10^{-8}\), far below the \(3/n\) that \(n\) trials can measure. Nasr et al. (2023) avoid the tail by assuming a Gaussian trade-off curve. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function. A single test then bounds the separation \(\mu\) from below, \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}), \tag{47.5}\] read at a moderate FPR, where trials are cheap. Its conversion to \(\varepsilon\) holds only if the curve really is Gaussian.
On the running example, the rigorous bound Equation 47.3 reaches 3.63 with 50,000 trials per hypothesis, about half the claim. The Gaussian-shape estimate reaches 5.33.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.7 One-run auditing
Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023) get many trials from one run. Choose a number \(m\) of canaries, include each one by its own independent fair coin, train once and score every canary. For a list of \(r\) guesses, guess “in” for the \(r/2\) highest scores and “out” for the \(r/2\) lowest. Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the number \(W\) of correct guesses is no more likely to reach any count \(v\) than a binomial count is: \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{47.6}\] The certified bound is the largest level whose tail at the observed count is below \(\beta\).
The coins must be independent and fair, and trying several list lengths needs a Bonferroni correction. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the paper adds a term of at most \(2m\delta\).
On the running example, one run with 1,000 white-box Dirac canaries certifies 2.22, against 2.84 from 10,000 runs per hypothesis.

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.8 Black-box audit of the trained network
text:
47.8 Black-box audit of the trained network
To see what the released network gives away, plant mislabeled canaries and attack the final model with a loss score or the likelihood-ratio attack of Membership inference. Run a non-private control next to it.
The non-private model memorizes its canaries and certifies 2.96, but the DP-SGD model certifies only 0.13. A model with clipping but no noise, which has no finite \(\varepsilon\) at all, certifies only 0.24. So a black-box bound of 0.5 against a claimed 8 does not show that the model is safe, or that its real \(\varepsilon\) is 0.5. It measures this attacker only.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.9 Auditing in continuous integration
The per-step audit is cheap enough to run as a unit test on every commit. Feed the code’s own clip-and-noise step a Dirac canary’s gradient, written by hand. In Opacus, for example, write it into a parameter’s p.grad_sample before the DPOptimizer runs clip_and_accumulate and add_noise, and read the noisy gradient afterwards. Test the code path that ships, not a copy of it. Run the steps with the canary and without, record each step’s noisy value on the canary’s coordinate, and bound \(\mu\) with Equation 47.5. The test fails when the bound exceeds \(1/\sigma\).
Fix the seeds so that a failure can be reproduced, and use a \(\beta\) below 5%, or correct code fails for one seed in twenty.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.10 Code
This snippet computes the certified bound of Equation 47.3 from counts, and prints the number quoted in the text.
from collections.abc import Callable
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def binom_cdf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Pr[Bin(n, p) <= k], summed in logs so that large n is safe."""
    log_terms = (lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(i + 1) - lgamma(n - i + 1) + i * log(p) + (n - i) * log(1 - p) for i in range(k + 1))
    return min(1.0, sum(exp(t) for t in log_terms))


def bisect(f: Callable[[float], float], target: float, lo: float, hi: float) -> float:
    """The x in [lo, hi] with f(x) = target, for f decreasing in x."""
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if f(mid) > target else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def eps_lower_bound(fp: int, tp: int, n: int, delta: float, beta: float = 0.05) -> float:
    """The eps certified with confidence 1 - beta from fp false and tp true positives in n trials each."""
    fpr_hi = bisect(lambda p: binom_cdf(fp, n, p), beta / 2, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    tpr_lo = 1 - bisect(lambda p: binom_cdf(n - tp, n, p), beta / 2, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    return max(log((tpr_lo - delta) / fpr_hi), log((1 - fpr_hi - delta) / (1 - tpr_lo)))


print(f"{eps_lower_bound(1, 500, 1_000, 1e-5):.2f}")  # 4.43

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.1 Why this matters
Machine learning reuses its evaluation data all the time. For example, you tune hyperparameters on a validation set, look at the scores and try new settings, and a competition shows a leaderboard score after every submission. Each time, the next question depends on the answers to the earlier ones, which makes the analysis adaptive. The practical question is how many such questions one holdout set can answer before its answers stop telling you anything about new data.
The answer depends on how the questions are answered. Exact scores on a holdout set break quickly. Giving each question its own fresh slice of data keeps the answers valid, but it needs data in proportion to the number of questions. Differential privacy (DP) does better. Answers that reveal little about any single record cannot be used to overfit the records behind them. So with noisy answers, the data you need grows only like the square root of the number of questions.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.2 What to do in practice
What decides the cost is the number of adaptive rounds, not the number of queries. A round is a batch of questions fixed before any of its answers is seen. Table 48.1 gives the method for each situation.



Table 48.1: How to reuse a holdout set, by situation.

Grows like \(\sqrt k\)

Choosing the best of \(k\) models trained without the validation set is one round. With a number \(n\) of validation records, the winner’s score then overstates its true score by at most \(\sqrt{\ln(2k)/(2n)}\) on average. Your search may already be private in the validation set, at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with slack \(\delta\) (Hyperparameter tuning and private selection). Then the winner’s score overstates its true score by at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) on average (Section 48.5). On a leaderboard, Blum & Hardt’s Ladder reports a new score only when a submission beats the best so far by more than a fixed step.
The classical fix inside one dataset is nested cross-validation, which keeps the folds that score the search away from the folds that choose it. Whatever you use, report how many evaluations a validation number has survived. Practice is often milder than the worst case. The risk is real when the records are few, the adaptive rounds are many, and someone has an incentive to climb a leaderboard.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.3 Reusing a holdout set overfits
A statistical query asks a question about each record whose answer is a number between 0 and 1, such as “does this classifier get this record right?”. Its empirical value is its average over the \(n\) records you hold, and its population value is its average over new data. If all \(k\) queries are fixed before the data are drawn, then on average the largest error among their exact answers is at most \[\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{48.1}\] The number of queries hardly matters, because it enters only through a logarithm.
That guarantee fails as soon as a query depends on earlier answers. Blum & Hardt’s boosting attack shows it on a leaderboard whose holdout labels are fair coin flips, so that nothing can beat 50% on new data. The attacker submits \(k\) random labellings, reads their exact scores, and submits the majority vote of those that scored above 50%. With 1,000 submissions on 1,000 holdout records, the final submission reports 0.7182. The overfitting is close to \[\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{2n}}, \tag{48.2}\] so it depends only on the ratio of submissions to holdout records.
What goes wrong in practice is rarely a deliberate attack. A long hyperparameter search, run with scikit-learn’s GridSearchCV on one validation split, does the same thing, because the winner is the setting that happened to fit that split’s noise best. So its validation score overstates its test score.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.4 Sample splitting and its cost
The simplest fix never lets a record answer a question it helped to choose. Split the sample into \(k\) equal parts and answer each query on its own part. Then, however the queries were chosen, the largest error is on average at most \[\sqrt{\frac{k\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{48.3}\] The data you need now grows linearly with \(k\). With queries in \(r\) rounds, one part per round is enough, and the \(k\) in front of the logarithm becomes \(r\).
Take a validation set of 10,000 records and a sequential search over 1,000 configurations, each chosen from the earlier scores. Splitting restores validity but leaves the bound at 0.6165, useless for scores between 0 and 1. Bringing it down to 0.05 takes 1,520,181 records, against 1,521 for fixed queries.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.5 Differential privacy implies generalization
Both results below use \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for samples that differ by replacing one record, which doubles an add-or-remove \(\varepsilon\).
The transfer lemma covers a single query chosen by a private algorithm. If the algorithm is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the chosen query’s empirical and population values differ on average by at most \[e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.4}\] The transfer theorem covers a whole interaction. Suppose a mechanism answers \(k\) adaptive queries, the whole exchange is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and its answers are within \(\alpha\) of the empirical values on average. Then its largest error against the population is on average at most \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.5}\] The bound holds whatever the analyst does with the answers. For small \(\varepsilon\), privacy at level \(\varepsilon\) costs about \(\varepsilon\) in accuracy, so answering to within 0.05 needs \(\varepsilon\) around 0.05 or less. Bassily et al. (2016) proved versions of the theorem that hold with high probability rather than on average.
This DP protects the validity of the answers, not the people in the holdout set, so a holdout set of personal data needs its own privacy accounting.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.6 Answering with Gaussian noise
The simplest private mechanism adds Gaussian noise with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each empirical value. Composing the \(k\) answers gives a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) (Concentrated differential privacy), and with this level the transfer theorem bounds the expected largest error by \[\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)} + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.6}\] The first term is the noise, and the rest is the transfer term. More noise shrinks the transfer term but grows the noise term, so there is a best \(\sigma\). At that balance the records you need grow like \(\sqrt k\), because the privacy loss of \(k\) Gaussian answers grows like \(\sqrt k\).
To use it, choose the \(\sigma\) and \(\delta\) that minimize the bound, as the snippet below does. Table 48.2 compares the three approaches.

The constants are large, so even a single query needs 7,300 records with noise, because the transfer term must itself be below 0.05. So splitting stays cheaper up to a few hundred adaptive queries, and only beyond that does the square root win.
In the other direction, when each record has many features, no efficient mechanism can answer much more than about \(n^2\) adaptive queries (Hardt & Ullman 2014, assuming one-way functions exist).

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.7 The reusable holdout: Thresholdout
Thresholdout (Dwork et al. 2015) answers from the training set while they agree and pays privacy only when they do not. It takes a threshold \(T\), a noise scale \(\sigma\) and a budget of \(B\) detections. Below the noisy threshold it returns the training value at no cost, and above it, it counts an overfitting detection and returns a noisy holdout value. This is the sparse vector technique of Selection, and no mainstream library ships it, but it takes a few lines of NumPy:
rng = np.random.default_rng()
noisy_t = T + rng.laplace(scale=2 * sigma)
def answer(train_value, holdout_value):
    global noisy_t, detections
    if abs(holdout_value - train_value) + rng.laplace(scale=4 * sigma) <= noisy_t:
        return train_value
    detections += 1                     # stop answering once detections reaches B
    noisy_t = T + rng.laplace(scale=2 * sigma)
    return holdout_value + rng.laplace(scale=sigma)
Write \(\Delta\) for the most one holdout record can move a query. A run that stops at its \(B\)-th detection is DP in the holdout records at \[\varepsilon = \frac{2B\Delta}{\sigma}, \tag{48.7}\] however many queries were answered below the threshold. The threshold sets the resolution of every answer, and when the budget is spent the holdout set must stop answering.
In the full edition’s experiment, an analyst screens noise features on a training set and confirms them on a holdout set. A holdout set answered exactly then reports 0.6842 for a classifier whose true accuracy is 0.5, while Thresholdout reports 0.5217. But its formal guarantee is weak, because the run triggered 325.8 detections on average, about \(\varepsilon = 29.1\).

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.8 Code
This snippet computes the three bounds for 1,000 queries on 10,000 records, and checks one entry of Table 48.2.
from math import expm1, log, sqrt


def fixed_queries(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Expected largest error of k queries chosen before the data were drawn."""
    return sqrt(log(2 * k) / (2 * n))


def splitting(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Expected largest error when each adaptive query gets its own n/k records."""
    return sqrt(k * log(2 * k) / (2 * n))


def gaussian(n: int, k: int, sigma: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Transfer-theorem bound for k adaptive queries answered with Gaussian noise sigma."""
    rho = k / (2 * n**2 * sigma**2)
    eps = rho + 2 * sqrt(rho * log(1 / delta))
    return sigma * sqrt(2 * log(2 * k)) + expm1(min(eps, 50.0)) + delta  # cap avoids overflow


def best_gaussian(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    """The smallest Gaussian bound over a grid of noise levels and deltas."""
    grid = [10 ** (e / 100) for e in range(-600, 1)]
    return min(gaussian(n, k, s, d) for s in grid for d in grid)


print(f"{fixed_queries(10_000, 1000):.4f}")  # 0.0195
print(f"{splitting(10_000, 1000):.4f}")  # 0.6165
print(f"{best_gaussian(10_000, 1000):.4f}")  # 0.4095
print(f"{best_gaussian(764_337, 1000):.4f}")  # 0.0500
The full edition’s script runs the attacks and the reusable-holdout experiment:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/adaptive_data_analysis.py

Rules of thumb

Count adaptive rounds, not queries.
Keep a test set that is used once, at the end, and never for model selection.
Privacy at level \(\varepsilon\) costs about \(\varepsilon\) in accuracy, so validity needs a small \(\varepsilon\).
Below a few hundred adaptive queries, splitting is cheaper than noise.
A large holdout set does not make many rounds of tuning safe, since adaptive error grows with the number of rounds.
On a leaderboard, release improvements, never exact scores.
